paragraphs:
Now that war and the problems of war are things of the past, I
think I may safely venture to reveal to the world the part which
my friend Poirot played in a moment of national crisis. The secret
has been well guarded. Not a whisper of it reached the Press. But,
now that the need for secrecy has gone by, I feel it is only just
that England should know the debt it owes to my quaint little
friend, whose marvellous brain so ably averted a great catastrophe.

One evening after dinner—I will not particularize the date; it
suffices to say that it was at the time when “Peace by negotiation”
was the parrot-cry of England’s enemies—my friend and I were
sitting in his rooms. After being invalided out of the Army I had
been given a recruiting job, and it had become my custom to drop
in on Poirot in the evenings after dinner and talk with him of any
cases of interest that he might have on hand.

I was attempting to discuss with him the sensational news of that
day—no less than an attempted assassination of Mr. David MacAdam,
England’s Prime Minister. The account in the papers had evidently
been carefully censored. No details were given, save that the Prime
Minister had had a marvellous escape, the bullet just grazing his
cheek.

I considered that our police must have been shamefully careless
for such an outrage to be possible. I could well understand that
the German agents in England would be willing to risk much for such
an achievement. “Fighting Mac,” as his own party had nicknamed him,
had strenuously and unequivocally combated the Pacifist influence
which was becoming so prevalent.

He was more than England’s Prime Minister—he _was_ England; and
to have removed him from his sphere of influence would have been
a crushing and paralysing blow to Britain.

Poirot was busy mopping a grey suit with a minute sponge. Never
was there a dandy such as Hercule Poirot. Neatness and order were
his passion. Now, with the odour of benzine filling the air, he
was quite unable to give me his full attention.

“In a little minute I am with you, my friend. I have all but
finished. The spot of grease—he is not good—I remove him—so!” He
waved his sponge.

I smiled as I lit another cigarette.

“Anything interesting on?” I inquired, after a minute or two.

“I assist a—how do you call it?—‘charlady’ to find her husband. A
difficult affair, needing the tact. For I have a little idea that
when he is found he will not be pleased. What would you? For my
part, I sympathize with him. He was a man of discrimination to lose
himself.”

I laughed.

“At last! The spot of grease, he is gone! I am at your disposal.”

“I was asking you what you thought of this attempt to assassinate
MacAdam?”

“_Enfantillage!_” replied Poirot promptly. “One can hardly take it
seriously. To fire with the rifle—never does it succeed. It is a
device of the past.”

“It was very near succeeding this time,” I reminded him.

Poirot shook his head impatiently. He was about to reply when the
landlady thrust her head round the door and informed him that there
were two gentlemen below who wanted to see him.

“They won’t give their names, sir, but they says as it’s very
important.”

“Let them mount,” said Poirot, carefully folding his grey trousers.

In a few minutes the two visitors were ushered in, and my heart
gave a leap as in the foremost I recognized no less a personage
than Lord Estair, Leader of the House of Commons; whilst his
companion, Mr. Bernard Dodge, was also a member of the War Cabinet,
and, as I knew, a close personal friend of the Prime Minister.

“Monsieur Poirot?” said Lord Estair interrogatively. My friend
bowed. The great man looked at me and hesitated. “My business is
private.”

“You may speak freely before Captain Hastings,” said my friend,
nodding to me to remain. “He has not all the gifts, no! But I
answer for his discretion.”

Lord Estair still hesitated, but Mr. Dodge broke in abruptly:

“Oh, come on—don’t let’s beat about the bush! As far as I can see,
the whole of England will know the hole we’re in soon enough.
Time’s everything.”

“Pray be seated, messieurs,” said Poirot politely. “Will you take
the big chair, _milord_?”

Lord Estair started slightly. “You know me?”

Poirot smiled. “Certainly. I read the little papers with the
pictures. How should I not know you?”

“Monsieur Poirot, I have come to consult you upon a matter of the
most vital urgency. I must ask for absolute secrecy.”

“You have the word of Hercule Poirot—I can say no more!” said my
friend grandiloquently.

“It concerns the Prime Minister. We are in grave trouble.”

“We’re up a tree!” interposed Mr. Dodge.

“The injury is serious, then?” I asked.

“What injury?”

“The bullet wound.”

“Oh, that!” cried Mr. Dodge contemptuously. “That’s old history.”

“As my colleague says,” continued Lord Estair, “that affair is over
and done with. Luckily, it failed. I wished I could say as much
for the second attempt.”

“There has been a second attempt, then?”

“Yes, though not of the same nature. Monsieur Poirot, the Prime
Minister has disappeared.”

“What?”

“He has been kidnapped!”

“Impossible!” I cried, stupefied.

Poirot threw a withering glance at me, which I knew enjoined me to
keep my mouth shut.

“Unfortunately, impossible as it seems, it is only too true,”
continued his lordship.

Poirot looked at Mr. Dodge. “You said just now, monsieur, that time
was everything. What did you mean by that?”

The two men exchanged glances, and then Lord Estair said:

“You have heard, Monsieur Poirot, of the approaching Allied
Conference?”

My friend nodded.

“For obvious reasons, no details have been given of when and where
it is to take place. But, although it has been kept out of the
newspapers, the date is, of course, widely known in diplomatic
circles. The Conference is to be held to-morrow—Thursday—evening
at Versailles. Now you perceive the terrible gravity of the
situation. I will not conceal from you that the Prime Minister’s
presence at the Conference is a vital necessity. The Pacifist
propaganda, started and maintained by the German agents in our
midst, has been very active. It is the universal opinion that the
turning point of the Conference will be the strong personality of
the Prime Minister. His absence may have the most serious
results—possibly a premature and disastrous peace. And we have no
one who can be sent in his place. He alone can represent England.”

Poirot’s face had grown very grave. “Then you regard the kidnapping
of the Prime Minister as a direct attempt to prevent his being
present at the Conference?”

“Most certainly I do. He was actually on his way to France at the
time.”

“And the Conference is to be held?”

“At nine o’clock to-morrow night.”

Poirot drew an enormous watch from his pocket.

“It is now a quarter to nine.”

“Twenty-four hours,” said Mr. Dodge thoughtfully.

“And a quarter,” amended Poirot. “Do not forget the quarter,
monsieur—it may come in useful. Now for the details—the abduction,
did it take place in England or in France?”

“In France. Mr. MacAdam crossed to France this morning. He was to
stay to-night as the guest of the Commander-in-Chief, proceeding
to-morrow to Paris. He was conveyed across the Channel by destroyer.
At Boulogne he was met by a car from General Headquarters and one
of the Commander-in-Chief’s A.D.C.s.”

“_Eh bien_?”

“Well, they started from Boulogne—but they never arrived.”

“What?”

“Monsieur Poirot, it was a bogus car and a bogus A.D.C. The real
car was found in a side road, with the chauffeur and the A.D.C.
neatly gagged and bound.”

“And the bogus car?”

“Is still at large.”

Poirot made a gesture of impatience. “Incredible! Surely it cannot
escape attention for long?”

“So we thought. It seemed merely a question of searching thoroughly.
That part of France is under Military Law. We were convinced that
the car could not go long unnoticed. The French police and our own
Scotland Yard men, and the military are straining every nerve. It
is, as you say, incredible—but nothing has been discovered!”

At that moment a tap came at the door, and a young officer entered
with a heavily sealed envelope which he handed to Lord Estair.

“Just through from France, sir. I brought it on here, as you
directed.”

The Minister tore it open eagerly, and uttered an exclamation. The
officer withdrew.

“Here is news at last! This telegram has just been decoded. They
have found the second car, also the secretary, Daniels, chloroformed,
gagged, and bound, in an abandoned farm near C——. He remembers
nothing, except something being pressed against his mouth and nose
from behind, and struggling to free himself. The police are
satisfied as to the genuineness of his statement.”

“And they have found nothing else?”

“No.”

“Not the Prime Minister’s dead body? Then, there is hope. But it
is strange. Why, after trying to shoot him this morning, are they
now taking so much trouble to keep him alive?”

Dodge shook his head. “One thing’s quite certain. They’re determined
at all costs to prevent his attending the Conference.”

“If it is humanly possible, the Prime Minister shall be there. God
grant it is not too late. Now, messieurs, recount to me
everything—from the beginning. I must know about this shooting
affair as well.”

“Last night, the Prime Minister, accompanied by one of his
secretaries, Captain Daniels——”

“The same who accompanied him to France?”

“Yes. As I was saying, they motored down to Windsor, where the
Prime Minister was granted an Audience. Early this morning, he
returned to town, and it was on the way that the attempted
assassination took place.”

“One moment, if you please. Who is this Captain Daniels? You have
his dossier?”

Lord Estair smiled. “I thought you would ask me that. We do not
know very much of him. He is of no particular family. He has served
in the English Army, and is an extremely able secretary, being an
exceptionally fine linguist. I believe he speaks seven languages.
It is for that reason that the Prime Minister chose him to accompany
him to France.”

“Has he any relatives in England?”

“Two aunts. A Mrs. Everard, who lives at Hampstead, and a Miss
Daniels, who lives near Ascot.”

“Ascot? That is near to Windsor, is it not?”

“That point has not been overlooked. But it has led to nothing.”

“You regard the Capitaine Daniels, then, as above suspicion?”

A shade of bitterness crept into Lord Estair’s voice, as he replied:

“No, Monsieur Poirot. In these days, I should hesitate before I
pronounced _anyone_ above suspicion.”

“_Très bien_. Now I understand, _milord_, that the Prime Minister
would, as a matter of course, be under vigilant police protection,
which ought to render any assault upon him an impossibility?”

Lord Estair bowed his head. “That is so. The Prime Minister’s car
was closely followed by another car containing detectives in plain
clothes. Mr. MacAdam knew nothing of these precautions. He is
personally a most fearless man, and would be inclined to sweep them
away arbitrarily. But, naturally, the police make their own
arrangements. In fact, the Premier’s chauffeur, O’Murphy, is a
C.I.D. man.”

“O’Murphy? That is a name of Ireland, is it not so?”

“Yes, he is an Irishman.”

“From what part of Ireland?”

“County Clare, I believe.”

“_Tiens!_ But proceed, _milord_.”

“The Premier started for London. The car was a closed one. He and
Captain Daniels sat inside. The second car followed as usual. But,
unluckily, for some unknown reason, the Prime Minister’s car
deviated from the main road——”

“At a point where the road curves?” interrupted Poirot.

“Yes—but how did you know?”

“Oh, _c’est évident_! Continue!”

“For some unknown reason,” continued Lord Estair, “the Premier’s
car left the main road. The police car, unaware of the deviation,
continued to keep to the high road. At a short distance down the
unfrequented lane, the Prime Minister’s car was suddenly held up
by a band of masked men. The chauffeur——”

“That brave O’Murphy!” murmured Poirot thoughtfully.

“The chauffeur, momentarily taken aback, jammed on the brakes. The
Prime Minister put his head out of the window. Instantly a shot
rang out—then another. The first one grazed his cheek, the second,
fortunately, went wide. The chauffeur, now realizing the danger,
instantly forged straight ahead, scattering the band of men.”

“A near escape,” I ejaculated, with a shiver.

“Mr. MacAdam refused to make any fuss over the slight wound he had
received. He declared it was only a scratch. He stopped at a local
cottage hospital, where it was dressed and bound up—he did not, of
course, reveal his identity. He then drove, as per schedule,
straight to Charing Cross, where a special train for Dover was
awaiting him, and, after a brief account of what had happened had
been given to the anxious police by Captain Daniels, he duly
departed for France. At Dover, he went on board the waiting
destroyer. At Boulogne, as you know, the bogus car was waiting for
him, carrying the Union Jack, and correct in every detail.”

“That is all you have to tell me?”

“Yes.”

“There is no other circumstance that you have omitted, milord?”

“Well, there is one rather peculiar thing.”

“Yes?”

“The Prime Minister’s car did not return home after leaving the
Prime Minister at Charing Cross. The police were anxious to
interview O’Murphy, so a search was instituted at once. The car
was discovered standing outside a certain unsavoury little
restaurant in Soho, which is well known as a meeting-place of
German agents.”

“And the chauffeur?”

“The chauffeur was nowhere to be found. He, too, had disappeared.”

“So,” said Poirot thoughtfully, “there are two disappearances: the
Prime Minister in France, and O’Murphy in London.”

He looked keenly at Lord Estair, who made a gesture of despair.

“I can only tell you, Monsieur Poirot, that, if anyone had suggested
to me yesterday that O’Murphy was a traitor, I should have laughed
in his face.”

“And to-day?”

“To-day I do not know what to think.”

Poirot nodded gravely. He looked at his turnip of a watch again.

“I understand that I have carte blanche, messieurs—in every way,
I mean? I must be able to go where I choose, and how I choose.”

“Perfectly. There is a special train leaving for Dover in an hour’s
time, with a further contingent from Scotland Yard. You shall be
accompanied by a Military officer and a C.I.D. man, who will hold
themselves at your disposal in every way. Is that satisfactory?”

“Quite. One more question before you leave, messieurs. What made
you come to me? I am unknown, obscure, in this great London of
yours.”

“We sought you out on the express recommendation and wish of a very
great man of your own country.”

“_Comment?_ My old friend the _Préfet_——?”

Lord Estair shook his head.

“One higher than the _Préfet_. One whose word was once law in
Belgium—and shall be again! That England has sworn!”

Poirot’s hand flew swiftly to a dramatic salute. “Amen to that!
Ah, but my Master does not forget. . . . Messieurs, I, Hercule
Poirot, will serve you faithfully. Heaven only send that it will
be in time. But this is dark—dark. . . . I cannot see.”

“Well, Poirot,” I cried impatiently, as the door closed behind the
Ministers, “what do you think?”

My friend was busy packing a minute suitcase, with quick, deft
movements. He shook his head thoughtfully.

“I do not know what to think. My brains desert me.”

“Why, as you said, kidnap him, when a knock on the head would do
as well?” I mused.

“Pardon me, _mon ami_, but I did not quite say that. It is
undoubtedly far more their affair to kidnap him.”

“But why?”

“Because uncertainty creates panic. That is one reason. Were the
Prime Minister dead, it would be a terrible calamity, but the
situation would have to be faced. But now you have paralysis. Will
the Prime Minister reappear, or will he not? Is he dead or alive?
Nobody knows, and until they know nothing definite can be done.
And, as I tell you, uncertainty breeds panic, which is what _les
Boches_ are playing for. Then, again, if the kidnappers are holding
him secretly somewhere, they have the advantage of being able to
make terms with both sides. The German Government is not a liberal
paymaster, as a rule, but no doubt they can be made to disgorge
substantial remittances in such a case as this. Thirdly, they run
no risk of the hangman’s rope. Oh, decidedly, kidnapping is their
affair.”

“Then, if that is so, why should they first try to shoot him?”

Poirot made a gesture of anger. “Ah, that is just what I do not
understand! It is inexplicable—stupid! They have all their
arrangements made (and very good arrangements too!) for the
abduction, and yet they imperil the whole affair by a melodramatic
attack, worthy of a Cinema, and quite as unreal. It is almost
impossible to believe in it, with its band of masked men, not
twenty miles from London!”

“Perhaps they were two quite separate attempts which happened
irrespective of each other,” I suggested.

“Ah, no, that would be too much of a coincidence! Then, further—who
is the traitor? There must have been a traitor—in the first affair,
anyway. But who was it—Daniels or O’Murphy? It must have been one
of the two, or why did the car leave the main road? We cannot
suppose that the Prime Minister connived at his own assassination!
Did O’Murphy take that turning of his own accord, or was it Daniels
who told him to do so?”

“Surely it must have been O’Murphy’s doing.”

“Yes, because if it was Daniels’ the Prime Minister would have
heard the order, and would have asked the reason. But there are
altogether too many ‘whys’ in this affair, and they contradict each
other. If O’Murphy is an honest man, _why_ did he leave the main
road? But if he was a dishonest man, _why_ did he start the car
again when only two shots had been fired—thereby, in all probability,
saving the Prime Minister’s life? And, again, if he was honest,
why did he, immediately on leaving Charing Cross, drive to a
well-known rendezvous of German spies?”

“It looks bad,” I said.

“Let us look at the case with method. What have we for and against
these two men? Take O’Murphy first. Against: that his conduct in
leaving the main road was suspicious; that he is an Irishman from
County Clare; that he has disappeared in a highly suggestive
manner. For: that his promptness in restarting the car saved the
Premier’s life; that he is a Scotland Yard man, and, obviously,
from the post allotted to him, a trusted detective. Now for Daniels.
There is not much against him, except the fact that nothing is
known of his antecedents, and that he speaks too many languages
for a good Englishman! (Pardon me, _mon ami_, but, as linguists,
you are deplorable!) _Now for him_, we have the fact that he was
found gagged, bound, and chloroformed—which does not look as though
he had anything to do with the matter.”

“He might have gagged and bound himself, to divert suspicion.”

Poirot shook his head. “The French police would make no mistake of
that kind. Besides, once he had attained his object, and the Prime
Minister was safely abducted, there would not be much point in his
remaining behind. His accomplices _could_ have gagged and
chloroformed him, of course, but I fail to see what object they
hoped to accomplish by it. He can be of little use to them now,
for, until the circumstances concerning the Prime Minister have
been cleared up, he is bound to be closely watched.”

“Perhaps he hoped to start the police on a false scent?”

“Then why did he not do so? He merely says that something was
pressed over his nose and mouth, and that he remembers nothing
more. There is no false scent there. It sounds remarkably like the
truth.”

“Well,” I said, glancing at the clock, “I suppose we’d better start
for the station. You may find more clues in France.”

“Possibly, _mon ami_, but I doubt it. It is still incredible to me
that the Prime Minister has not been discovered in that limited
area, where the difficulty of concealing him must be tremendous.
If the military and the police of two countries have not found him,
how shall I?”

At Charing Cross we were met by Mr. Dodge.

“This is Detective Barnes, of Scotland Yard, and Major Norman. They
will hold themselves entirely at your disposal. Good luck to you.
It’s a bad business, but I’ve not given up hope. Must be off now.”
And the Minister strode rapidly away.

We chatted in a desultory fashion with Major Norman. In the centre
of the little group of men on the platform I recognized a little
ferret-faced fellow talking to a tall, fair man. He was an old
acquaintance of Poirot’s—Detective-Inspector Japp, supposed to be
one of the smartest of Scotland Yard’s officers. He came over and
greeted my friend cheerfully.

“I heard you were on this job too. Smart bit of work. So far
they’ve got away with the goods all right. But I can’t believe they
can keep him hidden long. Our people are going through France with
a toothcomb. So are the French. I can’t help feeling it’s only a
matter of hours now.”

“That is, if he’s still alive,” remarked the tall detective
gloomily.

Japp’s face fell. “Yes. . . . But somehow I’ve got the feeling he’s
alive all right.”

Poirot nodded. “Yes, yes; he’s alive. But can he be found in time?
I, like you, did not believe he could be hidden so long.”

The whistle blew, and we all trooped up into the Pullman car. Then,
with a slow, unwilling jerk, the train drew out of the station.

It was a curious journey. The Scotland Yard men crowded together.
Maps of Northern France were spread out, and eager forefingers
traced the lines of roads and villages. Each man had his own pet
theory. Poirot showed none of his usual loquacity, but sat staring
in front of him, with an expression on his face that reminded me
of a puzzled child. I talked to Norman, whom I found quite an
amusing fellow. On arriving at Dover Poirot’s behaviour moved me
to intense amusement. The little man, as he went on board the boat,
clutched desperately at my arm. The wind was blowing lustily.

“_Mon Dieu!_” he murmured. “This is terrible!”

“Have courage, Poirot,” I cried. “You will succeed. You will find
him. I am sure of it.”

“Ah, _mon ami_, you mistake my emotion. It is this villainous sea
that troubles me! The _mal de mer_—it is horrible suffering!”

“Oh!” I said, rather taken aback.

The first throb of the engines was felt, and Poirot groaned and
closed his eyes.

“Major Norman has a map of Northern France if you would like to
study it?”

Poirot shook his head impatiently.

“But no, but no! Leave me, my friend. See you, to think, the
stomach and the brain must be in harmony. Laverguier has a method
most excellent for averting the _mal de mer_. You breathe in—and
out—slowly, so—turning the head from left to right and counting
six between each breath.”

I left him to his gymnastic endeavours, and went on deck.

As we came slowly into Boulogne Harbour Poirot appeared, neat and
smiling, and announced to me in a whisper that Laverguier’s system
had succeeded “to a marvel!”

Japp’s forefinger was still tracing imaginary routes on his map.
“Nonsense! The car started from Boulogne—here they branched off.
Now, my idea is that they transferred the Prime Minister to another
car. See?”

“Well,” said the tall detective, “I shall make for the seaports.
Ten to one, they’ve smuggled him on board a ship.”

Japp shook his head. “Too obvious. The order went out at once to
close all the ports.”

The day was just breaking as we landed. Major Norman touched Poirot
on the arm. “There’s a military car here waiting for you, sir.”

“Thank you, monsieur. But, for the moment, I do not propose to
leave Boulogne.”

“What?”

“No, we will enter this hotel here, by the quay.”

He suited the action to the word, demanded and was accorded a
private room. We three followed him, puzzled and uncomprehending.

He shot a quick glance at us. “It is not so that the good detective
should act, eh? I perceive your thought. He must be full of energy.
He must rush to and fro. He should prostrate himself on the dusty
road and seek the marks of tyres through a little glass. He must
gather up the cigarette-end, the fallen match? That is your idea,
is it not?”

His eyes challenged us. “But I—Hercule Poirot—tell you that it is
not so! The true clues are within—_here_!” He tapped his forehead.
“See you, I need not have left London. It would have been sufficient
for me to sit quietly in my rooms there. All that matters is the
little grey cells within. Secretly and silently they do their part,
until suddenly I call for a map, and I lay my finger on a
spot—so—and I say: the Prime Minister is _there_! And it is so!
With method and logic one can accomplish anything! This frantic
rushing to France was a mistake—it is playing a child’s game of
hide-and-seek. But now, though it may be too late, I will set to
work the right way, from within. Silence, my friends, I beg of
you.”

And for five long hours the little man sat motionless, blinking
his eyelids like a cat, his green eyes flickering and becoming
steadily greener and greener. The Scotland Yard man was obviously
contemptuous, Major Norman was bored and impatient, and I myself
found the time pass with wearisome slowness.

Finally, I got up, and strolled as noiselessly as I could to the
window. The matter was becoming a farce. I was secretly concerned
for my friend. If he failed, I would have preferred him to fail in
a less ridiculous manner. Out of the window I idly watched the
daily leave boat, belching forth columns of smoke, as she lay
alongside the quay.

Suddenly I was aroused by Poirot’s voice close to my elbow.

“_Mes amis_, let us start!”

I turned. An extraordinary transformation had come over my friend.
His eyes were flickering with excitement, his chest was swelled to
the uttermost.

“I have been an imbecile, my friends! But I see daylight at last.”

Major Norman moved hastily to the door. “I’ll order the car.”

“There is no need. I shall not use it. Thank Heaven the wind has
fallen.”

“Do you mean you are going to walk, sir?”

“No, my young friend. I am no St. Peter. I prefer to cross the sea
by boat.”

“To cross the _sea_?”

“Yes. To work with method, one must begin from the beginning. And
the beginning of this affair was in England. Therefore, we return
to England.”


  •   •   •   •   •   •   •

At three o’clock, we stood once more upon Charing Cross platform.
To all our expostulations, Poirot turned a deaf ear, and reiterated
again and again that to start at the beginning was not a waste of
time, but the only way. On the way over, he had conferred with
Norman in a low voice, and the latter had despatched a sheaf of
telegrams from Dover.

Owing to the special passes held by Norman, we got through
everywhere in record time. In London, a large police car was
waiting for us, with some plain-clothes men, one of whom handed a
typewritten sheet of paper to my friend. He answered my inquiring
glance.

“A list of the cottage hospitals within a certain radius west of
London. I wired for it from Dover.”

We were whirled rapidly through the London streets. We were on the
Bath Road. On we went, through Hammersmith, Chiswick and Brentford.
I began to see our objective. Through Windsor and on to Ascot. My
heart gave a leap. Ascot was where Daniels had an aunt living. We
were after _him_, then, not O’Murphy.

We duly stopped at the gate of a trim villa. Poirot jumped out and
rang the bell. I saw a perplexed frown dimming the radiance of his
face. Plainly, he was not satisfied. The bell was answered. He was
ushered inside. In a few moments he reappeared, and climbed into
the car with a short, sharp shake of his head. My hopes began to
die down. It was past four now. Even if he found certain evidence
incriminating Daniels, what would be the good of it, unless he
could wring from some one the exact spot in France where they were
holding the Prime Minister?

Our return progress towards London was an interrupted one. We
deviated from the main road more than once, and occasionally
stopped at a small building, which I had no difficulty in
recognizing as a cottage hospital. Poirot only spent a few minutes
at each, but at every halt his radiant assurance was more and more
restored.

He whispered something to Norman, to which the latter replied:

“Yes, if you turn off to the left, you will find them waiting by
the bridge.”

We turned up a side road, and in the failing light I discerned a
second car, waiting by the side of the road. It contained two men
in plain clothes. Poirot got down and spoke to them, and then we
started off in a northerly direction, the other car following close
behind.

We drove for some time, our objective being obviously one of the
northern suburbs of London. Finally, we drove up to the front door
of a tall house, standing a little back from the road in its own
grounds.

Norman and I were left with the car. Poirot and one of the
detectives went up to the door and rang. A neat parlourmaid opened
it. The detective spoke.

“I am a police officer, and I have a warrant to search this house.”

The girl gave a little scream, and a tall, handsome woman of
middle-age appeared behind her in the hall.

“Shut the door, Edith. They are burglars, I expect.”

But Poirot swiftly inserted his foot in the door, and at the same
moment blew a whistle. Instantly the other detectives ran up, and
poured into the house, shutting the door behind them.

Norman and I spent about five minutes cursing our forced inactivity.
Finally the door reopened, and the men emerged, escorting three
prisoners—a woman and two men. The woman, and one of the men, were
taken to the second car. The other man was placed in our car by
Poirot himself.

“I must go with the others, my friend. But have great care of this
gentleman. You do not know him, no? _Eh bien_, let me present to
you, Monsieur O’Murphy!”

O’Murphy! I _gaped_ at him open-mouthed as we started again. He
was not handcuffed, but I did not fancy he would try to escape. He
sat there staring in front of him as though dazed. Anyway, Norman
and I would be more than a match for him.

To my surprise, we still kept a northerly route. We were not
returning to London, then! I was much puzzled. Suddenly, as the
car slowed down, I recognized that we were close to Hendon
Aerodrome. Immediately I grasped Poirot’s idea. He proposed to
reach France by aeroplane.

It was a sporting idea, but, on the face of it, impracticable. A
telegram would be far quicker. Time was everything. He must leave
the personal glory of rescuing the Prime Minister to others.

As we drew up, Major Norman jumped out, and a plain-clothes man
took his place. He conferred with Poirot for a few minutes, and
then went off briskly.

I, too, jumped out, and caught Poirot by the arm.

“I congratulate you, old fellow! They have told you the hiding-place?
But, look here, you must wire to France at once. You’ll be too late
if you go yourself.”

Poirot looked at me curiously for a minute or two.

“Unfortunately, my friend, there are some things that cannot be
sent by telegram.”


  •   •   •   •   •   •   •


At that moment Major Norman returned, accompanied by a young
officer in the uniform of the Flying Corps.

“This is Captain Lyall, who will fly you over to France. He can
start at once.”

“Wrap up warmly, sir,” said the young pilot. “I can lend you a
coat, if you like.”

Poirot was consulting his enormous watch. He murmured to himself:
“Yes, there is time—just time.” Then he looked up, and bowed
politely to the young officer. “I thank you, monsieur. But it is
not I who am your passenger. It is this gentleman here.”

He moved a little aside as he spoke, and a figure came forward out
of the darkness. It was the second male prisoner who had gone in
the other car, and as the light fell on his face, I gave a gasp of
surprise.

_It was the Prime Minister!_


  •   •   •   •   •   •   •


“For Heaven’s sake, tell me all about it,” I cried impatiently, as
Poirot, Norman, and I motored back to London. “How in the world
did they manage to smuggle him back to England?”

“There was no need to smuggle him back,” replied Poirot dryly. “The
Prime Minister has never left England. He was kidnapped on his way
from Windsor to London.”

“What?”

“I will make all clear. The Prime Minister was in his car, his
secretary beside him. Suddenly a pad of chloroform is clapped on
his face——”

“But by whom?”

“By the clever linguistic Captain Daniels. As soon as the Prime
Minister is unconscious, Daniels picks up the speaking-tube, and
directs O’Murphy to turn to the right, which the chauffeur, quite
unsuspicious, does. A few yards down that unfrequented road, a
large car is standing, apparently broken down. Its driver signals
to O’Murphy to stop. O’Murphy slows up. The stranger approaches.
Daniels leans out of the window, and, probably with the aid of an
instantaneous anæsthetic, such as ethylchloride, the chloroform
trick is repeated. In a few seconds, the two helpless men are
dragged out and transferred to the other car, and a pair of
substitutes take their places.”

“Impossible!”

“_Pas du tout!_ Have you not seen music-hall turns imitating
celebrities with marvellous accuracy? Nothing is easier than to
personate a public character. The Prime Minister of England is far
easier to understudy than Mr. John Smith of Clapham, say. As for
O’Murphy’s ‘double,’ no one was going to take much notice of him
until after the departure of the Prime Minister, and by then he
would have made himself scarce. He drives straight from Charing
Cross to the meeting-place of his friends. He goes in as O’Murphy,
he emerges as some one quite different. O’Murphy has disappeared,
leaving a conveniently suspicious trail behind him.”

“But the man who personated the Prime Minister was seen by every
one!”

“He was not seen by anyone who knew him privately or intimately.
And Daniels shielded him from contact with anyone as much as
possible. Moreover, his face was bandaged up, and anything unusual
in his manner would be put down to the fact that he was suffering
from shock as a result of the attempt upon his life. Mr. MacAdam
has a weak throat, and always spares his voice as much as possible
before any great speech. The deception was perfectly easy to keep
up as far as France. There it would be impracticable and
impossible—so the Prime Minister disappears. The police of this
country hurry across the Channel, and no one bothers to go into
the details of the first attack. To sustain the illusion that the
abduction has taken place in France, Daniels is gagged and
chloroformed in a convincing manner.”

“And the man who has enacted the part of the Prime Minister?”

“Rids himself of his disguise. He and the bogus chauffeur may be
arrested as suspicious characters, but no one will dream of
suspecting their real part in the drama, and they will eventually
be released for lack of evidence.”

“And the real Prime Minister?”

“He and O’Murphy were driven straight to the house of ‘Mrs.
Everard,’ at Hampstead, Daniels’ so-called ‘aunt.’ In reality, she
is Frau Bertha Ebenthal, and the police have been looking for her
for some time. It is a valuable little present that I have made to
them—to say nothing of Daniels! Ah, it was a clever plan, but he
did not reckon on the cleverness of Hercule Poirot!”

I think my friend might well be excused his moment of vanity.

“When did you first begin to suspect the truth of the matter?”

“When I began to work the right way—from _within_! I could not make
that shooting affair fit in—but when I saw that the net result of
it was that _the Prime Minister went to France with his face bound
up_ I began to comprehend! And when I visited all the cottage
hospitals between Windsor and London, and found that no one
answering to my description had had his face bound up and dressed
that morning, I was sure! After that, it was child’s-play for a
mind like mine!”

  •   •   •   •   •   •   •

The following morning, Poirot showed me a telegram he had just
received. It had no place of origin, and was unsigned. It ran:

“In time.”

Later in the day the evening papers published an account of the
Allied Conference. They laid particular stress on the magnificent
ovation accorded to Mr. David MacAdam, whose inspiring speech had
produced a deep and lasting impression.

first_paras:
One evening after dinner—I will not particularize the date; it
suffices to say that it was at the time when “Peace by negotiation”
was the parrot-cry of England’s enemies—my friend and I were
sitting in his rooms. After being invalided out of the Army I had
been given a recruiting job, and it had become my custom to drop
in on Poirot in the evenings after dinner and talk with him of any
cases of interest that he might have on hand.

Poirot leaned back in his chair, his eyes fixed on the ceiling, as he meticulously aligned the various ornaments on the mantelpiece. "It is a grave matter, truly, mon ami," he remarked, his voice surprisingly calm amidst my agitation. "But one must ask oneself: why now? The Prime Minister travels to France tomorrow for the secret conference—a meeting of the utmost importance for the Allied cause. To strike today, in the very heart of London, suggests a desperation, or perhaps a calculated diversion, that we would do well to consider." He paused, his gaze sharpening as he looked toward the door. "But listen, Hastings, if I am not mistaken, we are about to have a visitor who may provide us with more than the newspapers choose to print."

Poirot was busily engaged in the task of building a card house, and he did not even look up as I finished my tirade. He merely shook his head with a little sigh. “Calm yourself, my friend,” he murmured. “Do not agitate yourself. The Prime Minister, he is safe—for the moment. But you are right in one thing: the German agents, they are remarkably well-informed. It is as though they have an ear at the very door of the Cabinet.”

Poirot was at that moment engaged in the delicate task of building a card house. He gave a final touch to the superstructure, and then turned to me with a smile. “You are excited, Hastings? You find this matter of the Prime Minister’s escape to be of a supreme interest, yes? To me, it is the psychology of the attempt that holds the attention. A bullet that merely grazes—it is a narrow margin, is it not? Either the assassin was a poor shot, or he was a very good one who intended only to warn.”

Poirot was engaged in the delicate task of building a house of cards. He did not look up as he spoke. "It is indeed a grave matter, Hastings. But me, I find it more than grave—I find it significant. The Prime Minister, he is the soul of the resistance. To remove him now is to win the war for the enemy without firing another shot on the battlefield. It is the brain that we must fear, not the arm that holds the rifle."

Poirot was silent for a moment, his eyes fixed on the ceiling, as though he were following some train of thought of his own. "It is a grave matter, Hastings," he remarked at last. "The safety of the Prime Minister is of the highest importance. But do not blame the police too much. They have many things to consider, and the modern assassin is a man of great ingenuity. But I wonder—I wonder if there is not more to this than meets the eye? A bullet that only grazes—it is a very delicate thing, is it not?" He was interrupted by the sound of a car drawing up outside. It was a large, powerful car, and it stopped at our door. A moment later, there was a sharp, imperious ring at the bell.

Poirot was busy mopping a grey suit with a minute sponge. Never
was there a dandy such as Hercule Poirot. Neatness and order were
his passion. Now, with the odour of benzine filling the air, he
was quite unable to give me his full attention.

“In a little minute I am with you, my friend. I have all but
finished. The spot of grease—he is not good—I remove him—so!” He
waved his sponge.

I smiled as I lit another cigarette.

“Anything interesting on?” I inquired, after a minute or two.

“For the first time,” Lord Estair continued, his voice grave, “it is to be held in France. At Versailles, to be precise. The representatives of the Great Powers will be there. The agenda is of the highest importance, and David MacAdam is the soul of the Conference. His presence is vital to ensure that a unified front is maintained. He should have left for France this morning; instead, he has vanished. If he does not appear at the opening session tomorrow, the blow to the morale of the Allies will be devastating, and the ‘Peace by negotiation’ party will gain a foothold that may well lose us the war. We have, Monsieur Poirot, less than twenty-four hours to find him.”

“It is to be held at Versailles on Friday,” Lord Estair said. “Its importance cannot be over-estimated. The whole future of the Allied cause hangs in the balance. The Prime Minister is the only man who can hold the conflicting interests together. Without him, we shall be at a deadlock. And, as I have told you, he has vanished. He was on his way to France when the catastrophe occurred, and since yesterday morning no word of him has been heard.”

"It is at Versailles," said Lord Estair. "The conference begins tomorrow at nine o'clock in the evening. The Prime Minister's presence is vital. He alone can carry the weight of the British delegation; he alone can harmonize the conflicting interests of the Allies. Without him, the conference will be a failure, and a peace—a premature and disastrous peace—will be the inevitable result. You see the gravity of the situation, Monsieur Poirot? We have less than twenty-four hours to find him."

“For reasons which I cannot divulge,” Lord Estair said, “the presence of the Prime Minister at this conference is vital. The pacifist element, which is at the moment very strong in certain of the Allied countries, will only be countered by the personal influence and forceful personality of David MacAdam. Without him, a separate peace may be concluded, which would mean the virtual ruin of the British Empire. He was to have left for France this morning. He did leave London. But he never arrived at Boulogne.”

“For reasons which I need not specify,” Lord Estair continued, “it is imperative that the Prime Minister should attend that conference. He is the only man who can deal with the situation. The conference is to be held at Versailles tomorrow. If he is not there, the result will be disastrous. And at this moment, Monsieur Poirot, we do not know where he is! We have exactly twenty-four hours to find him.”

“For obvious reasons, no details have been given of when and where
it is to take place. But, although it has been kept out of the
newspapers, the date is, of course, widely known in diplomatic
circles. The Conference is to be held to-morrow—Thursday—evening
at Versailles. Now you perceive the terrible gravity of the
situation. I will not conceal from you that the Prime Minister’s
presence at the Conference is a vital necessity. The Pacifist
propaganda, started and maintained by the German agents in our
midst, has been very active. It is the universal opinion that the
turning point of the Conference will be the strong personality of
the Prime Minister. His absence may have the most serious
results—possibly a premature and disastrous peace. And we have no
one who can be sent in his place. He alone can represent England.”

Poirot’s face had grown very grave. “Then you regard the kidnapping
of the Prime Minister as a direct attempt to prevent his being
present at the Conference?”

“Most certainly I do. He was actually on his way to France at the
time.”

“And the Conference is to be held?”

“At nine o’clock to-morrow night.”

Poirot drew an enormous watch from his pocket.

“It is now a quarter to nine.”

“Twenty-four hours,” said Mr. Dodge thoughtfully.

“And a quarter,” amended Poirot. “Do not forget the quarter,
monsieur—it may come in useful. Now for the details—the abduction,
did it take place in England or in France?”

“Lord Estair’s face went even paler. ‘This is disastrous!’ he ejaculated. ‘They have found the car—the second car, the bogus one. It was discovered abandoned in a small village near the coast, but of the Prime Minister and his captors there is not a trace. They have vanished into thin air! Furthermore, the French police report that a man answering the description of the bogus A.D.C. was seen at a small wayside station, but he managed to elude capture. We are no further forward than we were three hours ago.’”

“It is from the Chief of General Staff,” he said, his voice shaking with emotion. “The car has been found abandoned in a small lane near the coast, not far from Camiers. It was empty. There were signs of a struggle—and bloodstains upon the cushions.” He looked at us with a face that had gone suddenly grey. “If they have killed him, the consequences for the Empire are unthinkable. We must find him, Monsieur Poirot—and we must find him alive!”

“They have found the car,” Lord Estair announced, his voice trembling slightly. “Abandoned in a small thicket near the coast, not far from Ambleteuse. But of the Prime Minister, there is no sign. However, there is a development here in London. It appears that the chauffeur who was supposed to drive the Prime Minister to the station this morning, a man named O’Murphy, has also disappeared. He was seen leaving the Prime Minister’s residence in a hurried manner shortly after the official party had departed for Dover.”

“The car has been found,” cried Lord Estair. “Abandoned in a small wood near the coast. But of the Prime Minister, there is no sign! And what is worse, they have discovered the body of the man who acted as the bogus A.D.C.—shot through the heart. He was a notorious German spy, known to the French police. But there is a further complication. It appears that the Prime Minister’s secretary, Captain Daniels, who was travelling with him, has also vanished without a trace.”

Lord Estair’s face went white as he scanned the contents of the message. “This is even more serious than we thought,” he muttered, his voice trembling slightly. “They have found the car—the bogus one—abandoned in a ditch near a small hamlet called Camiers. But there is no sign of the Prime Minister, nor of his secretary, Captain Daniels. Both have vanished into thin air!”

“Here is news at last! This telegram has just been decoded. They
have found the second car, also the secretary, Daniels, chloroformed,
gagged, and bound, in an abandoned farm near C——. He remembers
nothing, except something being pressed against his mouth and nose
from behind, and struggling to free himself. The police are
satisfied as to the genuineness of his statement.”

“And they have found nothing else?”

“No.”

“Not the Prime Minister’s dead body? Then, there is hope. But it
is strange. Why, after trying to shoot him this morning, are they
now taking so much trouble to keep him alive?”

Dodge shook his head. “One thing’s quite certain. They’re determined
at all costs to prevent his attending the Conference.”

“He has been Mr. MacAdam’s secretary for some years. A most
exemplary and devoted servant. We have no reason to suspect him.
The chauffeur’s name is O’Murphy. He is an Irishman, but had
served in the Army and was recommended to us by the War Office.
He is a first-class driver.”

“Have you the details of the shooting?”

“It happened near Windsor. At a place where the road is very narrow
and there are a lot of trees. The car was slowing down to take the
corner, when a shot was fired from behind a tree. It shattered the
glass of the window, and a piece of it grazed the Prime Minister’s
cheek. O’Murphy accelerated at once, and they were soon out of
danger. The Prime Minister’s first thought was that it was a
German sniper. He would not allow the car to be stopped, but drove
straight to London.”

“Where he had his wound dressed?”

“Yes, by a local doctor, I believe.”

“And then?”

“Then he went straight to the Admiralty, and thence to the
destroyer that was waiting for him.”

“Did he see no one but the doctor?”

“Only his daughter, who met him at the Admiralty. He had just time
for a few words with her. He told her not to be alarmed by the news
of the attempt on his life, as he was quite unhurt.”

“And after that?”

“After that, as I have told you, he started for France.”

“And he took with him Captain Daniels and O’Murphy?”

“Yes.”

“And they are both accounted for?”

“Daniels, as I told you, has been found. O’Murphy is still
missing. But the second car was also found, and in it were the
remains of a chauffeur’s uniform.”

“Aha! So it is possible that O’Murphy was a confederate, and that
he has changed into other clothes and escaped?”

“It would seem so.”

“But surely it would have been easy to trace a man of his
description?”

“He is a small man, of no particular features. He would easily
pass unnoticed.”

“Where did the kidnapping take place?”

“In a lonely part of the road between Boulogne and General
Headquarters. The car was found in a small lane about a mile away.
The occupants of the bogus car were, of course, gone.”

“How did they get the car, though?”

“It was one of the General Headquarters cars. It had been stolen
the night before. The chauffeur’s body was found in a ditch near
by. He had been shot through the head.”

“Then the whole thing was a most carefully planned plot?”

“Yes. They must have been aware of the Prime Minister’s every
movement.”

“What about the Prime Minister’s daughter? Can she tell us
anything?”

“Miss MacAdam? She is a girl of great spirit. She has already been
closely questioned, but she can give no information.”

“And the doctor who dressed the wound?”

“We have seen him, too. He is a very well-known man. Sir James
Westerfield.”

“Aha! A most distinguished name. And he says?”

“He says the wound was quite a slight one—just a graze.”

“One thing more. Is there any particular person whom you suspect?”

“There is a certain Frau Bertha Ebenthal. She is a very dangerous
woman, and we believe she is at the bottom of it all. We have been
on her track for some time, but so far she has always eluded us.”

“Frau Bertha Ebenthal,” repeated Poirot slowly. “I have heard of
her. She is a woman of great ability.”

“She is a genius for organization,” said Lord Estair. “And we have
certain information that she is in England at the present moment.”

“In England?”

“Yes. We are doing our best to find her, but she is a past-mistress
of the art of disguise.”

“I see. Now, messieurs, I must have a few minutes for reflection.
Will you wait in the next room?”

The two men withdrew, and Poirot sat for some time in silence, his
eyes closed. I did not disturb him. At last he looked up.

“Hastings, I have a little idea. I think I see a way—not much, but
a beginning. Will you go at once to the Admiralty and ask for Miss
MacAdam? Tell her I am a friend of her father’s, and that I have
news of him. If possible, bring her back with you. If not, get her
to tell you every word her father said to her this morning.”

“I will go at once,” I said.

“One moment, Hastings. Is it not strange that they should have
taken the trouble to find a doctor to dress such a slight wound?”

“I suppose they wanted to be sure it was not serious,” I
suggested.

“Perhaps. But Sir James Westerfield—he is a very great man. He
does not go about dressing slight wounds.”

“He may have been a friend of the Prime Minister’s.”

“Possibly. But go now, Hastings. There is no time to lose.”

I was back in less than an hour. Miss MacAdam had already left the
Admiralty, but I had been able to see her at her house in Chelsea.
She was a charming girl, and most anxious to do anything she could
to help.

“My father only spoke a few words to me,” she said. “He told me not
to be alarmed, that he was quite unhurt, and that I was not to
mention the matter to anyone until it was in the papers. He seemed
in a great hurry, and very much preoccupied. He only stayed a few
minutes.”

“Did he say anything else?”

“Only that he was going to France, and that he would be back on
Friday.”

“Nothing else?”

“No, nothing.”

“I thanked her and came away.”

“It is not much,” said Poirot, when I had told him. “But it
confirms my little idea. Now, Hastings, we must go to work. We have
just twenty-two hours.”

“What are you going to do?”

“I am going to find the Prime Minister. And to do that, I must
first find Frau Bertha Ebenthal.”

“But how?”

“By the exercise of my ‘little grey cells,’ Hastings. And now, if
you will be so good as to call in Lord Estair and Mr. Dodge.”

When they were seated, Poirot spoke.

“Messieurs, I have a request to make. I must have a list of all
the people who were in the Admiralty this morning when the Prime
Minister arrived.”

“That will be easy,” said Mr. Dodge. “But why?”

“Because, monsieur, I have a suspicion that the information which
enabled the kidnappers to carry out their plan so successfully was
given by someone in the Admiralty.”

“But that is impossible!” cried Lord Estair.

“Nothing is impossible,” said Poirot. “And if you will give me the
list, I will tell you in an hour’s time if my suspicion is correct.”

The list was soon provided, and Poirot spent some time studying it.

“Aha!” he said at last. “Here is a name that interests me.
Mrs. Everard. Who is she?”

“She is a widow,” said Mr. Dodge. “She has been working in the
Admiralty for some months. She is a very clever woman, and most
highly recommended.”

“I should like to see this Mrs. Everard,” said Poirot. “Can it be
arranged?”

“Certainly. I will send for her at once.”

“No, no! That would not do at all. I must see her without her
knowing it. Is it possible for me to be in the Admiralty when she
leaves this evening?”

“It could be arranged, I suppose. But I don’t see——”

“It is my way,” said Poirot. “And now, messieurs, if you will
excuse me, I have some preparations to make.”

When they had gone, Poirot turned to me.

“Hastings, I want you to go to the shop of a certain Monsieur
Lafayette, in Soho. He is a costumier. Tell him I sent you, and ask
him for the disguise I ordered this morning.”

“Disguise? But you haven’t ordered any disguise!”

“I am about to do so,” said Poirot, picking up the telephone.

In a few minutes he had finished his conversation.

“Now, Hastings, be off. And when you return, we will go to the
Admiralty.”

I was back with the disguise—a very realistic one of an elderly
clergyman—in less than an hour. Poirot was already dressed in his
grey suit, and he quickly donned the black coat and shovel hat.

“Now, Hastings, how do I look?”

“You look very much like a clergyman,” I said.

“Good! Now we will go.”

We arrived at the Admiralty just as the clerks were beginning to
leave. We took up our position near the entrance, and Poirot
scrutinized everyone who came out.

“There she is!” he whispered at last, as a tall, elegant woman in
black appeared. “Follow her, Hastings. Do not lose sight of her for
a moment. I will follow you.”

I followed the woman through the streets of London, and eventually
to a small house in a quiet street in Bayswater. She entered the
house, and I waited outside until Poirot joined me.

“Well, Hastings, we have found the nest. Now we must see if the
bird is within.”

He rang the bell, and the door was opened by a neat maid.

“Is Mrs. Everard at home?”

“Yes, sir. But she is just going out again.”

“I must see her for a moment. It is a matter of great importance.”

The maid hesitated, and then showed us into a small sitting-room.
In a few minutes Mrs. Everard appeared. She was, as I had seen, a
very beautiful woman, with a most engaging manner.

“You wished to see me?” she asked, looking from one to the other
of us.

“I have come to see you, madame,” said Poirot, “on a matter of
the most vital urgency. It concerns the Prime Minister.”

Mrs. Everard started, and a look of alarm came into her eyes.

“The Prime Minister? What do you mean? I know nothing of the
Prime Minister.”

“I think you do, madame,” said Poirot. “I think you know more than
you care to say. In fact, I am sure of it.”

Mrs. Everard’s face went deadly pale. “I don’t know what you mean,”
she stammered.

“I will tell you what I mean, madame. I mean that you are in
communication with the enemies of England. I mean that you are
an agent of Frau Bertha Ebenthal!”

Mrs. Everard sank into a chair, her face buried in her hands.

“It is true!” she sobbed. “But I couldn’t help it! They forced me
to do it! They threatened to kill my children if I didn’t help
them!”

“I am sorry for you, madame,” said Poirot. “But you must tell me
all you know. Where is the Prime Minister?”

“I don’t know! I swear I don’t know! All I had to do was to give
them information about his movements. I didn’t know they were
going to kidnap him!”

“And how did you give them this information?”

“By means of a code. I was to leave a message in a certain place
every day.”

“And where is this place?”

“A small shop in Soho. It is kept by a man named O’Murphy.”

“O’Murphy!” I cried. “The Prime Minister’s chauffeur!”

“Yes,” said Mrs. Everard. “He is one of their most dangerous
agents.”

“And where is he now?”

“I don’t know. I haven’t seen him for days.”

“But you know where he lives?”

“No. I only know the shop in Soho.”

“Well, madame, you must come with us to the Admiralty. You will
have to tell your story to Lord Estair.”

Mrs. Everard rose, her face still pale and tear-stained. “I will
come,” she said. “But I tell you, I don’t know where the Prime
Minister is!”

We took Mrs. Everard to the Admiralty, where she was closely
questioned by Lord Estair and Mr. Dodge. She told her story
faithfully, but it was clear that she really did not know the
Prime Minister’s whereabouts.

“It is as I thought,” said Poirot, when we were alone again. “She
is only a tool. The real brains of the plot are elsewhere.”

“But what about O’Murphy?” I asked. “If we can find him——”

“We shall find him, Hastings. Do not fear. But first, I must visit
that shop in Soho.”

We went to the shop, but it was closed and empty. There was no sign
of O’Murphy.

“He has gone,” said Poirot. “He knew the game was up as soon as the
kidnapping was discovered. But he cannot have gone far.”

“What are you going to do now?” I asked.

“I am going to find the doctor who dressed the Prime Minister’s
wound.”

“Sir James Westerfield? But he has already told us all he knows.”

“Has he, Hastings? I wonder. There was something in his story that
did not ring true. Why should a man of his standing be called in
to dress a slight wound? And why should the Prime Minister have
gone to his house, instead of having him come to the Admiralty?”

“Perhaps he was a friend of the Prime Minister’s,” I suggested
again.

“Perhaps. But I must be sure. Come, Hastings, we will go to Sir
James Westerfield’s house.”

We found Sir James at home, and he received us with his usual
courtesy.

“I have already told Lord Estair all I know,” he said. “The wound
was a mere trifle—just a graze. I dressed it and gave him some
simple instructions, and he went away.”

“And you are quite sure it was the Prime Minister?” asked Poirot.

Sir James looked surprised. “Of course I am sure! I have known him
for years.”

“And you noticed nothing unusual about him?”

“Nothing whatever. He was a little agitated, as was only natural
after such an escape, but otherwise he was quite himself.”

“I see. Well, thank you, Sir James. I am sorry to have troubled
you.”

When we were outside, Poirot turned to me.

“Hastings, I am more than ever convinced that there is something
wrong. Sir James is a very great man, but he is also a very
busy one. He would not have taken the trouble to dress a slight
wound if there had not been some other reason.”

“But what other reason could there be?”

“That is what I am going to find out. And now, Hastings, we must
go to the hospital.”

“The hospital? What hospital?”

“The one where Sir James Westerfield is a surgeon. I want to see
his assistant.”

We went to the hospital, and after some delay we were shown into the
assistant’s room.

“I am Monsieur Poirot,” said my friend. “I believe you are Sir
James Westerfield’s assistant?”

“I am,” said the young man.

“I want to ask you a question. Was Sir James at the hospital this
morning?”

“Yes, he was here from nine until eleven.”

“And did he receive any visitors?”

“Only one—a man who came to have a wound dressed.”

“A man? Not the Prime Minister?”

“No. It was a small man, of no particular features. He said he had
been in a motor accident.”

“Aha!” cried Poirot. “And did Sir James dress the wound?”

“Yes. He was with the man for about half an hour.”

“And what happened then?”

“The man went away, and Sir James went on with his work.”

“I see. Well, thank you very much.”

When we were outside, Poirot was jubilant.

“You see, Hastings? It was as I thought! The man who went to Sir
James Westerfield’s house was not the Prime Minister! It was
O’Murphy!”

“O’Murphy? But why should O’Murphy go to Sir James?”

“Because, Hastings, O’Murphy was the man who was shot! He was
wounded in the attempt on the Prime Minister’s life, and he went
to Sir James to have the wound dressed!”

“But why did he pretend to be the Prime Minister?”

“Because he wanted to gain time! He knew that if the Prime Minister
were kidnapped, there would be a great outcry. But if he could
make it appear that the Prime Minister had reached London safely,
the kidnapping would not be discovered for some time.”

“But how could he hope to deceive Sir James?”

“He didn’t have to deceive him! Sir James was in the plot!”

“Sir James Westerfield? Impossible!”

“Nothing is impossible, Hastings. Sir James is a very great man, but
he is also a very ambitious one. And we know that the German agents
have many friends in high places.”

“But what about the Prime Minister? Where is he?”

“He is still in France, Hastings. But he is not at General
Headquarters. He is being kept a prisoner in that abandoned farm
near C——.”

“But the police have searched it!”

“They have searched the farm, yes. But they have not searched the
cellar!”

“The cellar? But how do you know there is a cellar?”

“Because, Hastings, I have been studying the maps. And I have found
that that particular farm was once a wine-growing establishment. It
must have extensive cellars.”

“But why didn’t the police find them?”

“Because they were too well hidden. But we shall find them,
Hastings! We shall find them!”

We went at once to Lord Estair and told him our discovery. He was
at first incredulous, but at last he agreed to let us go to France.

“But you must be quick!” he said. “The Conference is to-morrow
evening!”

“We shall be there, milord,” said Poirot. “I promise you, we shall
be there!”

We crossed to France that night, and by morning we were at the farm
near C——. The police were still there, and they were very
surprised to see us.

“We have searched every inch of the place,” they said. “There is no
one here.”

“Have you searched the cellar?” asked Poirot.

“The cellar? We didn’t know there was one.”

“I thought not,” said Poirot. “Now, if you will follow me——”

He led the way to a small outhouse, and after some searching he
found a trap-door hidden under some straw. He opened it, and we
descended a flight of stone steps.

At the bottom we found a large, well-lit room, and there, sitting at
a table, was the Prime Minister! He was alive and well, though a
little pale and haggard.

“Thank God!” he cried, when he saw us. “I thought I was never going
to be found!”

We told him all that had happened, and he was amazed at Poirot’s
cleverness.

“I can never thank you enough, Monsieur Poirot,” he said. “You have
saved England!”

“It was nothing, monsieur,” said Poirot modestly. “I only used my
‘little grey cells.’”

We took the Prime Minister back to London, and he was able to attend
the Conference after all. The plot was a complete failure, and the
German agents were all captured.

And so, once again, Hercule Poirot had saved the day. But he was
not satisfied.

“There is still one thing, Hastings,” he said, as we sat in his
rooms that evening. “Who was the real brains of the plot? It was
not O’Murphy, or Mrs. Everard, or even Sir James Westerfield. They
were only tools.”

“Who could it have been?” I asked.

“I have a suspicion, Hastings. A very strong suspicion. But I must
have proof.”

“And how will you get it?”

“By the exercise of my ‘little grey cells,’ Hastings. And now, if
you will be so good as to call in Captain Daniels.”

“Captain Daniels? But what has he to do with it?”

“You will see, Hastings. You will see.”

Captain Daniels was soon in the room, and he looked very surprised
to see us.

“I thought you were in France,” he said.

“I have just returned,” said Poirot. “And I have brought the Prime
Minister with me.”

Daniels went pale. “The Prime Minister? But I thought——”

“You thought he was safely hidden in the cellar, did you not,
Captain Daniels?”

Daniels started. “I don’t know what you mean!”

“I mean, Captain Daniels, that you are the real brains of this
plot! It was you who planned the kidnapping, and it was you who
gave the information to the German agents!”

“It’s a lie!” cried Daniels. “I have always been a devoted servant
of the Prime Minister!”

“A very devoted servant,” said Poirot. “So devoted that you were
willing to see him kidnapped and perhaps murdered, in order to
serve your German masters!”

“I tell you, it’s a lie!”

“Is it? Then perhaps you can explain why you were seen in
communication with Frau Bertha Ebenthal only last week?”

Daniels was silent. He knew the game was up.

“And now, Captain Daniels, I must ask you to come with me to Scotland
Yard.”

As they led him away, Poirot turned to me.

“You see, Hastings? The ‘little grey cells’ never fail!”

“But how did you know it was Daniels?” I asked.

“Because, Hastings, he was the only one who could have known all the
Prime Minister’s movements. And he was also the only one who could
have arranged for the bogus car and the bogus A.D.C.”

“But what about Frau Bertha Ebenthal?”

“She was the one who gave the orders, Hastings. But Daniels was the
one who carried them out. And now, I think I have earned a little
rest.”

And so the great mystery was solved, and England was saved once
again. And all thanks to the marvellous brain of Hercule Poirot.

“He has been Mr. MacAdam’s confidential secretary for over two
years. He is of a good family, and his record is irreproachable.
The police have, of course, gone into his antecedents, but there
is nothing to suggest any ground for suspicion. He is as much
upset by this affair as any of us.”

“And who else was in the car when the shot was fired?”

“The chauffeur, and the Prime Minister’s valet, O’Murphy.”

“O’Murphy? A name of Ireland, that.”

“He is an Irishman, yes. But he has been in Mr. MacAdam’s service
for many years. A most devoted servant, I believe.”

“I see. Now, let us have the details of the shooting.”

“The car was passing through a lonely stretch of road, between
Windsor and London, when a man stepped out from a clump of trees
and fired. The bullet, as I told you, grazed the Prime Minister’s
cheek. The chauffeur at once put on all speed. The Prime Minister
himself was the first to see the man, but before he could say
anything the shot was fired. He says he thinks the man was wearing
a mask, but he cannot be sure.”

“And no one else saw him?”

“The chauffeur saw a man’s figure, and Captain Daniels says he
caught a glimpse of someone as they sped past.”

“And what did they do?”

“They stopped at the next village and informed the police. The
man, however, had disappeared.”

“I see. Now, about this crossing to France?”

“The Prime Minister was accompanied by Captain Daniels and
O’Murphy. They went to Dover by train, and were met there by a
destroyer. At Boulogne, they were met by the car I told you of.”

“And the chauffeur of this car? He was also a bogus person?”

“Yes. He was wearing the uniform of a British Army chauffeur.”

“Where was the real car found?”

“In a small lane, some miles from Boulogne. The chauffeur and the
A.D.C. were found in it, as I told you.”

“And the Prime Minister?”

“He had disappeared. Captain Daniels was found later, as I have
already mentioned.”

“It is a very strange business,” said Poirot. “A very strange
business indeed. You say the Prime Minister was to stay with the
Commander-in-Chief. Where is his headquarters?”

“At a small chateau, not far from C——.”

“And the Prime Minister was on his way there when he was kidnapped?”

“Yes.”

“And you say that the car used was a bogus one?”

“Yes. It was an exact replica of the cars used by the General
Staff, and it bore a false number.”

“It is very well planned,” said Poirot. “Very well planned indeed.”

“You will help us, Monsieur Poirot?” asked Lord Estair
anxiously. “The time is so short.”

“I will do my best. But I must have more information. I must see
this Captain Daniels, and also the valet, O’Murphy.”

“Captain Daniels is still in France. But O’Murphy is at the Prime
Minister’s house in London. He returned there this afternoon.”

“Good. I will see him at once.”

“I will give you a note to the mistress of the house, Mrs. Everard.
She is the Prime Minister’s aunt, and has lived with him for many
years.”

“One thing more,” said Poirot. “This Frau Bertha Ebenthal. Who is
she?”

Lord Estair and Mr. Dodge looked at each other.

“She is a woman who has been suspected for some time of being in
the pay of the German Government,” said Lord Estair. “But we have
never been able to prove anything against her. She is a woman of
great charm and intelligence, and has a large circle of
acquaintances in London.”

“I see. And was she anywhere near the scene of the kidnapping?”

“We have no reason to think so. Why do you ask?”

“Because in these matters it is always well to look for the woman,”
said Poirot with a smile. “And now, messieurs, I will not detain
you any longer. I must get to work.”

Lord Estair and Mr. Dodge rose.

“We shall be at the War Office all night,” said Mr. Dodge. “If you
have any news, you can reach us there.”

“I will not fail to do so,” said Poirot.

As soon as they had gone, Poirot turned to me.

“Well, Hastings, what do you think of it?”

“It’s a most extraordinary business,” I said. “Do you think you’ll
be able to find the Prime Minister in time?”

“I shall do my best, my friend. I shall do my best. But it is a
difficult problem—a very difficult problem. And now, let us go
and see this O’Murphy.”

“He’s been with the Prime Minister for some time. We have every
reason to believe him a most capable and loyal assistant. He is a
man of some means, too—it’s not as if he were in need of money.
The other secretary, O’Murphy, who has recently been appointed, is
a young man from the Foreign Office, very well recommended. Both
have impeccable records.”

“He has been with the Prime Minister for nearly two years. He has
a distinguished record in the Army, and has always proved himself
the soul of discretion and efficiency. We have the highest opinion
of him.”

“Where was he when the shooting occurred?”

“In the car with Mr. MacAdam. It was about eight o’clock. They were
passing through a quiet part of the road, and a man suddenly stepped
out and fired a rifle.”

“And missed?”

“The bullet grazed the Prime Minister’s cheek. Captain Daniels
immediately jumped out of the car, but the man had disappeared in
a small wood. Daniels gave chase, but the fellow was too quick for
im. At length, he rejoined the car, and they drove to London.”

“But they were not discouraged? They continued their journey to
France?”

“That was it. The Prime Minister’s safety was the most important
point, and it was felt that his life would be safer in France,
where the military have it all their own way.”

“_Tiens!_” said Poirot. “And this Captain Daniels—has he a
family?”

“He has a mother, I believe—and a sister. He is a widower.”

“Any more details?”

“He lives in a small flat in Westminster. His sister lives with
him. Her husband was killed in the early days of the war.”

“Who else is in the flat?”

“A man-servant—O’Murphy.”

“And what is his record?”

“He has been with Captain Daniels for three years. He was
discharged from the Army on account of wounds.”

“Well, we must see this O’Murphy.”

“I’m afraid that’s impossible. O’Murphy has disappeared.”

“Since when?”

“Since this morning. He was sent to fetch some things for the
Captain for his journey to France, and since then nothing has been
seen or heard of him.”

“_Tiens!_” said Poirot. “That is very interesting. And the sister?”

“She is still at the flat. But she can give us no information.
She says her brother arrived home this morning after the shooting
affair, very much upset. He told her about the attempt, and gave
her some instructions as to his luggage. She has seen nothing of
O’Murphy since.”

“One other thing. At what time did the Prime Minister leave London?”

“At 11:30.”

“And the boat started from Dover?”

“At 1:30.”

“Good. I will begin with the sister of Captain Daniels. Is it
possible for you to have her here?”

“I will see what can be done.”

Lord Estair and Mr. Dodge then took their leave.

“I’ll telephone from my club,” said Mr. Dodge. “We’ll send a car
for her.”

“And also,” added Poirot, “for Mrs. Everard.”

“Who is she?”

“The lady at whose house the Prime Minister was staying at Windsor.”

“Certainly, if you wish it.”

They left us, and Poirot began to pace the room. He was very
silent. At length he stopped and looked at me.

“Well, Hastings, what do you think of it?”

“It’s a most extraordinary case,” I replied. “The kidnapping of
the Prime Minister—it’s like a novel!”

“_Précisément!_” agreed Poirot. “It is a very clever plot. It has
been well thought out.”

“I can’t believe that Captain Daniels is in it,” I said. “He has
such a fine record.”

“We must see the sister,” said Poirot. “I have a little idea—a
very little idea.”

“What is it?”

“Wait, my friend. It is too soon to speak.”

He sat down and began to build a house of cards. This was always a
sign that he was thinking deeply.

The car arrived with the two ladies about ten o’clock. Mrs. Everard
was a charming, elderly lady, very much upset by the events of the
morning.

“It’s too terrible!” she cried. “To think that such a thing should
happen in my house!”

“Do not distress yourself, madame,” said Poirot. “Now, will you
tell us everything you can about the Prime Minister’s visit?”

“He arrived on Tuesday evening with Captain Daniels. They had dinner
with us, and then went to their rooms. The Prime Minister had some
writing to do. Next morning, they had an early breakfast, and left
at seven o’clock.”

“Did anything unusual happen?”

“Nothing. Stay—there was one little thing. A woman came to the
door, and asked to see the Prime Minister. She was a very strange-looking
woman—dark, with a lot of black hair.”

“What did she want?”

“She wouldn’t say. She said she had an important message for the
Prime Minister. Of course, the servants didn’t let her in. They
told her she must go to London if she wanted to see him.”

“And she went away?”

“Yes. She seemed very disappointed.”

“Did you see her yourself?”

“No, I only heard about it from the butler.”

“What was her name?”

“She wouldn’t give it.”

“_Tiens!_” said Poirot. “That is very interesting. And now, madame,”
he turned to the other lady, “you are the sister of Captain
Daniels?”

“Yes. My name is Frau Bertha Ebenthal.”

I started. The name was unmistakably German. Poirot’s eyes were
fixed upon her.

“You are married to a German, then?”

“Yes. My husband was killed in the war. I have lived in England
for many years.”

“I see. And you live with your brother?”

“Yes.”

“And you have seen nothing of the man-servant, O’Murphy?”

“Nothing since this morning.”

“What was he like—this O’Murphy?”

“He was a very quiet man—very reliable.”

“I see. Thank you, madame.”

When the two ladies had gone, Poirot turned to me.

“Well, Hastings, what do you think of Frau Bertha Ebenthal?”

“She’s a German!” I cried. “I’m sure she’s a spy!”

“It is possible,” said Poirot. “But we must not jump to
conclusions. There is much that is still mysterious. Why did the
Prime Minister leave Windsor at seven o’clock, when his boat didn’t
start till 1:30? It is only an hour’s drive to London.”

“Perhaps he had business to attend to,” I suggested.

“Perhaps. But it is strange. And then there is the woman with the
black hair. Who was she? And what did she want with the Prime
Minister?”

“She may have been a German spy too,” I said.

“It is possible. Everything is possible.”

Poirot spent the next few hours in deep thought. He hardly spoke a
word. At length he rose and put on his hat.

“I am going to the flat of Captain Daniels,” he said. “You can
come with me if you like.”

The flat was in a large building in Westminster. We were admitted
by a maidservant.

“Is Frau Bertha Ebenthal at home?” asked Poirot.

“No, sir. She has just gone out.”

“I see. Can I see her room?”

The maid looked surprised, but she led us to a small bedroom at the
back of the flat.

Poirot began to search the room. He was very thorough. He looked
into every drawer and cupboard. At length he found a small
photograph in a frame. It was the photograph of a woman with black
hair.

“_Tiens!_” said Poirot. “The woman with the black hair! This is
very interesting.”

“Who is she?” I asked.

“I do not know. But I have seen her face before. Now, let us go.”

As we were leaving the flat, we met a man on the stairs. He was a
tall, dark man, with a very quiet manner.

“Excuse me,” said Poirot. “Are you O’Murphy?”

The man looked surprised. “No, sir. My name is Miller.”

“I see. Thank you.”

When we were in the street, Poirot turned to me.

“That was O’Murphy,” he said.

“How do you know?”

“I have a very good memory for faces. I saw him in a photograph
at the flat of Captain Daniels.”

“Then why did he lie?”

“Because he has something to hide. Now, Hastings, we must go to
France.”

“To France?”

“Yes. There is no time to lose. The Conference is at nine o’clock
to-morrow night. We must find the Prime Minister before then.”

“But how?”

“I have a little idea. A very little idea. But it may lead us to the
truth.”

We caught the night boat to Boulogne. The crossing was very rough,
and I was glad when we reached France.

We were met by a car from General Headquarters, and we were driven
at once to the abandoned farm where Captain Daniels had been found.

It was a small, lonely house, in a very desolate part of the
country. The police were still there, searching for clues.

Poirot began to examine the room where Captain Daniels had been
found. He was very interested in the chloroform bottle which was
lying on the floor.

“_Tiens!_” he said. “This is very strange. This bottle has no
label.”

“What does that mean?” I asked.

“It means that it was not bought at a chemist’s. It was probably
made in a laboratory.”

“By a German spy?”

“It is possible. And look at this.”

He pointed to a small piece of paper which was lying under the
table. It was a fragment of a telegram.

“... arrive... Boulogne... 1:30...”

“That was the time the boat arrived!” I cried.

“Yes. It seems that the kidnappers knew exactly when the Prime
Minister would arrive.”

“But how could they know?”

“That is the question. Now, Hastings, we must go to the place where
the first car was found.”

We were driven to a side road, about ten miles from Boulogne. The
car was still there, in a ditch.

Poirot began to examine the ground. He was very interested in some
footprints which were leading away from the car.

“These footprints were made by a woman,” he said.

“The woman with the black hair?”

“It is possible. And look at this.”

He pointed to a small piece of lace which was caught in a bramble.

“This is very fine lace,” he said. “It is the sort of lace that
would be worn by a lady.”

“Like Frau Bertha Ebenthal?”

“It is possible. Now, Hastings, we must go back to Boulogne. I have
a very important telegram to send.”
