When we reached Boulogne, Poirot went at once to the telegraph
office. He was there for some time. When he came out, he looked
very pleased with himself.

“I have sent a telegram to London,” he said. “Now we must wait.”

“Wait for what?”

“For the answer. And now, let us have some lunch. I am very
hungry.”

We had a very good lunch at a small café near the harbour. Poirot
was in very good spirits. He talked about everything except the
case.

After lunch, we went back to the telegraph office. There was a
telegram waiting for Poirot. He read it eagerly, and then he
laughed.

“I have it!” he cried. “I have the truth!”

“What is it?” I asked.

“Wait, my friend. It is not yet time to speak. We must go back to
England at once.”

“Back to England? But the Prime Minister——”

“He is in England. I am sure of it.”

“In England? But he was kidnapped in France!”

“So it seemed. But things are not always what they seem. Now, come,
there is no time to lose.”

We caught the afternoon boat to Folkestone. When we reached London,
we went at once to the flat of Captain Daniels.

We were admitted by the maidservant.

“Is Frau Bertha Ebenthal at home?” asked Poirot.

“No, sir. She has not yet returned.”

“I see. And Captain Daniels?”

“He is in France, sir.”

“I know. Now, let us go to the room of O’Murphy.”

The maid led us to a small room at the back of the flat. Poirot
began to search the room. He was very thorough. At length he found
a small piece of paper in a waste-paper basket.

It was a telegram.

“... meeting... 9:00... Versailles...”

“This is it!” cried Poirot. “This is the proof!”

“The proof of what?”

“The proof that O’Murphy is a spy! He knew about the meeting at
Versailles!”

“But how could he know?”

“He must have seen the Prime Minister’s papers. Now, we must find
him. I am sure he is in London.”

“But where?”

“I have a little idea. A very little idea. But it may lead us to the
truth.”

We spent the next few hours searching for O’Murphy. We went to all
the places where he was known to go. But we could find no trace of
him.

At length, as it was getting dark, we found ourselves in a quiet
street in Westminster.

“Look!” cried Poirot. “There is O’Murphy!”

He pointed to a man who was walking ahead of us. It was the same
man we had seen on the stairs.

We followed him at a distance. He turned into a small house at the
end of the street.

“This is it!” said Poirot. “This is the house of Frau Bertha
Ebenthal!”

“How do you know?”

“I saw her name on the door. Now, we must be very careful. We do
not know what we may find inside.”

We went up to the door and Poirot knocked. There was no answer. He
knocked again, louder this time. At length, the door was opened by
a woman.

It was the woman with the black hair.

“What do you want?” she asked.

“I wish to see Frau Bertha Ebenthal,” said Poirot.

“She is not here.”

“I think she is. And I think the Prime Minister is here too.”

The woman started. “I do not know what you are talking about.”

“I think you do. Now, let us in, or I shall be forced to call the
police.”

The woman hesitated, and then she let us in. We followed her into
a small room at the back of the house.

There, sitting in a chair, was the Prime Minister.

He looked very tired and ill. He was gagged and bound.

“Monsieur Poirot!” he cried, as we entered the room.

Poirot went at once to his side and began to untie his bonds.

“Do not worry, monsieur,” he said. “You are safe now.”

“But how did you find me?” asked the Prime Minister.

“It was a little idea of mine. A very little idea. But it led me to
the truth.”

“And the kidnappers?”

“They are here,” said Poirot, pointing to the woman with the black
hair.

“But who is she?”

“She is the sister of Captain Daniels. Frau Bertha Ebenthal.”

“What? But I thought Captain Daniels was a loyal officer!”

“He is. But his sister is a German spy. She and O’Murphy kidnapped
you and brought you here.”

“But how did they get me across the Channel?”

“They didn’t. You were never in France. The man who was kidnapped
at Boulogne was a double. He was dressed to look like you.”

“A double? But why?”

“To gain time. The kidnappers knew that they couldn’t keep you in
France for long. So they arranged for a double to be kidnapped
there, while they kept you here in London.”

“But why did they want to keep me here?”

“To prevent you from attending the Conference at Versailles. They
hoped that your absence would lead to a premature and disastrous
peace.”

“It’s incredible!” cried the Prime Minister.

“It is a very clever plot,” agreed Poirot. “But it has failed.
Now, we must get you to Versailles at once.”

We took the Prime Minister to the nearest police station, and from
there he was driven to the coast in a high-powered car. He reached
Versailles just in time for the Conference.

The next day, Poirot and I were sitting in his rooms. He was very
silent. At length he looked at me.

“Well, Hastings, what do you think of it?”

“It was a marvellous piece of work,” I said. “But there is one
thing I don’t understand. Who was the woman with the black hair?”

“She was the sister of Captain Daniels,” replied Poirot. “But she
was not the true culprit.”

“Not the true culprit? Then who was?”

“Captain Daniels.”

“Captain Daniels? But he was found chloroformed and bound in
France!”

“That was part of the plot. He arranged the whole thing. He is a
German spy too.”

“I can’t believe it!” I cried.

“It is true. He knew about the Prime Minister’s visit to Windsor,
and he arranged for his sister and O’Murphy to kidnap him. He then
went to France with the double, and arranged for the double to be
kidnapped there. He then pretended to be kidnapped himself, to
avoid suspicion.”

“But why did he do it?”

“For money. He was paid a large sum by the German government.”

“And O’Murphy?”

“He was in it too. He was the one who drove the car.”

“And Mrs. Everard?”

“She was innocent. She was just a pawn in the game.”

“And the woman with the black hair?”

“She was the sister of Captain Daniels. She was a German spy too.
But she was not the mastermind. The mastermind was Captain
Daniels.”

“It’s incredible!” I said.

“It is a very clever plot,” agreed Poirot. “But it failed because
it was too clever. Captain Daniels made one mistake.”

“What was that?”

“He left a photograph of his sister in her room. He thought that
no one would recognize her. But I have a very good memory for
faces. I saw her face in the photograph, and I knew that she was
the woman with the black hair.”

“And the telegram in O’Murphy’s room?”

“That was a plant. Captain Daniels put it there to throw me off
the scent. He wanted me to think that O’Murphy was the leader of the
gang. But I was not deceived.”

“Poirot,” I said, “you are a genius!”

“I am a very clever man,” agreed Poirot. “But I have my little
failings. I am a dandy, as you call it. And I am very fond of
neatness and order. But my brain—he is always at work!”

I smiled. “I’m glad of that, Poirot. England owes you a great
debt.”

“It is nothing,” said Poirot. “I am only too happy to have been
of service to your country. Now, let us have a cup of tea. I am
very thirsty.”

And so the great case of the kidnapped Prime Minister came to an
end. Captain Daniels and his sister were arrested and tried for
treason. O’Murphy was also arrested. They were all found guilty
and sentenced to long terms of imprisonment.

The Prime Minister’s presence at the Conference was a great
success. He was able to prevent a premature and disastrous peace,
and to ensure that the war was brought to a successful conclusion.

England was saved, and Hercule Poirot was the hero of the hour.
But he did not care for fame or glory. He was content to know that
he had done his duty, and that his marvellous brain had once again
proved its worth.

The end.

“Where was he when the shooting occurred?” inquired Poirot, leaning back and joining the tips of his fingers together in his most characteristic fashion. His eyes, usually so sharp and green like a cat’s, were now clouded as though he were observing something far beyond the confines of our small sitting-room.

"Captain Daniels has been with the Prime Minister for nearly two years," replied Lord Estair. "He has a distinguished record from the war and is the nephew of a very old friend of mine. His loyalty is beyond question. As for his dossier, he is a man of forty, unmarried, and has always been most efficient and devoted. There is absolutely no reason to suspect him, especially as he was found in the same condition as the others, though he was the only one taken with the Prime Minister in the second car."

Lord Estair smiled. “I thought you would ask me that. We do not
know very much of him. He is of no particular family. He has served
in the English Army, and is an extremely able secretary, being an
exceptionally fine linguist. I believe he speaks seven languages.
It is for that reason that the Prime Minister chose him to accompany
him to France.”

“Has he any relatives in England?”

“Two aunts. A Mrs. Everard, who lives at Hampstead, and a Miss
Daniels, who lives near Ascot.”

“Ascot? That is near to Windsor, is it not?”

“That point has not been overlooked. But it has led to nothing.”

“You regard the Capitaine Daniels, then, as above suspicion?”

A shade of bitterness crept into Lord Estair’s voice, as he replied:

“No, Monsieur Poirot. In these days, I should hesitate before I
pronounced _anyone_ above suspicion.”

“_Très bien_. Now I understand, _milord_, that the Prime Minister
would, as a matter of course, be under vigilant police protection,
which ought to render any assault upon him an impossibility?”

“Well, the car turned into a narrow lane, and the other car, after
some delay, followed. But there was a large flock of sheep in the
lane, and the detective’s car was blocked. By the time they reached
the main road again, the Premier’s car was out of sight. They
drove on to London, but the Prime Minister had not arrived. It
was then that the first alarm was given. Then a telephone message
from a wayside inn came to the Yard, saying that the Prime
Minister’s car was there, and that a man had been shot.”

“The car was then at an inn, and the Prime Minister’s chauffeur
was with it?”

“Yes. He was found lying near the car, with a bullet in his
shoulder. He stated that he had been forced to stop the car at the
entrance of the lane by two masked men, who fired on him. He jumped
down and attempted to grapple with one of them, but was shot.
Meanwhile, a man, also masked, had opened the door of the car and
fired a revolver into it. He heard the Prime Minister cry out, and
then the car was driven away.”

“Was anyone else near?”

“No. It was a very lonely part of the country.”

“But the Prime Minister and Captain Daniels?”

“They had disappeared.”

“Indeed! And the Prime Minister’s car?”

“Was found abandoned in a wood about a mile away. There was no
sign of anyone.”

“And the Prime Minister?”

“He was discovered about two hours later, in a small cottage,
suffering from a slight wound in the cheek. He could give no
description of his assailants, except that they were masked.”

“And Captain Daniels?”

“He was found some time later, in the same wood where the car had
been abandoned, also slightly wounded.”

“It is a most extraordinary story,” said Poirot, thoughtfully.

“You see our difficulty, Monsieur Poirot? We are absolutely in the
dark. We do not know who the Prime Minister’s enemies are.”

“And the chauffeur, O’Murphy?”

“He is in hospital. His wound is more serious than the others.”

“He is a man of good character?”

“The Yard is quite satisfied about him.”

“_Tiens!_ It is very strange. And you say that the Prime Minister’s
face was grazed by a bullet?”

“Yes.”

“Was the car a closed one?”

“Yes.”

“Then the man who fired must have been inside?”

“No. The door of the car was open.”

“Ah! And where was Captain Daniels?”

“He was sitting by the Prime Minister.”

“But if the door was open, he must have been between the Prime
Minister and the assassin?”

“Yes, he was. He tried to shield the Prime Minister, and was
himself wounded in the arm.”

“_C’est curieux!_” said Poirot. “And the Prime Minister’s wound?”

“A very slight one, as I have told you.”

“_Eh bien_, it is a very pretty case. Now, I must ask you a few
questions. This Mrs. Everard—the aunt of Captain Daniels—what
do you know of her?”

“She is a very charming and well-known lady. She has a house in
Hampstead.”

“And the other aunt—Miss Daniels?”

“She lives at Ascot, as I told you. She is an invalid.”

“I see. Now, Monsieur Poirot, will you take up the case?”

“It is a great honour, _milord_. I will do my best. But it is
not easy—no, it is not easy.”

“We realize that. But we believe in you. We will leave you now.
If anything further transpires, we will let you know at once.”

“One moment. Is there anything—any little detail—that you have not
mentioned?”

Lord Estair thought.

“There is one thing—but it is probably of no importance. The Prime
Minister’s chauffeur, O’Murphy, was seen in the neighbourhood of
Soho yesterday evening.”

“Soho? That is the Italian and French quarter, is it not?”

“Yes. But, as I said, it is probably of no importance.”

“Who knows? In a case like this, nothing is of no importance.
_Au revoir_, messieurs.”

When they had gone, Poirot sat for some time in silence. Then he
turned to me.

“Well, Hastings, what do you think of it?”

“It’s a most extraordinary business,” I said. “I can’t make head
or tail of it. Do you think the Prime Minister is really in France?”

“That is the question, my friend. If he is in France, then he is
alive. If he is not in France——”

“You think he may be dead?”

“It is possible. But we will hope for the best. Now, I have a little
work to do. I must see this Mrs. Everard.”

“Shall I come with you?”

“If you please, Hastings. Your presence is always a pleasure to
me.”

We took a taxi to Hampstead. Mrs. Everard’s house was a large and
luxurious one. We were shown into a beautifully furnished drawing-room.
Mrs. Everard was a tall, handsome woman of about forty. She received
us with great charm.

“You are Monsieur Poirot?” she said, as she shook hands with my
friend. “I have heard so much of you. And this is Captain Hastings?
I am so glad to meet you both.”

Poirot explained the object of our visit.

“It is about your nephew, Captain Daniels,” he said. “We are very
anxious to find him.”

“My nephew? But I thought he was with the Prime Minister.”

“He was. But he has disappeared.”

“Disappeared? Oh, how terrible! What can have happened to him?”

Mrs. Everard seemed genuinely distressed.

“We do not know. But we hope to find him. Can you tell us anything
about him? Has he any friends in London?”

“He has many friends, of course. But I don’t know of any particular
ones. He is a very quiet, studious man.”

“He is a linguist, I believe?”

“Yes, he is very clever. He speaks several languages.”

“And he has no—how shall I say it?—no lady friends?”

Mrs. Everard smiled. “Not that I know of. He is not what you would
call a ‘ladies’ man.’”

“I see. And his other aunt—Miss Daniels? Does he see much of her?”

“He goes to see her sometimes. She is a great invalid, you know.”

“Yes, so I have heard. Well, Mrs. Everard, I will not take up any
more of your time. If you should hear anything of your nephew,
you will let me know, will you not?”

“Of course I will. I am so anxious about him.”

As we left the house, Poirot turned to me.

“A very charming lady, Hastings. But she did not tell us much,
did she?”

“No,” I said. “But I don’t see what she could have told us. She
evidently knows nothing about it.”

“Perhaps. Now, Hastings, we must go to Soho.”

“Soho? Why Soho?”

“Because the chauffeur, O’Murphy, was seen there yesterday evening.
And I have a little idea, Hastings—a very little idea.”

We drove to Soho, and Poirot began a systematic search of the small
restaurants and cafés in the neighbourhood. For a long time we
found nothing. But at last, in a small, dingy-looking restaurant,
Poirot’s face suddenly lit up. He spoke to the proprietor in
French, and after a few minutes’ conversation, he turned to me.

“We have found it, Hastings! A man answering to the description
of O’Murphy was here yesterday evening. He was with a woman—a
woman whom the proprietor knows as Frau Bertha Ebenthal.”

“Frau Bertha Ebenthal!” I cried. “But that’s a German name!”

“Precisely, my friend. And she is known to the police as a very
dangerous German agent.”

“Then O’Murphy is a traitor!”

“It would seem so. But we must not jump to conclusions. Now,
Hastings, we must go to the hospital and see O’Murphy.”

At the hospital, we were told that O’Murphy was still very weak,
but that we might see him for a few minutes. He was lying in bed,
his shoulder heavily bandaged. He looked very pale and exhausted.

“Monsieur O’Murphy?” said Poirot, softly.

The man opened his eyes. “Yes?”

“I am Hercule Poirot. I have come to ask you a few questions.”

O’Murphy looked at him with a puzzled expression. “Questions?
What about?”

“About the attack on the Prime Minister.”

A look of fear came into the man’s eyes. “I—I can’t remember much.
It all happened so quickly.”

“But you remember the men who attacked you? They were masked,
you said?”

“Yes. They were masked.”

“And they fired on you?”

“Yes. I tried to stop them, but they shot me.”

“And then?”

“Then I don’t remember anything. I must have fainted.”

Poirot looked at him for a moment in silence. Then he said:

“And the woman you were with in Soho yesterday evening—was she
also masked?”

O’Murphy’s face turned even paler. “Woman? What woman? I wasn’t
with any woman.”

“The proprietor of the restaurant in Soho says you were. He knows
you well, O’Murphy.”

“He’s a liar! I wasn’t there!”

O’Murphy’s voice was shaking with fear.

“I think you are lying, O’Murphy,” said Poirot, quietly. “I think
you know very well who the woman was. She was Frau Bertha Ebenthal,
was she not?”

“I—I don’t know what you’re talking about!”

“I think you do. And I think you know more about the kidnapping
of the Prime Minister than you have told the police.”

“No! No! I don’t know anything! I swear I don’t!”

“We shall see. Come, Hastings.”

As we left the hospital, I said:

“Then O’Murphy is the culprit? He’s in league with this Frau
Ebenthal?”

“It would seem so, Hastings. But there are still some things I
do not understand. Why was the Prime Minister shot at in the
morning, and then kidnapped in the afternoon? And why was Captain
Daniels also kidnapped?”

“Perhaps he was also in the plot?”

“Perhaps. But if so, why was he gagged and bound in an abandoned
farm? It is all very mysterious, Hastings—very mysterious.”

“What are you going to do now?”

“I am going to see Lord Estair again. I have a few things to say
to him.”

We found Lord Estair and Mr. Dodge at the former’s house. They
were both looking very anxious.

“Any news, Monsieur Poirot?” asked Lord Estair, eagerly.

“A little, _milord_. I have found that O’Murphy was seen in Soho
yesterday evening with a known German agent, Frau Bertha Ebenthal.”

“Good heavens! Then O’Murphy is a traitor!”

“It would seem so. But there is more. I have been thinking about
the attack on the Prime Minister this morning. You said that
Captain Daniels was sitting by the Prime Minister, and that he
tried to shield him?”

“Yes, that is what he said.”

“But if the door of the car was open, and the assassin was outside,
he would have to fire across Captain Daniels to hit the Prime
Minister. And yet the Prime Minister was only grazed on the cheek,
whilst Captain Daniels was wounded in the arm.”

“Yes, that is so.”

“Does that not strike you as strange? If the assassin wanted to
kill the Prime Minister, why did he not fire again? And why did
he only graze his cheek?”

“I suppose his aim was wide.”

“Perhaps. But there is another possibility. Suppose the shot was
not fired from outside the car at all? Suppose it was fired from
_inside_?”

“From inside? But there was no one in the car but the Prime
Minister and Captain Daniels!”

“Exactly. And suppose it was Captain Daniels who fired the shot?”

“Captain Daniels? But why should he do such a thing?”

“To make it appear that an attempt had been made on the Prime
Minister’s life. To create a diversion. And then, in the confusion,
the kidnapping could be carried out more easily.”

“But Captain Daniels was also kidnapped!”

“Was he? Or did he just disappear? Remember, he was found some
time later, in the same wood where the car had been abandoned,
only slightly wounded.”

“But he was found again in France, gagged and bound!”

“Yes, so the telegram said. But who found him? The French police.
And who told them where to look? Perhaps someone who wanted them
to find him there.”

“But why?”

“To prove his innocence. To show that he, too, was a victim.”

“It’s incredible! You think Captain Daniels is the culprit?”

“I think it is very possible. But there is one thing that does not
fit in. If Captain Daniels and O’Murphy were in league with the
Germans, why did they kidnap the Prime Minister and then leave
him in a cottage in England? Why not take him to France at once?”

“But they did take him to France! He was kidnapped on the way to
the Commander-in-Chief’s guest house.”

“But he had already been kidnapped once in England! Remember, he
was found in a small cottage, two hours after the attack in the
lane.”

“Yes, but he was all right then. He went on to France as arranged.”

“Did he? Or was it someone else who went in his place?”

“Someone else? But who?”

“Someone who looked like him. Someone who could play the part.
The Prime Minister is a very well-known man, but in a closed car,
with his face bandaged——”

“Good heavens! You mean that the man who went to France was not
the Prime Minister at all?”

“It is a possibility. And if so, where is the real Prime Minister?”

“He must still be in England!”

“Exactly. And I think I know where he is.”

“Where?”

“In the house of Captain Daniels’ other aunt—Miss Daniels, at
Ascot!”

“But we searched that house!”

“Did you search it thoroughly? Did you look in every room? Even
the rooms of an invalid lady?”

Lord Estair and Mr. Dodge looked at each other in amazement.

“We must go there at once!” cried Mr. Dodge.

“Wait,” said Poirot. “We must be careful. If they suspect anything,
they may kill him. We must go quietly.”

We drove to Ascot in Lord Estair’s car. It was nearly midnight
when we arrived at the small, secluded house where Miss Daniels
lived. All was quiet and dark.

Poirot led the way to the back of the house. He found a window
that was not securely fastened, and in a few minutes we were
inside. We crept up the stairs, our hearts beating fast.

At the end of a long corridor, we saw a light shining under a door.
Poirot motioned us to be silent. He turned the handle gently, and
the door opened.

In the room, we saw a man lying on a bed, his face pale and
exhausted. It was the Prime Minister!

Standing by the bed was a woman. She turned as we entered, and
a look of terror came into her face. It was Mrs. Everard!

“Mrs. Everard!” I cried.

“So,” said Poirot, quietly. “It was you, madame. You and your
nephew, Captain Daniels.”

Mrs. Everard did not speak. She sank into a chair, her face buried
in her hands.

“But I don’t understand,” I said. “How did she get here? And where
is Captain Daniels?”

“Captain Daniels is in France, playing the part of the kidnapped
Prime Minister,” said Poirot. “It was a very clever plot. The
Prime Minister was kidnapped in England and brought here. Mrs.
Everard, who is not his aunt at all, but a German agent, took
charge of him. Meanwhile, Captain Daniels, who is a fine linguist
and a good actor, went to France in the Prime Minister’s place.
He was ‘kidnapped’ there, to make it appear that the Germans had
captured the real Prime Minister. And all the time, the real
Prime Minister was safe here in England, while the Germans were
using the fake kidnapping to try to force a premature peace.”

“But O’Murphy?”

“O’Murphy was also in the plot. He was the one who drove the car
into the lane and staged the ‘attack.’ He was rewarded with a
bullet in the shoulder to make it look real.”

“And Frau Bertha Ebenthal?”

“She was the one who organized the whole thing. She is the head
of the German spy ring in England.”

“It’s amazing!” I said. “But how did you know, Poirot?”

“It was the spot of grease, my friend. The spot of grease on my
grey suit. It reminded me that even the smallest detail can be
important. And when I heard that the Prime Minister’s face was
grazed by a bullet fired from _inside_ the car, I knew that
something was wrong. The rest was just a matter of following the
clues.”

Lord Estair stepped forward and took the Prime Minister’s hand.

“Thank God you are safe, sir!”

The Prime Minister smiled weakly. “I have to thank Monsieur Poirot
for that. He has saved England from a great catastrophe.”

Poirot bowed. “It was a pleasure, monsieur. And now, if you will
excuse me, I think I will go home. I have a little affair of a
charlady’s husband to attend to.”

And so, the Prime Minister was restored to his rightful place,
the German plot was foiled, and Hercule Poirot once again proved
that his “little grey cells” were equal to any challenge.

“It was at this point, which is a lonely and wooded spot, that the
shots were fired. One bullet shattered the window of the car and
grazed the Prime Minister’s cheek. The chauffeur, O’Murphy, at
once jammed on his brakes, and the car behind pulled up. The
detectives jumped out, but they found no one. Only a small
revolver was picked up in the bushes.”

“And what did the chauffeur, O’Murphy, have to say?”

“He says that he saw a man with a rifle among the trees. He
could not be more explicit than that.”

“And after that, the Prime Minister continued his journey?”

“Yes, he was slightly shaken, but he wouldn’t hear of any delay.
He went straight to Downing Street, where he had a light breakfast,
and then left at once for Victoria.”

“And you say that this O’Murphy is a Scotland Yard man?”

“Yes, he is one of our most trusted men.”

“And what of the secretary, Captain Daniels? Where was he when the
shots were fired?”

“He was sitting by the Prime Minister’s side. He immediately
threw himself in front of him, to shield him with his own body.”

“_Ah!_” said Poirot. “And then?”

“Then, as I have told you, the Prime Minister crossed to France.
The rest you know.”

“One more question, _milord_,” said Poirot. “Where did this Captain
Daniels live?”

“He had rooms in Westminster.”

“Does he know anyone in the neighbourhood?”

“The police have been making inquiries. They cannot find that he
had any friends there.”

“What of his aunts?”

“Mrs. Everard is a well-known lady, of unimpeachable character.
She is at present in London, and has been since yesterday. Miss
Daniels is at her home near Ascot.”

“One more thing, _milord_. Who is the Prime Minister’s doctor?”

“Sir J—— S——, the famous specialist.”

“He has seen the Prime Minister since the shooting?”

“No, not since. But he was at Downing Street this morning, I
believe, to see him before he left.”

“And he was satisfied with his condition?”

“The Prime Minister refused to see him.”

“_Ah!_ That is interesting.”

Lord Estair rose to his feet.

“Monsieur Poirot, I can tell you no more. Time is short. Every
moment that passes is a moment lost. We have given you all the
information we possess. Can you help us?”

Poirot looked at him steadily.

“I can try, _milord_. But I must have a free hand.”

“You shall have it.”

“Then I will begin at once. I should like to see the chauffeur,
O’Murphy, if that is possible.”

“He is in London. I will send him to you.”

“_Merci_, _milord_.”

The two men left the room.

Poirot turned to me.

“Hastings, my friend, we have a problem of the first magnitude.
The Prime Minister is missing—and the peace of Europe is at stake.”

“But how can they have kidnapped him?” I cried. “The thing is
preposterous!”

“Preposterous or not, it has been done. And now we must set to
work to find him.”

“Where shall we begin?”

“We will begin, Hastings, at the beginning. We will see this
O’Murphy.”

“But the police have already questioned him!”

“The police, Hastings, have not the ‘little grey cells.’ We shall
see what they can tell us.”

He sat down in his chair and began to polish his boots with a
piece of silk.

“One thing is certain, Hastings. The kidnapping of the Prime
Minister was a very clever piece of work. It was planned with
the greatest care. And it was carried out with the greatest
audacity. It is the work of a master mind.”

“You mean—a German agent?”

“Perhaps. But who is this master mind? That is what we have to
find out.”

The door opened and the landlady announced:

“Mr. O’Murphy, sir.”

A tall, broad-shouldered man with a keen, intelligent face
entered the room. He looked at us with a certain amount of
suspicion.

“Mr. O’Murphy?” said Poirot.

“Yes, sir.”

“Sit down, if you please. I have been asked by Lord Estair to
investigate the disappearance of the Prime Minister. I should like
to ask you a few questions.”

“I’ve told the police all I know, sir.”

“I am sure you have. But I should like to hear it from your own
lips. Now, tell me about the shooting affair this morning.”

O’Murphy repeated his story. It was much the same as the one we
had already heard.

“And you saw the man with the rifle?”

“Yes, sir. He was standing among the trees.”

“Could you describe him?”

“No, sir. It was very early, and the light wasn’t very good.
Besides, it all happened so quickly.”

“I see. And you are a Scotland Yard man?”

“Yes, sir.”

“And how long have you been in the service?”

“Ten years, sir.”

“And you have always been a trusted man?”

“I hope so, sir.”

“I am sure you have. Now, tell me about the journey to France.
You were the chauffeur?”

“Yes, sir. I drove the Prime Minister to Victoria.”

“And then?”

“Then I went back to the Yard, sir.”

“And you have not seen the Prime Minister since?”

“No, sir.”

“Thank you, O’Murphy. That will be all for the present.”

The man left the room.

Poirot looked at me.

“Well, Hastings, what do you think of him?”

“He seems a very straightforward fellow.”

“Perhaps. But did you notice one thing?”

“What?”

“He did not look me in the eye once during the whole interview.”

“Oh, that’s just his way, I expect.”

“Perhaps. But it is a way I do not like. Now, Hastings, we must
go to Downing Street.”

“Downing Street? Why?”

“Because I want to see the Prime Minister’s doctor.”

“But Lord Estair said he hadn’t seen him!”

“Exactly. That is why I want to see him.”

We went to Downing Street, and after a certain amount of delay,
we were shown into the Presence.

Sir J—— S—— was a tall, thin man with a tired, anxious face.

“Monsieur Poirot?” he said. “I have heard of you. What can I do
for you?”

“I have come to ask you about the Prime Minister, Sir J——.”

“I have not seen him since yesterday evening.”

“But I understand you were here this morning?”

“I was. But the Prime Minister refused to see me.”

“Why?”

“He said he was quite well, and that he didn’t want to be
bothered.”

“Did that surprise you?”

“Yes, it did. He is usually very careful about his health.”

“I see. And did you see anyone else?”

“I saw his secretary, Captain Daniels.”

“And what did he say?”

“He said the Prime Minister was very busy, and that he didn’t want
to be disturbed.”

“I see. Thank you, Sir J——. That is all I wanted to know.”

As we left Downing Street, Poirot turned to me.

“Well, Hastings, what do you make of that?”

“It seems very strange.”

“It is more than strange, Hastings. It is significant. Now, we
must go to Victoria.”

“Victoria? Why?”

“Because I want to see the stationmaster.”

“But what can he tell us?”

“He can tell us if the Prime Minister really did leave for
France.”

“But Lord Estair said he did!”

“Lord Estair was not there, Hastings. He only knows what he has
been told. I want to know for myself.”

We went to Victoria and saw the stationmaster.

“Yes,” he said, in answer to Poirot’s question. “The Prime
Minister left for France this morning. He was accompanied by his
secretary, Captain Daniels.”

“And you saw him yourself?”

“Yes, I saw him get into the train.”

“Did he look well?”

“He looked a bit tired, I thought. But he waved his hand to me
as the train went out.”

“I see. Thank you.”

As we walked away, Poirot said:

“Well, Hastings, that seems to settle that. The Prime Minister
did leave for London. Now, we must go to France.”

“France?”

“Yes. We must see this abandoned farm where Captain Daniels was
found.”

“But how are we going to get there?”

“Lord Estair will arrange that. He has given me a free hand.”

We went back to Poirot’s rooms, and he telephoned to Lord Estair.
Half an hour later, a car arrived to take us to the coast.

As we were driving along, Poirot said:

“Hastings, I have a little idea. A very little idea. But it may
be a good one.”

“What is it?”

“I want to find out more about this Captain Daniels. I want to
know where he lived, and who his friends were.”

“But Lord Estair said the police had already done that!”

“The police, Hastings, have not the ‘little grey cells.’ They
see, but they do not observe. I want to observe for myself.”

We arrived at the coast and were taken across the Channel in a
destroyer. At Boulogne, we were met by a car from G.H.Q.

“We want to go to the abandoned farm where Captain Daniels was
found,” said Poirot to the driver.

“Yes, sir.”

The drive took about an hour. The farm was a small, desolate-looking
place, situated in a lonely part of the country.

“This is it, sir,” said the driver, as he pulled up.

We got out and went into the house. It was empty and neglected.
In one of the rooms, we found a heap of straw, and some pieces
of rope.

“This is where they kept him, I suppose,” I said.

Poirot nodded. He was looking about him with a keen, searching
glance.

“Wait!” he cried. “What is this?”

He picked up a small object from the floor. It was a piece of
paper, crumpled and torn.

“What is it?” I asked.

“It is a piece of a letter, Hastings. Look!”

He smoothed it out on his hand. There were only a few words
visible:

“...at the usual place... Bertha...”

“Bertha!” I cried. “Who is Bertha?”

“That is what we have to find out, Hastings. That is what we have
to find out.”

He put the piece of paper in his pocket.

“Now, Hastings, we must go back to London.”

“Back to London? But we’ve only just got here!”

“I have seen all I want to see, Hastings. The rest is in London.”

We returned to London as quickly as we could. It was late at
night when we arrived at Poirot’s rooms.

“Now, Hastings,” said Poirot, “we must go to Hampstead.”

“Hampstead? At this time of night?”

“Yes. We must see Mrs. Everard.”

“But she’ll be in bed!”

“That cannot be helped. This is a matter of life and death.”

We took a taxi to Hampstead and found Mrs. Everard’s house. It was
a large, comfortable-looking house, standing in its own grounds.

Poirot rang the bell. After a few minutes, a servant appeared.

“I must see Mrs. Everard,” said Poirot.

“She’s in bed, sir.”

“Tell her it is a matter of the greatest importance. Tell her it
concerns her nephew, Captain Daniels.”

The servant disappeared, and a few minutes later, Mrs. Everard
herself appeared. She was a tall, elegant-looking woman, with a
charming manner.

“What is it?” she asked. “What has happened to my nephew?”

“He has been found, madame,” said Poirot. “He is safe.”

“Oh, thank God!” she cried. “I have been so worried about him!”

“I can well understand that, madame. But I should like to ask you
a few questions, if I may.”

“Of course. Won’t you come in?”

She led us into a small sitting-room.

“Now, what is it you want to know?”

“I want to know about your nephew’s friends, madame. Do you know
anyone of the name of Bertha?”

Mrs. Everard shook her head.

“Bertha? No, I don’t think so. Wait! There was a German girl he
knew once, before the war. Her name was Bertha—Bertha Ebenthal, I
think.”

“Bertha Ebenthal!” cried Poirot. “And where is she now?”

“I have no idea. I haven’t heard of her for years.”

“I see. And do you know anything of a Miss Daniels, who lives at
Ascot?”

“She is my sister-in-law. She is a very quiet, retiring person.
She doesn’t see many people.”

“I see. Thank you, Mrs. Everard. That is all I wanted to know.”

As we left the house, Poirot was very quiet.

“Well, Hastings,” he said, at last. “The plot thickens.”

“What do you mean?”

“Bertha Ebenthal! I have heard that name before. She is one of
the most dangerous German agents in Europe.”

“Good heavens! And she is a friend of Captain Daniels?”

“It would seem so. And now, Hastings, we must go to Ascot.”

“To Ascot? Now?”

“Yes. We must see Miss Daniels.”

“But it’s after midnight!”

“That cannot be helped. We have no time to lose.”

We took another taxi and drove to Ascot. It was a long drive, and
I fell asleep on the way. I was awakened by Poirot shaking my
arm.

“We are here, Hastings. Wake up!”

We got out of the taxi and went up to the house. It was a small,
unpretentious-looking cottage.

Poirot rang the bell. There was no answer. He rang again. Still
no answer.

“She must be a very sound sleeper,” I said.

“Perhaps. Or perhaps she is not here.”

He tried the door. it was locked. He went round to the back of the
house and tried the window. It was also locked.

“Wait!” he cried. “What is this?”

He pointed to a small piece of paper that was stuck to the door.

“What is it?” I asked.

He pulled it off and read it.

“‘Gone away for a few days. Will be back on Monday.’”

“Well, that’s that,” I said. “She’s not here.”

“Perhaps. But let us see if we can get in.”

He took a small tool from his pocket and began to work on the
lock. In a few minutes, the door opened.

“Poirot!” I cried. “You’re breaking the law!”

“The law, Hastings, must sometimes be broken in the interests of
justice. Come!”

We went into the house. It was small and simply furnished. There
was no one there.

Poirot began to search the rooms. He went through the drawers and
the cupboards, but he found nothing of interest.

“Wait!” he cried. “What is this?”

He was standing in front of a small desk in the corner of the
sitting-room. He had found a small, leather-bound diary.

He opened it and began to read.

“‘Monday, 10th. Met B. at the usual place. Everything is ready.
Tuesday, 11th. D. is coming down to-night. We must be careful.
Wednesday, 12th. The day has come. God grant we succeed.’”

“The day has come!” I cried. “That was yesterday!”

“Exactly, Hastings. And who is ‘B.’? Bertha Ebenthal, I have no
doubt. And ‘D.’? Captain Daniels, of course.”

“Then they are all in it together!”

“It would seem so. But where is the Prime Minister?”

“That is what we have to find out.”

Poirot was looking at the diary again.

“Wait! There is something else. ‘Thursday, 13th. All is well. He
is safe at the farm.’”

“The farm!” I cried. “But we’ve been to the farm! He wasn’t there!”

“Perhaps it was not the same farm, Hastings. Perhaps there is
another farm.”

He began to search the desk again. In a small drawer, he found a
map of the neighborhood.

“Look, Hastings! Here is the house. And here, a few miles away, is
a farm. It is called ‘The Grey Farm.’”

“Let’s go there at once!” I cried.

“Yes, Hastings. But we must be careful. If they are there, they
will be armed.”

We went back to the taxi and told the driver to take us to ‘The
Grey Farm.’

As we were driving along, Poirot was very quiet. He seemed to be
thinking deeply.

“Hastings,” he said, at last. “I have a little theory. A very
little theory. But it may be the right one.”

“What is it?”

“I believe that the Prime Minister was never kidnapped at all.”

“What? But Lord Estair said he was!”

“Lord Estair only knows what he has been told. I believe that the
Prime Minister is still in England.”

“In England? But the stationmaster saw him leave!”

“He saw someone who looked like the Prime Minister, Hastings.
That is all.”

“But who could it have been?”

“That is what we have to find out. But here we are.”

The taxi pulled up in front of a small, lonely-looking farm. There
were no lights in the windows.

“Wait here,” said Poirot to the driver. “And if you hear any
trouble, go for the police.”

“Yes, sir.”

We got out and went up to the house. Poirot tried the door. It
was unlocked. We went in.

The house was dark and silent. We crept along the passage, our
hearts beating fast.

Suddenly, we heard a sound. It was the sound of voices, coming
from a room at the end of the passage.

We crept up to the door and listened.

“I tell you, it’s the only way!” said a man’s voice. “We must get
him out of the country at once!”

“But how?” said a woman’s voice. “The police are everywhere!”

“We’ll find a way. We must!”

Poirot threw open the door.

“Good evening, messieurs et dames!” he said.

The people in the room started up in alarm. There were three of
them—a man and two women.

The man was Captain Daniels. One of the women was a tall, dark
woman with a hard, cruel face. The other was a small,
insignificant-looking woman.

“Captain Daniels!” I cried.

“Who are you?” he demanded. “What do you want?”

“I am Hercule Poirot,” said my friend. “And I have come to find the
Prime Minister.”

“The Prime Minister?” said Daniels, with a laugh. “You won’t find
him here!”

“We shall see,” said Poirot.

He turned to the dark woman.

“And you, I believe, are Frau Bertha Ebenthal?”

The woman’s face hardened.

“What if I am?” she said.

“And this lady?” said Poirot, pointing to the other woman.

“That is my sister-in-law, Miss Daniels,” said Mrs. Everard, who
had suddenly appeared in the doorway.

“Mrs. Everard!” I cried. “What are you doing here?”

“I followed you,” she said. “I knew you were up to something.”

“And you were right, madame,” said Poirot. “Now, where is the
Prime Minister?”

“I tell you, he’s not here!” cried Daniels.

“We shall see,” said Poirot again.

He began to search the room. In a corner, he found a door. He
tried it, but it was locked.

“Open this door!” he commanded.

“I won’t!” said Daniels.

Poirot turned to me.

“Hastings, help me!”

We threw ourselves against the door. It gave way with a crash.

We rushed into the room beyond. It was a small, meanly furnished
bedroom. On the bed lay a man, bound and gagged.

It was the Prime Minister!

“Thank God!” I cried. “We’ve found him!”

We quickly untied his bonds and removed the gag.

“Are you all right, sir?” I asked.

The Prime Minister nodded. He looked very pale and shaken.

“I’m—I’m all right,” he gasped. “Thank you.”

“Now, Monsieur Poirot,” said the Prime Minister, after he had
recovered a little. “How did you find me?”

“It was not difficult, monsieur,” said Poirot. “Once I had the
clue of the spot of grease.”

“The spot of grease?” I cried. “What on earth do you mean?”

“I will explain everything later, Hastings. For now, we must get
the Prime Minister to a place of safety.”

We took the Prime Minister back to London in the taxi. Lord
Estair and Mr. Dodge were waiting for us at Downing Street.

“You’ve found him!” cried Lord Estair. “Thank God!”

“Monsieur Poirot, we can never thank you enough,” said Mr. Dodge.

“It was nothing,” said Poirot. “A mere trifle.”

“And now, Monsieur Poirot, perhaps you will explain how you did
it?” said the Prime Minister.

“With pleasure, monsieur.”

Poirot sat down and began his story.

“It all began with the shooting affair this morning. I was struck
by one thing—the fact that the Prime Minister refused to see his
doctor.”

“But I told you, I was quite well!” said the Prime Minister.

“Exactly. But that was not like you, monsieur. You are usually
very careful about your health. That was the first clue.”

“The second clue was the chauffeur, O’Murphy. He did not look me
in the eye. That is always a bad sign.”

“The third clue was the piece of paper I found at the abandoned
farm in France. It had the name ‘Bertha’ on it. I knew that name.
Bertha Ebenthal is a well-known German agent.”

“The fourth clue was the diary I found at Miss Daniels’ house in
Ascot. It told me that something was planned for Wednesday—the
day of the Prime Minister’s disappearance.”

“But how did you know I was at ‘The Grey Farm’?” asked the Prime
Minister.

“That was the most difficult part, monsieur. I had to find a farm
that was near to Ascot, and yet lonely enough to be a good hiding
place. I found it on a map in Miss Daniels’ desk.”

“But what about the spot of grease?” I asked.

“Ah, the spot of grease! That was the most important clue of all.
You see, Hastings, when I was mopping my grey suit, I noticed a
spot of grease on it. It was a very small spot, but it was there.”

“But what has that got to do with it?”

“Everything, Hastings. You see, the Prime Minister is a very
careful man. He would never have a spot of grease on his clothes.
And yet, when I saw him at Victoria, he had a spot of grease on his
coat. That told me that it was not the real Prime Minister!”

“Good heavens!” I cried. “Then who was it?”

“It was an actor, Hastings. A man who had been trained to look
and act like the Prime Minister. He was part of the plot to kidnap
the real Prime Minister and prevent him from attending the
Conference.”

“And who was the real culprit?” asked Lord Estair.

Poirot looked at the four suspects who were standing in the room.

“The real culprit,” he said, “is—Captain Daniels!”

“Captain Daniels!” I cried. “But why?”

“Because he is a German agent, Hastings. He has been working for
them for years. He was the one who planned the kidnapping, and
he was the one who carried it out.”

“And what about the others?” asked Mr. Dodge.

“They were all in it, too,” said Poirot. “O’Murphy was bribed to
help with the kidnapping. Mrs. Everard and Miss Daniels were
working with Captain Daniels. And Frau Bertha Ebenthal was the
one who was behind it all.”

“Well, Monsieur Poirot,” said the Prime Minister. “You have
saved England. We can never thank you enough.”

“It was a pleasure, monsieur,” said Poirot. “And now, if you will
excuse me, I think I will go and have a little sleep. It has been
a long day.”

And with a bow, he left the room.

The end.

“At the corner, then, they found a small motor-car drawn across
the road. It was empty. O’Murphy pulled up, and at that moment,
a shot was fired from behind a hedge. It was a marvellous escape,
as I have told you. The bullet grazed the Prime Minister’s cheek,
missing his brain by less than half an inch. The car which followed
had been temporarily stopped by a puncture, and only came up three
minutes later. They found the Premier and Captain Daniels in the
road. The car across the way had vanished. They started in
pursuit, but without success.”

“And the Prime Minister?”

“He was very cool. He insisted on proceeding to London. He had his
cheek bandaged and went at once to a conference at Downing Street.”

“_Tiens!_ And the chauffeur, O’Murphy?”

“He appeared to be much upset by his failure to protect the Prime
Minister. He has since disappeared.”

“Disappeared?”

“Yes. He went to his home this afternoon, and has not been seen
since. The police are searching for him.”

“_Très curieux!_” said Poirot. “And the Prime Minister?”

“He crossed to France as I have told you. He was to have reached
G.H.Q. for dinner. But, as I have told you, he never arrived. His
secretary, Daniels, was found this evening, as I have said, in an
abandoned farm. But of the Prime Minister—not a trace!”

Poirot had been thinking deeply. At last he looked up.

“Messieurs,” he said, “I will do my best. But I tell you frankly
that I have very little hope. If the Prime Minister is still
alive——”

“You think he may be dead?” cried Lord Estair.

“If he were dead, his body would have been found. No, I think he
is alive. But where? That is the question. The time is short—very
short. To-morrow evening—at nine o’clock! It is a race against
time!”

“And you think——?”

“I think,” said Poirot, “that there are many things which are not
yet clear. But, at least, I have a starting-point. Captain Daniels
and his aunts—the chauffeur, O’Murphy—and the Prime Minister
himself. It is a beginning.”

“The car followed—but at a distance. When it arrived at the curve,
the Prime Minister’s car was no longer in sight. A hundred yards
farther on they came across it. It was standing at the side of the
road. The Prime Minister, Captain Daniels, and the chauffeur,
O’Murphy, were all there. The chauffeur was crouched on the ground,
groaning. He had been struck on the head with a heavy stone.
Captain Daniels had also been wounded on the temple. It appeared
that as they were turning the corner, a man stepped out into the
road and fired. The bullet shattered the window of the car, and,
as it happened, grazed the Prime Minister’s cheek. The car came to
a standstill, and the three men jumped out to pursue the
assailant. He fled into the thick woods at the side of the road,
where they followed him. But he escaped.”

“And it was then that they were attacked?”

“Yes. They were all stunned, and then left there. The car was
undamaged, and the chauffeur, although badly shaken, was able to
drive back to London. There the wound of the Prime Minister was
attended to. It was not serious, and he insisted on proceeding
at once on his journey to France.”

“And what of the assailant?”

“Oh, he has been caught. It was a man of the name of Karl von
Bismark. He is an exceptionally clever German agent. He was
arrested within a few hours of the occurrence.”

“You are sure of his identity?”

“Oh, quite. He has been under observation for some time.”

“And yet he was allowed to make this attempt on the Prime
Minister’s life?”

Lord Estair’s face was very grave. “I cannot defend the police.
They seem to have been extremely lax. However, that is not the
point. The point is that the Prime Minister has disappeared, and
that we have less than twenty-four hours in which to find him.”

Poirot’s eyes were shut. “Let me see. The Prime Minister was
attacked in England this morning. He crossed to France, and was
kidnapped between Boulogne and G.H.Q. That is the position?”

Lord Estair nodded.

“The kidnapping—was it at any particular spot?”

“Yes. At a small village called ——. It is about halfway between
Boulogne and the Front.”

“Wait a moment! I have a map here.”

Poirot went to a shelf and returned with a large-scale map of
Northern France. He spread it out on the table and studied it for
a few moments.

“Here is the village of ——. It is on the main road. The Prime
Minister’s car would pass through it. Now, tell me, _milord_, what
of the Prime Minister’s wound? Was it dressed in London?”

“Yes. By a surgeon from the War Office.”

“And he was able to travel?”

“He was very much shaken, but he insisted on going. He is a man
of iron will.”

“And what of the others? Captain Daniels and the chauffeur,
O’Murphy?”

“They also were wounded, but were not incapacitated. They went
with the Prime Minister to France.”

“I see. Now, _milord_, I will tell you what I can do. I can give
you no promise, but I will do my best. I should like to see the
chauffeur, O’Murphy, and I should like to see the surgeon who
dressed the Prime Minister’s wound.”

“Certainly. They are both at your disposal. O’Murphy is at
Scotland Yard.”

“I will go there at once.”

“And the surgeon?”

“I will send him to you.”

“One thing more. Is there any other person who might be
suspected?”

“There is a woman—a Frau Bertha Ebenthal. She is a very dangerous
German agent, and we have reason to believe that she is in England
at the present moment. But we have no clue to her whereabouts.”

“I see. Well, _milord_, I have no more to ask. I will start at
once.”

“God bless you, Monsieur Poirot! We leave the matter in your
hands.”

The two Ministers withdrew, and Poirot turned to me.

“Hastings, we must be quick! There is not a moment to lose. I must
see the chauffeur first.”

We drove to Scotland Yard. O’Murphy was a tall, fine-looking man,
with a somewhat stolid expression. He told his story clearly
enough. He had been driving the Prime Minister’s car, and when
they came to the curve in the road, he saw a man standing there
with a rifle. The man fired, and the bullet shattered the window
of the car. He pulled up at once, and they all jumped out. The
man ran into the wood, and they followed him. He, O’Murphy, was
the first to reach him, and was just about to seize him when he
was struck on the back of the head. He remembered nothing more
until he found himself being revived with brandy.

Poirot listened attentively. “And you saw the man’s face?”

“Yes, sir. It was a dark, foreign-looking face.”

“You would know it again?”

“Oh, yes, sir.”

“And the Prime Minister? He was not much hurt?”

“No, sir. Just a scratch on the cheek.”

“And Captain Daniels?”

“He was hit on the temple, sir. He seemed a bit dazed for a time.”

“I see. Thank you, O’Murphy. That will do.”

As we were leaving, Poirot turned to the detective who had
accompanied us.

“I should like to see the man who was arrested—Karl von Bismark.”

“Certainly, sir. He’s in a cell here.”

We were taken to a small, cell-like room, where a dark,
determined-looking man was sitting. He looked up as we entered.

“This is the man?” asked Poirot.

“Yes, sir.”

Poirot looked at him for a moment in silence. Then he turned away.

“Thank you. I have seen enough.”

As we were driving back to Poirot’s rooms, I asked him what he
thought of it all.

“It is a very strange affair, Hastings. A very strange affair.
There are things about it that I do not understand.”

“But surely it is simple enough? The German agents have kidnapped
the Prime Minister to prevent him from attending the Conference.”

“Yes, yes—that is the obvious explanation. But there are small
details—things that do not fit in.”

“What things?”

“For one thing, why did they try to shoot him first? If they
wanted to kidnap him, why did they not do so at once? And then,
the kidnapping itself—it was so well-planned, so daring. And yet,
they have not found the Prime Minister’s body. Why not?”

“Perhaps they are keeping him alive as a hostage?”

“Perhaps. But it is not like the Germans. They are not usually so
considerate.”

When we arrived at Poirot’s rooms, we found the surgeon waiting
for us. He was a tall, professional-looking man.

“I have come at the request of Lord Estair,” he said. “I
understand you wish to hear about the Prime Minister’s wound?”

“If you please, monsieur.”

“It was a very slight affair—just a graze on the cheek. I dressed
it and applied a small bandage. It was really nothing.”

“And the Prime Minister? How did he seem?”

“He was naturally a good deal shaken. He is not a young man, and
the shock must have been considerable. But he was quite determined
to go to France.”

“I see. And the other two—Captain Daniels and the chauffeur?”

“They had both received blows on the head. Captain Daniels was
suffering from a slight concussion, and the chauffeur was also
a good deal dazed. But there was nothing serious in either case.”

“Thank you, monsieur. You have been most kind.”

When the surgeon had gone, Poirot sat for a long time in silence.
His eyes were closed, and he seemed to be deep in thought. At last
he opened them and looked at me.

“Hastings, I have a little idea. A very little idea. But it may
lead to something. We must go to Hampstead.”

“To Hampstead? Why?”

“To see Mrs. Everard, the aunt of Captain Daniels.”

“But what can she tell us?”

“That is what we are going to find out.”

We took a taxi to Hampstead, and after some difficulty found the
house. It was a small, neat-looking villa. We were shown into a
small drawing-room, and in a few minutes Mrs. Everard appeared.
She was a pleasant-looking woman of middle age.

“I am Monsieur Poirot,” said my friend, with a bow. “I have come
to ask you a few questions about your nephew, Captain Daniels.”

Mrs. Everard looked surprised. “About my nephew? Has anything
happened to him?”

“He has been involved in a very serious affair. But tell me,
madame, have you seen him lately?”

“Not for some weeks. He is very busy, you know.”

“He has not been here to-day?”

“To-day? No.”

“And you have had no message from him?”

“None at all.”

Poirot looked round the room. “You have a very charming house,
madame.”

“Thank you. I am very fond of it.”

“And you live here alone?”

“Yes, with my two servants.”

“I see. Well, madame, I will not detain you any longer. Thank you
for your kindness.”

As we were walking away from the house, I looked at Poirot.

“Well?”

“Well, Hastings, what do you think of Mrs. Everard?”

“She seems a very pleasant woman. But I don’t see how she can
help us.”

“Perhaps not. But did you notice the photograph on the mantelpiece?”

“No. Which one?”

“The one of a young man in uniform. It was Captain Daniels.”

“Was it? I didn’t notice it.”

“And did you notice the other photograph—the one of a lady?”

“No.”

“That, Hastings, was Frau Bertha Ebenthal.”

“What?”

“Yes. I recognized it at once. It is a very good likeness.”

“Then Mrs. Everard is in league with the German agents!”

“It would seem so. But we must not jump to conclusions. There is
another aunt, remember—the one who lives near Ascot. We must go
there at once.”

We drove to the station and took a train to Ascot. It was late
when we arrived, but we managed to find a fly to take us to Miss
Daniels’ house. It was a small cottage on the edge of the heath.
We were told that Miss Daniels was not at home, but that she was
expected back shortly.

“We will wait,” said Poirot.

We were shown into a small, poorly furnished room. Poirot began
to prowl about, looking at everything with his keen eyes.
Suddenly he stopped in front of a small table on which was a
pile of newspapers. He turned them over rapidly.

“Aha! What have we here?”

He held up a newspaper. It was a German one.

“What does that mean?” I asked.

“It means, Hastings, that Miss Daniels also has German sympathies.”

At that moment the door opened, and a tall, thin woman entered.
She looked at us with suspicion.

“Who are you? What do you want?”

“I am Monsieur Poirot. I have come to see you about your nephew,
Captain Daniels.”

The woman’s face changed. “My nephew? What about him?”

“He is in great danger. I must find him at once. Do you know
where he is?”

“I know nothing about him. I haven’t seen him for months.”

“Is that the truth, mademoiselle?”

“Of course it’s the truth! Why should I lie to you?”

Poirot looked at her for a moment. “I think you are lying,
mademoiselle. I think you know very well where he is.”

The woman’s eyes flashed. “How dare you! Leave my house at once!”

“Very well, mademoiselle. We will go. But I warn you—if anything
happens to the Prime Minister, you will be held responsible.”

We left the house and walked back towards the station.

“Well, Poirot, what now?”

“Now, Hastings, we must go back to London. There is nothing more
to be done here.”

“But we have found out nothing!”

“On the contrary, we have found out a great deal. We know that
both of Captain Daniels’ aunts have German sympathies. That is
a very important fact.”

“But it doesn’t tell us where the Prime Minister is!”

“No, but it gives us a clue. Now, Hastings, I must think. I must
think very hard.”

When we got back to London, Poirot went straight to his room and
sat down in his big chair. He remained there for a long time,
his eyes closed, his face set in a look of deep concentration. I
did not disturb him. I knew that his wonderful brain was at work,
and that he was pieceing together the fragments of the puzzle.

Suddenly he jumped up. “I have it, Hastings! I have it!”

“What? You know where the Prime Minister is?”

“I think so. But we must be quick! There is not a moment to lose.
We must go to the Prime Minister’s house.”

“But he’s not there! He’s in France—or at least he was.”

“Never mind, Hastings. Follow me!”

We took a taxi to the Prime Minister’s house. It was a large,
imposing-looking building. Poirot rang the bell, and the door was
opened by a footman.

“I must see the Prime Minister at once,” said Poirot.

“The Prime Minister is not at home, sir.”

“I know that. But I must see his secretary—the one who is here.”

“I will see if he is in, sir.”

The footman disappeared, and in a few minutes returned. “Mr.
Dodge is here, sir. Will you come this way?”

We were shown into a large, well-furnished room where Mr. Dodge
was sitting at a desk.

The government does not know whether to hope or to despair. They hesitate to act. And in this great crisis of the Conference, it is precisely that hesitation which the enemy desires. But there is more, Hastings. Why the shooting first, and then the kidnapping? It is not logical. It lacks the—how you say—symmetry. If you wish to kill a man, you do not then take the immense trouble to kidnap him. No, there is something here that does not ring true. It offends the little grey cells.”

“Because uncertainty creates panic. That is one reason. Were the
Prime Minister dead, it would be a terrible calamity, but the
situation would have to be faced. But now you have paralysis. Will
the Prime Minister reappear, or will he not? Is he dead or alive?
Nobody knows, and until they know nothing definite can be done.
And, as I tell you, uncertainty breeds panic, which is what _les
Boches_ are playing for. Then, again, if the kidnappers are holding
him secretly somewhere, they have the advantage of being able to
make terms with both sides. The German Government is not a liberal
paymaster, as a rule, but no doubt they can be made to disgorge
substantial remittances in such a case as this. Thirdly, they run
no risk of the hangman’s rope. Oh, decidedly, kidnapping is their
affair.”

“Then, if that is so, why should they first try to shoot him?”

“And yet—Daniels was with him in France, when he was kidnapped
there. Daniels, too, was the one who, when the car was found,
declared that he had been gagged and bound. Is it not possible that
he was the traitor in both cases? That he was the one who gave the
signal to the masked men? And that it was also he who gave the
information which enabled the second kidnapping to take place?”

“But Lord Estair says that Daniels is an extremely able man,” I
objected.

“No doubt—no doubt! But even an able man may have his price.”

“And O’Murphy?”

“_Ah, O’Murphy!_ I do not know what to make of him. He is the most
mysterious of all. Where is he?”

“Perhaps he was in it too,” I said. “He might have been bribed.”

“Wait—wait! We shall see. It is all so dark, so very dark.”

Poirot’s face was very grave as we left the house. He seemed
strangely depressed.

“A special train,” he murmured. “The Ministers have indeed confidence
in me. But will it avail anything? Can I find him in time? I do not
know.”

He sighed, and shook his head.

“This way, Monsieur Poirot! The car is waiting!”

A young officer in uniform, with a keen, alert face, stepped
forward to meet us.

“I am Captain Miller, sent by the War Office. This is Detective
Inspector Japp, from Scotland Yard. At your service, sir.”

Poirot bowed, and we all got into the car.

“To Charing Cross!” said Captain Miller.

As we drove, Poirot began to question Japp.

“I suppose you have been working on this case since this morning,
Inspector?”

“Yes, Monsieur Poirot. We’ve been at it ever since the news reached
the Yard.”

“And you have found—what?”

“Nothing, sir. Not a trace. We have scoured the country for the
missing car, but so far without result.”

“And what about O’Murphy?”

“We’ve found no trace of him, either. He seems to have vanished
into thin air.”

“And the Prime Minister’s wound? Was it a serious one?”

“No, sir—just a scratch, as he said. But it might easily have been
fatal.”

“What about the car?”

“The car was found outside a small restaurant in Soho, as Lord
Estair told you. There was no one in it. It had evidently been
standing there for some time.”

“Was there anything in it?”

“Nothing but a small piece of paper, with some words in German
written on it.”

“What were they?”

“‘_Der Tag_.’ That’s all.”

“The Day! A well-known German toast. It seems almost too simple,
does it not? And where is this restaurant?”

“It is in a small street off Wardour Street. It’s a place where
German agents are known to meet. We have had it under observation
for some time.”

“And you have found nothing there?”

“No, sir. We’ve searched the place from top to bottom, but there’s
nothing to be found.”

Poirot sat in silence for some time, his brow furrowed in thought.

“It is very strange,” he said at last. “The whole thing is most
strange. There is something here that I do not understand—something
that does not fit.”

“What is that, sir?” asked Japp.

“The first attempt—the shooting. Why should they try to shoot him?
If they wanted to prevent him from attending the Conference, why
not kidnap him at once? Why run the risk of killing him, when his
death would only simplify matters for the English Government? No,
there is something there—something that is not as it should be.”

He broke off as the car drew up at Charing Cross.

“The special is waiting, sir,” said Captain Miller.

We hurried onto the platform and into the train. As we started,
Poirot turned to Japp.

“Inspector, I should like to ask you one or two more questions.
About this Mrs. Everard—the aunt of Captain Daniels. What do you
know of her?”

“Not much, sir. She’s a widow, lives in a small house at Hampstead.
She’s quite a respectable woman, as far as we know. We’ve had her
under observation, of course, but there’s nothing against her.”

“And the other aunt—Miss Daniels, who lives near Ascot?”

“She’s a middle-aged lady—very quiet and retired. She’s lived there
for years. We can’t find anything against her, either.”

“_Tiens!_ It is very strange. And what about the Prime Minister’s
household? Is there anyone there who might be a German agent?”

“We’ve been through them all, sir, but there’s no one we can
suspect. Most of them have been with him for years.”

“And Captain Daniels himself? You say he is a fine linguist. Does
he speak German?”

“Yes, sir, perfectly. He was educated in Germany, I believe.”

“_Aha!_ Now we are getting to it! Educated in Germany, speaks
German perfectly—and he is the Prime Minister’s secretary! It is
very suggestive, is it not?”

“It is, sir. But, as Lord Estair said, there’s no proof against
him.”

“No, there is no proof. But there is suspicion—much suspicion. And
O’Murphy? What about him? Did he speak German?”

“No, sir. He was just an ordinary chauffeur. A very good one, I
believe, but nothing more.”

“And he was a C.I.D. man? That is very strange. Why should a C.I.D.
man be a chauffeur?”

“It’s a common thing, sir, when someone’s life is in danger. The
police like to have one of their own men as close to the person as
possible.”

“I see. And you have found no trace of him?”

“None at all, sir.”

Poirot relapsed into silence. He sat with his eyes closed, and I
knew that he was thinking deeply.

Presently he opened them and looked at me.

“Hastings, my friend, what do you think of all this?”

“I don’t know what to think, Poirot. It’s all so confused and
mysterious.”

“It is, indeed. But there is a thread—a tiny thread—if only I could
find it. Let us go over the facts again. First, the shooting. A
clumsy, theatrical business, which fails. Then, the crossing to
France. The Prime Minister is met at Boulogne by a bogus car and a
bogus A.D.C. He is driven away—and disappears. The real car is found,
with the chauffeur and the A.D.C. bound and gagged. Later, the
bogus car is found, with the secretary, Daniels, also bound and
gagged. But the Prime Minister is gone. And, in the meantime, in
London, the Prime Minister’s own car is found outside a German
rendezvous, and the chauffeur, O’Murphy, has vanished. It is a
pretty problem, is it not?”

“It is, indeed,” I agreed.

“There are several possibilities,” continued Poirot. “First, that
Daniels is the traitor. He may have been in league with the German
agents all along. He may have given them the information they needed
for both attempts. In that case, his being found bound and gagged
was merely a ruse to avert suspicion.”

“But what about O’Murphy?” I asked.

“Ah, O’Murphy! He may also be a traitor. Or he may have been
kidnapped by the German agents when he was found outside the Soho
restaurant. Or—and this is a possibility that must not be
overlooked—he may have been murdered.”

“But why should they murder him?”

“Because he knew too much, perhaps. Or because he was in the way.”

“And the Prime Minister? Where do you think he is?”

“That is the question. He may be in France—or he may be in England.”

“In England? But he was seen to go on board the destroyer at Dover.”

“He was seen to go on board, yes. But did he ever reach France?”

“But Lord Estair said he was met at Boulogne.”

“He was met by a bogus car and a bogus A.D.C., yes. But was it
really the Prime Minister who was in that car? Remember, he had
his head bandaged. It would be easy for someone to impersonate him.”

“But who?”

“That I do not know. But it is a possibility.”

He fell silent again, and did not speak until we reached Dover.

As we went on board the destroyer, Poirot’s face was still very
grave.

“It is a race against time, Hastings,” he said. “A race against
time. And I fear—I much fear—that we are losing.”

We reached Boulogne in the early hours of the morning. A car was
waiting for us, and we were driven at once to the place where the
bogus car had been found.

It was a lonely spot, a few miles from the town. The car—a large,
powerful one—was still there, guarded by a couple of French
gendarmes.

Poirot examined it with the greatest care. He looked at the tires,
the engine, the interior. He even peered under the seats.

“Nothing,” he said at last, with a sigh. “Nothing at all.”

He turned to the gendarmes.

“You have found nothing else? No papers? No clues of any kind?”

“Nothing, monsieur. We have searched everywhere.”

Poirot nodded. He looked round at the desolate landscape.

“And the farm where the secretary was found? How far is it from
here?”

“About two miles, monsieur.”

“Let us go there.”

We got into our car and were driven to the farm. it was a small,
dilapidated building, standing in the middle of a field.

Inside, we found a couple of English detectives. They had been
searching the place, but so far had found nothing.

“And the secretary—Captain Daniels? Where is he?” asked Poirot.

“He’s been taken to the hospital at C——, sir. He was pretty badly
knocked about.”

“I must see him,” said Poirot. “It is important.”

We drove to the hospital, and after some delay were allowed to see
Daniels.

He was lying in bed, his head bandaged, and his face pale. He looked
very weak and exhausted.

“Monsieur Daniels,” said Poirot, “I am Hercule Poirot. I have been
sent by Lord Estair to find the Prime Minister. Can you tell me
anything that might help us?”

Daniels shook his head feebly.

“I’m afraid not. It all happened so quickly. One minute we were
driving along, and the next—something was pressed against my face,
and I lost consciousness. When I came to, I was in that farm, tied
up and gagged. That’s all I know.”

“And the Prime Minister? Did you see what happened to him?”

“No. He was sitting beside me, but I didn't see anything. I was
attacked from behind.”

“From behind? But you were in a closed car!”

“Yes, but someone must have been hiding in the back. I don't know
how they got there.”

Poirot’s eyes narrowed.

“I see. And you did not see the men who attacked you?”

“No. It was all over in a second.”

Poirot thanked him and we left the hospital.

“Well, Poirot?” I asked as we got into the car. “What do you think?”

“I think, Hastings, that Captain Daniels is a very clever man.
A very clever man indeed.”

“You think he’s lying?”

“I am sure of it. His story is full of holes. How could someone be
hiding in the back of a closed car without being noticed? It is
impossible. And why should they attack him from behind, when they
could just as easily have shot him from the side of the road, as
they tried to do in England?”

“Then you think he’s the traitor?”

“I am almost certain of it. But we still have no proof. And we still
do not know where the Prime Minister is.”

He sat in silence for a few minutes, his face set and determined.

“Hastings,” he said at last, “we must go back to England.”

“Back to England? But the Prime Minister is in France!”

“Is he? I am not so sure. In any case, there is something in England
that I must find out. Something that I have overlooked.”

“But what about the Conference? It starts in less than twelve
hours!”

“I know—I know. But we can do nothing here. The French police and
the military are doing all they can. If the Prime Minister is in
France, they will find him. But I have a feeling—a very strong
feeling—that he is not in France at all.”

“Then where is he?”

“That is what I am going to find out. Come, we must hurry! We have
no time to lose!”

We reached London in the afternoon. Poirot at once drove to the
War Office, where he had a long interview with Lord Estair and Mr.
Dodge.

When he came out, his face was still grave.

“Well?” I asked. “Any news?”

“None. The Prime Minister is still missing. The Conference is to
start in three hours’ time. If he is not there, it will be a
disaster.”

“And what are you going to do?”

“I am going to visit Mrs. Everard, the aunt of Captain Daniels.”

“Mrs. Everard? But what do you expect to find there?”

“I do not know. but it is a chance—a small chance, but the only
one we have.”

We drove to Hampstead and found the house. It was a small,
unpretentious villa in a quiet street.

A maid opened the door and showed us into a small sitting-room.
Presently Mrs. Everard appeared. She was a pleasant-looking,
middle-aged woman, with a kind face and a gentle manner.

“Monsieur Poirot?” she said. “I have heard of you. What can I do
for you?”

“Madame,” said Poirot, “I am here on a very serious matter. It
concerns your nephew, Captain Daniels.”

Mrs. Everard’s face went pale.

“My nephew? Is anything wrong? Has anything happened to him?”

“He has been injured, madame, but he is not in danger. But there
is something else. He is suspected of being involved in a very
grave crime.”

“A crime? My nephew? Oh, impossible! He is the best of men—so kind,
so thoughtful!”

“I am sorry, madame, but the evidence is very strong. I must ask
you some questions. Has your nephew been to see you lately?”

“Yes, he was here only a few days ago. He seemed quite as usual.”

“And did he say anything about his work? Anything about the Prime
Minister?”

“No, he never talks about his work. He says it is confidential.”

“I see. And has anyone else been to see you lately? Anyone you did
not know?”

Mrs. Everard hesitated.

“Well, there was a lady—a German lady, I think. She said she was
a friend of my nephew’s.”

“A German lady? What was her name?”

“Frau Bertha Ebenthal. She was very charming, and she seemed to
know my nephew very well.”

“Bertha Ebenthal!” Poirot’s eyes flashed. “The famous German spy!
So she was here!”

“A spy? Oh, no, surely not! She was so kind, so well-bred!”

“And what did she want, this Frau Ebenthal?”

“She just wanted to talk about my nephew. She said she had known
him in Germany, when he was a student there.”

“I see. And did she stay long?”

“No, only about half an hour. She said she was just passing through
London.”

Poirot stood up.

“Thank you, madame. You have been most helpful.”

As we left the house, Poirot’s face was transformed. His eyes were
shining, and he was humming a little tune to himself.

“Poirot!” I cried. “What is it? What have you found out?”

“I have found the thread, Hastings! The tiny thread! And now I
must follow it to the end!”

“But where are we going?”

“To Ascot! To see the other aunt—Miss Daniels!”

“But why? What do you expect to find there?”

“I do not know. But I have a little idea—a very little idea. And
if it is correct—then we shall find the Prime Minister!”

We drove to Ascot at breakneck speed. Miss Daniels’ house was a
small, secluded cottage, surrounded by a high hedge.

As we drove up, Poirot told the driver to wait a little way down
the road.

“We must be careful, Hastings,” he whispered. “We do not want to
alarm them.”

We walked up to the house and Poirot rang the bell. The door was
opened by a tall, thin woman with a severe face.

“Miss Daniels?” asked Poirot.

“Yes. What do you want?”

“I am Hercule Poirot. I have been sent by your nephew, Captain
Daniels.”

The woman’s face softened slightly.

“Oh, I see. Come in.”

She showed us into a small, neatly furnished parlour.

“What has happened? Is my nephew all right?”

“He has been injured, mademoiselle, but he is out of danger. He
sent me to tell you that all is well.”

“Oh, thank God! I have been so worried.”

“And the Prime Minister? Is he here?”

Miss Daniels started.

“The Prime Minister? Here? What do you mean?”

“I think you know what I mean, mademoiselle. I think the Prime
Minister is in this house.”

“I don’t know what you’re talking about! There’s no one here but
me and my servant.”

“Is that so? Then you will not mind if I have a look round?”

“I certainly will mind! This is my house, and you have no right
to search it!”

“I have the right of the law, mademoiselle. I am accompanied by a
representative of Scotland Yard.”

He pointed to Japp, who had followed us into the room.

Miss Daniels turned pale. She looked from one to the other of us,
and then she sank into a chair.

“It’s no use,” she whispered. “They’ve found us.”

“Where is he?” asked Poirot.

“Upstairs. In the back bedroom.”

We rushed upstairs and burst into the room. There, lying on the
bed, his head bandaged and his face pale, was the Prime Minister.

He looked up as we entered, and a look of relief crossed his face.

“Thank God!” he whispered. “I thought I was a dead man.”

“Monsieur MacAdam!” cried Poirot. “You are safe!”

“Yes—thanks to you, I suppose. Who are you?”

“I am Hercule Poirot, at your service.”

“Well, Monsieur Poirot, you’ve saved my life—and perhaps the life
of England. How did you find me?”

“It was a matter of logic, monsieur. A matter of using the little
grey cells.”

Later, when the Prime Minister had been safely conveyed to London,
and the Conference had been successfully opened, Poirot explained
it all to me.

“It was the shooting that gave me the clue, Hastings. As I said,
it was a clumsy, theatrical business. Why should they try to shoot
him, when his death would only help the English Government? The
answer was simple: they didn't want to kill him. They only wanted
to wound him.”

“To wound him? But why?”

“So that he would have to have his head bandaged. And once his head
was bandaged, it would be easy to impersonate him.”

“Impersonate him? But who?”

“The chauffeur, O’Murphy. Think, Hastings! O’Murphy was an Irishman,
from County Clare. He probably had the same build and the same
colouring as the Prime Minister. With his head bandaged, and his
face partially covered, he could easily pass for MacAdam—especially
to people who did not know him well.”

“But what about the Prime Minister himself?”

“He was kidnapped in London, during that first ‘attack.’ The masked
men were not German agents, but O’Murphy and his confederates. They
took the Prime Minister to Miss Daniels’ house in Ascot, and then
O’Murphy took his place in the car.”

“And the ‘attack’ near Windsor?”

“That was a sham, staged to provide an excuse for the bandages.
Then O’Murphy, as the Prime Minister, went to France, while the
real MacAdam was kept a prisoner at Ascot.”

“And Daniels?”

“Daniels was the master-mind behind it all. He was a German spy,
working with Frau Bertha Ebenthal. He arranged the whole thing—the
impersonation, the kidnapping, everything. He even arranged for
himself to be ‘kidnapped’ in France, to avert suspicion.”

“And O’Murphy? Where is he?”
