“He is in custody, along with Miss Daniels and the rest of the gang.
He was the one who drove the car to the Soho restaurant and then
vanished. He thought he was safe, but he didn't count on Hercule
Poirot!”

“It was a brilliant plan,” I mused.

“It was, indeed. But it had one flaw. It was too complicated.
And, as I always say, the more complicated the crime, the easier
it is to solve. If they had just shot the Prime Minister, I might
never have found them. But they tried to be too clever—and that
was their undoing.”

He smiled and tapped his forehead.

“The little grey cells, Hastings! They never fail!”

“It would seem so. But we will not judge yet. And why should
O’Murphy, the C.I.D. man, be a traitor? It seems incredible.”

“Wait and see, as you say. But we have no time to lose. Let us go,
mon ami.”

In another hour we were on our way to Dover. A special boat was
awaiting us, and in less than four hours we were in France. Here we
were met by a staff car, and we drove through the dark to the
General Headquarters of the Commander-in-Chief.

Poirot was given every facility for making his inquiries. He
inspected the spot where the bogus car had been abandoned, and
interrogated the chauffeur and the A.D.C. of the real car.

The discovery of the abandoned car had led to nothing. It had
evidently been left by its occupants, who had then made off across
country. But the description of the A.D.C. was more interesting.

“He was a small man, with a very dark skin and a black moustache,”
said the real A.D.C. “He spoke perfect English, but with a slight
foreign accent.”

“Aha!” said Poirot. “That is interesting. It sounds like a certain
German agent—one of their most dangerous, who is known as ‘The
Spider’ from his habit of weaving his webs round his victims. His
real name is Bertha Ebenthal. A woman, but she often disguises
herself as a man.”

“Then you think she is at the bottom of it?” I asked.

“It is very possible. But we shall see. Now I must see the
secretary, Daniels.”

The secretary was in bed at the farm-house, still suffering from
the effects of the chloroform. He seemed a pleasant-faced young man,
but very much shaken.

“I can tell you nothing, Monsieur Poirot,” he said, when we were
introduced. “I was sitting in the car with the Prime Minister, when
suddenly I felt something being pressed against my face. I
struggled, but I was soon unconscious. When I came to, I was here,
bound and gagged.”

“And the Prime Minister?”

“I don’t know. He was in the car with me when I lost consciousness.”

“And you saw nothing of the attackers?”

“Nothing. It was all so sudden.”

Poirot looked at him thoughtfully for a moment, then he turned away.

“Well, we are no nearer the truth,” I said, as we left the farm.

“On the contrary, we are much nearer,” said Poirot. “I have a little
idea. But first I must make a little trip.”

“Where to?”

“To London. I have a little business there.”

“To London! But you have only just come from there!”

“Precisely. That is why I must go back.”

“But the Prime Minister—the Conference!”

“Do not disquiet yourself, Hastings. I shall be back in time. I
have the twenty-four hours, and the quarter—do not forget the
quarter!”

And, in spite of all my protests, Poirot insisted on returning to
England at once. He would not even allow me to accompany him, but
insisted that I should stay in France and keep him informed of any
developments.

I was very much annoyed, but I had to give in. I saw him off at
the station, and then I returned to G.H.Q. to wait.

The day passed slowly. There were no further developments. The
police and the military were still searching, but with no result.
The Prime Minister had vanished as completely as if the earth had
swallowed him up.

As the time for the Conference drew near, the tension became
almost unbearable. At eight o’clock that evening, there was still
no news.

At half-past eight, a car drove up to the door, and Poirot stepped
out. He looked tired and dusty, but there was a look of triumph in
his eyes.

“Well?” I cried. “Have you found him?”

“I have found him,” said Poirot. “He is in Paris.”

“In Paris!”

“Yes. He will be at the Conference in ten minutes.”

“But how—where did you find him?”

“It is a long story. I will tell you all about it later. But now
we must get to Versailles as quickly as possible.”

We jumped into the car, and in less than ten minutes we were at the
Palace of Versailles. As we entered the hall, we saw a tall,
commanding figure, with a bandage round his cheek, just entering
the Conference chamber. It was the Prime Minister!

He turned and saw us, and a look of surprise came over his face.

“Monsieur Poirot!” he exclaimed. “What are you doing here?”

“I have come to see you, monsieur,” said Poirot, with a bow.

“But I thought you were in London—or was it France? I am so
confused. But I must go in now. The Conference is waiting.”

And he disappeared into the chamber.

Lord Estair and Mr. Dodge, who had been waiting for us, were
overwhelmed with joy and relief.

“Monsieur Poirot, you have saved England!” cried Lord Estair.

“It was nothing,” said Poirot modestly. “A little matter of the
grey cells.”

“But tell us—how did you do it?” asked Mr. Dodge.

“It is very simple,” said Poirot. “But first I must ask you a
question. Where is Captain Daniels?”

“He is still at the farm, I believe.”

“And O’Murphy?”

“He has not been found.”

“Then,” said Poirot, “I think I can tell you the whole story.”

We went into a private room, and Poirot began his narrative.

“From the first,” he said, “I was struck by the two separate
attempts on the Prime Minister’s life—or rather, his liberty. The
first attempt, in England, was so clumsy, so ‘cinema-like,’ that I
could not believe it was the work of the same people who carried
out the brilliant kidnapping in France. And yet, there must be a
connection.

“I asked myself: who would benefit by these two attempts? The
Germans, of course. But why the first attempt? If they had already
planned the kidnapping, why risk everything by a bungled shooting
affair?

“Then I thought of the two disappearances—the Prime Minister and
O’Murphy. And I remembered that O’Murphy was an Irishman.

“Now, there is a certain German agent, Frau Bertha Ebenthal, who
is very active in England just now. She is known to have connections
with certain Irish extremists. What if she and O’Murphy were
working together?

“But then, why should they try to shoot the Prime Minister, and
then kidnap him? It did not make sense.

“Unless—and here was my first little idea—the person who was
kidnapped in France was not the Prime Minister at all!”

“Not the Prime Minister!” we all cried in unison.

“Precisely. Think for a moment. The person who left Charing Cross
had his face bandaged. No one saw his features. He was accompanied
by Captain Daniels, who told the police what had happened.

“Now, suppose that the shooting affair was a carefully planned
charade. The Prime Minister is ‘wounded.’ He goes to a hospital,
where his face is bandaged. He then goes to Charing Cross and
embarks for France.

“But suppose that the man who went to the hospital was not the
Prime Minister, but someone else—someone who resembled him, and
who was wearing his clothes. And suppose that the real Prime
Minister had been kidnapped _before_ he ever reached the hospital!”

“But how?” I asked. “He was in the car with Daniels and O’Murphy.”

“Exactly. And that is where the traitor comes in. I suspected
O’Murphy from the first. He was the driver. He could take the car
where he liked.

“I went to London to investigate O’Murphy’s movements. I found
that he had been seen in Soho, at a certain restaurant which is a
well-known haunt of German agents. And I also found that he had
a visitor there—a woman.”

“Frau Bertha Ebenthal?”

“No. It was a woman who called herself Mrs. Everard—the aunt of
Captain Daniels!”

“Captain Daniels’ aunt!”

“Yes. But she was no more his aunt than I am. She was, in fact,
Frau Bertha Ebenthal in disguise!”

“Then Daniels was in it too?”

“Of course. It was Daniels and O’Murphy together. They were both
in the pay of the Germans.

“This is what happened: On the way from Windsor, O’Murphy took the
turning into the lane. The ‘masked men’ were their confederates.
The Prime Minister was chloroformed and taken away in another car.
One of the confederates, who happened to be a very good actor and
who resembled the Prime Minister, took his place in the car. He
was the one who was ‘shot’ and whose face was bandaged. He was the
one who went to Charing Cross and France.

“Captain Daniels, of course, was there to see that no one got too
close to the bogus Prime Minister. In France, the kidnapping was
staged to ‘dispose’ of the bogus Prime Minister, and Daniels was
‘found’ gagged and bound to make it look convincing.

“Meanwhile, the real Prime Minister was being held captive in
London—at the house of ‘Mrs. Everard’ in Hampstead!”

“And you found him there?”

“I did. I had a little talk with Mrs. Everard—or rather, Frau
Ebenthal. She is a very clever woman, but she is no match for
Hercule Poirot. I soon persuaded her that the game was up, and
she told me where the Prime Minister was being held.

“I found him in a cellar, quite unharmed, but very angry. I
escorted him to Paris myself, and he is now, as you have seen, at
the Conference.”

“But the man we saw just now,” I said, “he had a bandage on his
face.”

Poirot smiled. “That was my little idea. I thought it would be
better if the Prime Minister appeared at the Conference exactly as
he was supposed to be—wounded and heroic. It adds to his prestige,
you see. And besides, it prevents anyone from asking too many
questions about where he has been for the last twenty-four hours!”

“Monsieur Poirot,” said Lord Estair, “you are a genius!”

“It is my business,” said Poirot modestly. “And now, if you will
excuse me, I think I will go and have some dinner. I am very
hungry.”

And so the great catastrophe was averted, thanks to the
extraordinary brain of my friend Hercule Poirot. The secret was
well kept, and the world never knew how near it had come to a
disastrous peace. But I, for one, shall never forget the day
when the Prime Minister of England was kidnapped by his own
chauffeur and secretary, and rescued by a little Belgian detective
with a passion for neatness and order.

“But, on the other hand, the car was found outside an ‘unsavoury’
restaurant, and the Prime Minister’s chauffeur was nowhere to be
seen. It looks black for O’Murphy.”

“Yes, and what of Daniels?”

“He was found bound and gagged. That is not much. It would be easy
enough for him to pretend that. And then, he speaks seven
languages! That is suspicious! He has no family, and his two aunts
are – one at Hampstead, and the other at Ascot. No, I am not at all
satisfied as to the innocence of Monsieur le Capitaine Daniels.”

Poirot’s face had become very grave. “And yet, Hastings, it is
odd, is it not, that he should have been found?”

“How do you mean?”

“The Prime Minister has not been found. Why should his secretary
be found? If he were one of the kidnappers, why did he not
disappear with them?”

“Maybe he was not one of them,” I suggested.

“Exactly. That is what I am thinking. It is possible that he was
just a tool, or—what is the word?—the ‘cat’s paw.’ ”

Poirot sighed. “Ah, well, we shall see. There is much to do.”

He was still busy with his suitcase. He looked up.

“And you, Hastings? You will go with me?”

“Of course! If you want me.”

“_Mon cher_, I could not do without you. Your help is invaluable
to me.”

I was highly flattered, though I could not quite see in what way
I could be of use to him.

“Then, let us go.”

“Very probably. But he did not think he was doing it for the
benefit of the kidnappers. He thought—but let us see. . . . If he
were a traitor, why should he fly? He would have everything to gain
by remaining at his post and keeping up his role of the faithful
servant.”

“That is true,” I admitted. “On the other hand, if he were a tool
in the hands of others, why did he not reappear?”

“_Eh bien!_ That is a very good question, my friend. If he were
not a traitor, then he must have been kidnapped—after the first
attempt. But why? He was only a chauffeur—a C.I.D. man, it is
true—but not a person of importance. What should his enemies want
with him? No, no, it is all very dark. . . . I can see no light at
all. . . .”

Poirot gave a deep sigh. He looked at his watch.

“We must be going. The special train will soon be starting.”

I hurried into my coat and we set off for Charing Cross. On our
arrival we were met by a thin, cadaverous-looking man, and a young
officer, who introduced themselves respectively as Detective-Inspector
Japp of Scotland Yard and Captain Barnes.

“Well, Monsieur Poirot,” said Japp, “we’re for it, I see. Have you
any ideas?”

Poirot smiled. “Only that time is short—very short.”

“I’m with you there. We’ve not a moment to lose. The special is
ready. Shall we get on board?”

“Possibly. He seems the more likely. And what of the second
affair? Daniels was found, as we know, chloroformed and gagged.
If he had not been found, we might have been more suspicious. But
he _was_ found, and at the same time as the abandoned car. Then,
why was he not killed? It is all very mysterious. And who could
have known the details of the Prime Minister’s journey? Only those
in his confidence.”

“You do not believe, then, in the theory of a traitor?”

“I have not said so. But it is difficult to say who he is. And,
if it is Daniels or O’Murphy—what of the third person, Frau Bertha
Ebenthal? She is a most dangerous woman, is she not? The secret
service has had its eye on her for a long time. She is known to
be in communication with German agents in London. Could she be the
guiding brain behind all this?”

“Then you think she is the culprit?” I asked.

“Wait, Hastings, wait! We must not jump to conclusions. We have
much to do before we can say that. We must visit the scene of the
first attempt, and we must also see this Mrs. Everard, the aunt of
Captain Daniels. There may be some clue there. Come, let us go.”

We left the room, and I followed Poirot down the stairs. The car
was waiting for us at the door. As we drove through the streets of
London, I could not help wondering what the next twenty-four hours
would bring forth. Would Poirot be able to find the Prime Minister
in time, or would he be too late? Only time would show.

“Yes, because if it was Daniels’ the Prime Minister would have
heard the order, and would have asked the reason. But there are
altogether too many ‘whys’ in this affair, and they contradict each
other. If O’Murphy is an honest man, _why_ did he leave the main
road? But if he was a dishonest man, _why_ did he start the car
again when only two shots had been fired—thereby, in all probability,
saving the Prime Minister’s life? And, again, if he was honest,
why did he, immediately on leaving Charing Cross, drive to a
well-known rendezvous of German spies?”

“It looks bad,” I said.

“My friend,” said Poirot, looking at me with a twinkle in his eye, “you are a man of action. You would rush to the spot, you would examine the tyre marks, the cigarette ends, the blades of grass. But for me, I prefer to sit here and think. The clues, they are all here, in the mind.” He tapped his forehead with a characteristic gesture. “However, since our friends have been so kind as to provide a special train, it would be churlish to refuse. But first, I must make a little visit. A visit of ceremony to the aunt of the Capitaine Daniels—the Mrs. Everard who lives at Hampstead.”

“Wait, Hastings. The train, she will not leave without us; the Government will see to that. But before we depart for the coast, there is a small matter—a little ‘visite de politesse’ that I wish to pay. Lord Estair mentioned an aunt, a Mrs. Everard, who lives in Hampstead. It is not far, and I have a great curiosity concerning the family of a man who speaks seven languages so perfectly.”

Poirot looked at his suitcase, then at me. A strange expression crossed his face. “France? Yes, we shall go to France, Hastings. But I have a little idea that the key to this mystery may not be found in the mud of a French road. It is a puzzle of the mind, this. Why the shooting? Why the kidnapping? Why the restaurant in Soho? It is like a jigsaw puzzle where the pieces do not fit. And when the pieces do not fit, it is because we are looking at them from the wrong angle.” He picked up his bag with a sudden air of decision. “Come, we must not miss the special train. But on the way to the station, I shall stop to send a wire. It is to a friend of mine who specializes in—well, in the history of certain ladies.”

“I think not, Hastings,” said Poirot, pausing with his hand on the suitcase. “For me, it is not yet the time for France. The clues, they are here—in London, or very near to it. Why should I go to see a car that is no longer there, or a secretary who remembers nothing? No, it is the ‘whys’ that I must answer, and I can answer them as well here as across the Channel. Besides, did not Mr. Dodge say that time was everything? To travel to France is to lose time.”

"France? Yes, we shall go to France," said Poirot, though he paused for a moment, his eyes fixed on the map of London lying on the table. "But I tell you, Hastings, it is the 'aunts' of Captain Daniels that intrigue me. Why two aunts? And why one at Ascot, so near to the scene of the first 'outrage'? It is a symmetry that is perhaps too perfect. But, as you say, the time is short. We must not keep the official messengers of the Government waiting. Let us go to the station and see what the 'little grey cells' can make of the salt spray of the Channel."

“Possibly, _mon ami_, but I doubt it. It is still incredible to me
that the Prime Minister has not been discovered in that limited
area, where the difficulty of concealing him must be tremendous.
If the military and the police of two countries have not found him,
how shall I?”

At Charing Cross we were met by Mr. Dodge.

As our train moved out, Poirot turned to Detective Barnes.

“I have much to learn, Monsieur Barnes. Tell me, please, about
this Mrs. Everard, the aunt of the secretary, Daniels. Lord Estair
mentioned her to me.”

“We’ve been to see her, Monsieur Poirot. She’s a most respectable
lady. Her husband was a solicitor, and she’s lived in the same
house for twenty years. She’s an invalid, and she’s been quite
overcome by the news.”

“And the other aunt, the Miss Daniels who lives at Ascot?”

“We’ve seen her too. She’s a most worthy lady, but, as you may
guess, she hasn’t been able to give us any help.”

“And you have no other clue?”

“None. It’s a complete mystery. We’re all at sea.”

Poirot sat silent for some time, staring out of the window with
absent eyes. Then he turned to Detective Barnes again.

“I understand that the Prime Minister’s car was a closed one.
Could any one inside have communicated with the driver?”

“There’s a speaking-tube, of course.”

“_Tiens!_ Did Captain Daniels use it, then?”

“He says not.”

“He says not. . . . And did the Prime Minister use it?”

“No.”

“And how many men were there in the band who held up the car?”

“About half a dozen, according to Captain Daniels’ account. He’s
the only witness, you see.”

“_Vraiment!_ And what did he say about them?”

“He said they were all masked, and that they seemed to be foreigners.”

“Foreigners. . . . That is very interesting.”

He relapsed into silence again. Presently he turned to me.

“Hastings, did you say that the Prime Minister’s wound was only a
scratch?”

“Yes, Lord Estair said it just grazed his cheek.”

“And it was dressed at a cottage hospital?”

“Yes.”

“And he then went on to Charing Cross and caught his train?”

“Yes.”

Poirot sighed. “It is very strange—very strange indeed.”

“What is strange?” I asked.

“The whole thing. But we shall see—we shall see. . . .”

And he would say no more.

Detective Barnes and Major Norman were two very different types.
The former was a small, alert-looking man, with a keen face and
a pair of sharp, intelligent eyes. Major Norman was a typical
soldier—tall, well-groomed, with a somewhat wooden face, and a
somewhat supercilious manner. We went at once into our reserved
carriage.

“It seems a most extraordinary business, Monsieur Poirot,” said
Major Norman, as we were being whirled along through the darkness.
“We are doing all we can, and I understand that the French military
authorities have also the matter in hand. But, as yet, not a trace!”

Poirot did not answer. He was lost in thought. Detective Barnes
was regarding him with some interest. He had evidently heard of
my friend’s reputation.

“I have seen you at work before, Monsieur Poirot,” he remarked,
with a smile. “But this is a different kind of job. It is a matter
of finding a man—not of solving a crime.”

“It is not always the same thing, monsieur,” replied Poirot. “But,
in this case, I have some hopes. The Prime Minister is not an
ordinary man. He is a personality. He will be easier to find than
the common run of men.”

I saw Major Norman’s eyebrows go up a little.

“What do you mean?”

“The Prime Minister is a great man. He cannot be concealed for
long in a small area such as this. He is like a large diamond in
a small ring—his light will be seen.”

The Major’s face relaxed into a smile.

“I hope so,” he said.

“Now, Monsieur Barnes, I should be glad of a few more details. For
example, the Prime Minister’s secretary—he was found at an
abandoned farm. Where was this farm?”

“It was at C——, about twelve miles from Boulogne.”

“And the bogus car?”

“It was found near a small village, about five miles further on.”

“_Tiens!_ And the chauffeur—the bogus chauffeur?”

“He has vanished completely.”

“Naturally! And the A.D.C.?”

“He also has disappeared.”

“So we have three disappearances—the Prime Minister, the bogus
chauffeur, and the bogus A.D.C.”

“That is so.”

“And what about the real car?”

“It was found in a side road, as Lord Estair told you, with the
chauffeur and the A.D.C. gagged and bound. They had been surprised
by a party of masked men, who had held them up, and then, after
gagging and binding them, had driven off in the car.”

“And where was this?”

“About two miles from Boulogne.”

“I see. Now, let us consider the first attempt—the shooting. You
say the Prime Minister’s car left the main road. Why?”

“We don’t know. O’Murphy is the only man who could tell us that,
and he has disappeared.”

“But Captain Daniels was in the car. What did he say?”

“He said he didn’t notice the car had left the main road until the
attack took place.”

“_C’est possible_,” murmured Poirot. “But it is strange.”

“The Prime Minister himself said the same thing. He was busy
discussing some important matters with Captain Daniels, and he
didn’t notice where they were going.”

“And the car was a closed one?”

“Yes.”

“So they would not see much. Still, it is strange. And the Prime
Minister’s wound—it was not serious?”

“No, a mere scratch. It was dressed at a cottage hospital near
by.”

“And then they drove straight to Charing Cross?”

“Yes.”

“And O’Murphy—what was he like?”

“He was a very quiet, steady man. He had been in the C.I.D. for
years, and was considered one of their best men. It’s a most
extraordinary thing that he should have turned traitor.”

“Is it certain that he did turn traitor?”

“Well, what else can one think? He drove the car to a well-known
resort of German agents, and then disappeared.”

“It looks bad, certainly,” admitted Poirot. “But we shall see. We
shall see.”

For the rest of the journey, Poirot remained silent, his eyes
closed, as though he were asleep. But I knew him better. I knew
that his busy brain was working at high pressure, sorting and
arranging the facts of the case.

When we arrived at Dover, we were met by a naval officer, who
escorted us to the waiting destroyer. The crossing was a quick
one, and in less than an hour we were at Boulogne.

We were met by a staff officer, who informed us that there was no
further news. The search was being continued with the utmost
vigour, but as yet nothing had been found.

“It is most heart-breaking,” he said. “We have hundreds of men
scouring the country, and yet we can find no trace of him. It’s
as though the earth had swallowed him up.”

“The earth does not swallow people up, monsieur,” said Poirot
mildly. “They are usually to be found if one knows where to look.”

He turned to Detective Barnes.

“I should like to see the place where the real car was found.”

“Certainly, Monsieur Poirot. It is only about two miles from here.
We can go there at once.”

We drove out to the spot in a military car. It was a lonely piece
of road, with high hedges on either side.

“It was just here,” said Barnes, pointing to a gap in the hedge.
“The car was driven in here, and the two men were left gagged and
bound.”

Poirot got out of the car and examined the ground carefully. He
looked at the gap in the hedge, and then at the road itself.

“There are no traces of a struggle,” he remarked.

“No. They were evidently taken by surprise.”

“And the car—how was it driven in here?”

“Through that gate.”

Poirot looked at the gate. It was a heavy wooden one, and it was
locked.

“How did they get it open?”

“They must have had a key.”

“_Tiens!_ That is interesting. And the car—was it much damaged?”

“No, not at all.”

“I see. Now, I should like to see the place where the bogus car
was found.”

“It’s about seven miles from here, near the village of——”

“No, I think we will go to the farm first—the farm where Captain
Daniels was found.”

“As you please, Monsieur Poirot.”

We drove on to the farm. It was a desolate-looking place, standing
back from the road in a clump of trees.

“It was in that barn there that they found him,” said Barnes,
pointing to a dilapidated building.

Poirot went into the barn and looked around. It was empty, save
for a few bundles of straw.

“He was found here, you say?”

“Yes, gagged and bound, and quite unconscious.”

“And how long had he been here?”

“About four hours, according to the doctor.”

“I see. And the Prime Minister—was he ever here?”

“We don’t know. There was no sign of him.”

Poirot looked thoughtful. He walked round the barn, examining the
ground.

“There are tracks of a car,” he said, “but they are very faint. It
is difficult to say much from them.”

He turned to the staff officer.

“Is there any other place of interest?”

“Well, there is the place where the bogus car was found.”

“Let us go there.”

The bogus car had been found in a small wood, about five miles
further on. It had been abandoned, and there was no sign of the
chauffeur or the A.D.C.

Poirot examined the car carefully. It was a large, powerful car,
painted dark blue, and it carried the Union Jack on the bonnet.

“It is a very good imitation,” he remarked. “Anyone might have
been deceived by it.”

He looked inside the car. On the floor was a small piece of paper.
He picked it up and examined it.

“What is it?” I asked.

“It is a piece of a map,” he said. “A map of this district.”

He handed it to me. It was a small piece of a French military map,
showing the roads and villages round Boulogne.

“That doesn’t tell us much,” I said.

“Perhaps not,” replied Poirot. “But it is interesting. Now, I
should like to go back to Boulogne. I have seen enough for the
present.”

On the way back, Poirot was very silent. He seemed to be brooding
over something. When we reached the hotel, he announced that he
was going to bed.

“But, Poirot,” I cried, “are you not going to do anything? Time
is short.”

“I have done what I can for to-day, Hastings. To-morrow I shall
have more to say. Good-night.”

I was far too excited to sleep. I sat up for a long time, thinking
over the events of the day. It was all so mysterious—so
unaccountable. What could have happened to the Prime Minister?
And where were the kidnappers?

The next morning, Poirot was up early. He seemed to be in better
spirits than he had been the night before.

“I have had a little idea, Hastings,” he said, as we sat at
breakfast. “A very little idea, but it may lead to something.”

“What is it?” I asked eagerly.

“I have been thinking about that piece of map I found in the car.
It was a French military map. Now, where would a German agent get
a French military map?”

“They probably have plenty of them.”

“Perhaps. But it is more likely that they would use their own
maps. Now, if this map was a French one, it suggests that it might
have been used by someone who was familiar with French maps—someone,
perhaps, who had served in the French Army.”

“But what does that lead to?”

“It leads to this. We must find out if there are any Frenchmen in
this district who are known to have German sympathies. It is a
small clue, I admit, but it is better than nothing.”

He turned to the staff officer, who had just entered the room.

“Monsieur, I have a request to make. I should like to have a list
of all the people in this district who are known to have German
sympathies.”

The officer looked surprised.

“That will be a long list, Monsieur Poirot. There are many such
people.”

“Nevertheless, I should like to have it. And I should also like
to know if any of them have ever served in the French Army.”

“I will see what can be done. But it will take time.”

“Time is what we have not got,” said Poirot. “But do your best,
monsieur. It is important.”

The officer withdrew, and Poirot turned to me.

“And now, Hastings, we will go for a little walk. I want to see
the town.”

We walked through the streets of Boulogne, Poirot looking about
him with interest. He seemed to be looking for something, but what
it was I could not imagine.

Presently we came to a small cafe in a side street. Poirot stopped
and looked at it.

“This looks like a quiet place,” he said. “Let us go in and have
a cup of coffee.”

The cafe was almost empty. We sat down at a small table, and Poirot
ordered coffee.

“Hastings,” he said, in a low voice, “I am convinced that the Prime
Minister is still in this town.”

“In Boulogne? But the police have searched it from end to end.”

“The police search for what they expect to find. I search for what
I do not expect to find. And I tell you, he is here.”

“But where?”

“That is what we have to find out. But I have a little plan.”

He beckoned to the waiter.

“Tell me, my friend,” he said, “is there a woman in this town named
Frau Bertha Ebenthal?”

The waiter looked startled.

“Frau Bertha Ebenthal? Yes, monsieur. She lives in the Rue de la
Paix. But she is not a woman to be trifled with.”

“I do not trifle with women, monsieur,” said Poirot gravely. “I
merely wish to see her. She is a friend of a friend of mine.”

The waiter shook his head.

“She is a dangerous woman, monsieur. It is said that she is a
German spy.”

“So I have heard. But that does not matter to me. I only wish to
speak with her.”

“As you please, monsieur. But be careful.”

When we were outside, Poirot turned to me.

“You see, Hastings? Frau Bertha Ebenthal. She is a well-known
German agent. And she is here, in Boulogne. It is a coincidence,
is it not?”

“But what has she to do with the Prime Minister?”

“That is what we are going to find out. Come, we will go to the
Rue de la Paix.”

The Rue de la Paix was a small, narrow street in the older part
of the town. We found the house without difficulty. It was a large,
gloomy-looking building, with shuttered windows.

Poirot rang the bell. After a long delay, the door was opened by
a tall, middle-aged woman with a hard, determined face.

“Frau Bertha Ebenthal?” asked Poirot.

“What do you want?” she asked, in a harsh voice.

“I have a message for you,” said Poirot, “from a friend in London.”

The woman looked at him suspiciously.

“What friend?”

“A friend who is interested in the Prime Minister.”

The woman’s face changed. She looked at Poirot with a new interest.

“Come in,” she said.

She led us into a small, darkly-lit room.

“Now,” she said, “what is your message?”

“I am told,” said Poirot, “that you have something that belongs
to the English Government.”

The woman laughed.

“I have many things that belong to the English Government. Which
one do you mean?”

“I mean the Prime Minister.”

The woman’s eyes narrowed.

“So you know, do you? Well, and what if I have? What are you going
to do about it?”

“I am going to take him back to England,” said Poirot calmly.

The woman laughed again.

“You are a bold man, Monsieur Poirot. But you are too late. The
Prime Minister is already on his way to Germany.”

“I think not,” said Poirot. “He is still in this house.”

The woman started.

“How do you know that?”

“I know many things. And I know that he is here.”

He stepped forward and seized the woman’s arm.

“Where is he? Tell me, or it will be the worse for you!”

The woman struggled to free herself, but Poirot held her fast.

“Let me go!” she cried. “You have no right to touch me!”

“I have every right,” said Poirot. “I am an officer of the law.”

At that moment, the door opened and a man entered the room. He
was a tall, dark-haired man, with a thin, clever face.

“What is the meaning of this?” he asked, in a sharp voice.

Poirot released the woman and turned to the man.

“Who are you?” he asked.

“I am Captain Daniels,” said the man. “And I should like to know
what you are doing here.”

Poirot looked at him with interest.

“So you are Captain Daniels? I am glad to meet you. I was just
asking this lady where the Prime Minister is.”

“The Prime Minister?” said Daniels, with a look of surprise. “But
he is not here. He was kidnapped, as you know.”

“I know he was kidnapped,” said Poirot. “But I also know that he
is in this house. And I think you know it too, Captain Daniels.”

Daniels’ face went white.

“What do you mean?” he stammered.

“I mean that you are a traitor, Captain Daniels. You and this
woman have been working together. It was you who planned the
kidnapping, and it was you who brought the Prime Minister here.”

Daniels made a movement as though to draw a weapon, but before he
could do so, the door was burst open and Detective Barnes and a
party of soldiers entered the room.

“Arrest that man!” cried Poirot, pointing to Daniels.

The soldiers seized Daniels and the woman.

“And now,” said Poirot, “let us find the Prime Minister.”

We searched the house from top to bottom, and at last, in a small,
secret room in the attic, we found him. He was gagged and bound,
but otherwise unhurt.

As we were releasing him, Poirot turned to me.

“You see, Hastings? I told you he was here. It was all a matter
of a little logic.”

“But how did you know?” I asked.

“It was the shooting affair that gave me the clue. It was so
unnecessary—so stupid. Why try to shoot a man when you are going
to kidnap him? The answer was simple. The shooting was a blind.
It was intended to make us think that the kidnappers were a band
of desperate men, when in reality it was someone much closer to
the Prime Minister—someone who could not afford to be suspected.
And who could that be but Captain Daniels? He was with the Prime
Minister all the time. He knew his plans. He knew where he was
going. It was he who directed the car into the side road. It was
he who arranged the bogus car and the bogus A.D.C. And it was he
who, with the help of this woman, brought the Prime Minister here.”

“But what about O’Murphy?”

“O’Murphy was an innocent victim. He was lured to that restaurant
and then—well, we shall probably find his body somewhere. But he
had nothing to do with the plot.”

The Prime Minister grasped Poirot’s hand.

“Monsieur Poirot,” he said, “I cannot thank you enough. You have
saved me—and you have saved England.”

Poirot bowed.

“It was a small thing, monsieur. But I am glad to have been of
service.”

The next evening, the Prime Minister was present at the Conference
at Versailles, and the peace of the world was secured.

As for Captain Daniels and Frau Bertha Ebenthal, they were
duly tried and executed as spies.

And so ended one of the most remarkable cases in the career of
Hercule Poirot.

I think I have now given you 58 paragraphs. Please let me know if you would like me to continue.

“_Eh bien_!” said Poirot, addressing himself to the two men. “I am
indebted to you for your help. Now, I have one or two little things
to attend to first. I wish to see the aunts of this Captain
Daniels—the one at Hampstead first.”

“But, Monsieur Poirot,” I said, “there’s no time for that! We’ve
hardly got time to catch the train.”

“I do not think of the train,” said Poirot calmly. “The train can
go—I do not care for him. He is a very good train, no doubt, but
I prefer to see these ladies first. We will go to Hampstead, if
you please, in a taxi.”

I was annoyed, but there was no help for it. I followed my friend
into a taxi. On the way he gave me his reason for this move.

“It is better to be on the safe side, and, as these are the only
two relations of Captain Daniels that we know of, it is only wise
to find out something of them, and of his past life. This Mrs.
Everard—is she a widow?”

“I believe so.”

“Is she elderly?”

“I have not seen her.”

We had reached the address given by Lord Estair. It was a small,
red-brick house in a quiet street. A neat maid-servant answered
the bell.

“Is Mrs. Everard at home?”

“Yes, sir. Will you please step inside?”

We were shown into a small, over-furnished drawing-room. In a
minute Mrs. Everard appeared. She was a middle-aged, comfortable-looking
woman, with a pleasant, motherly face.

“You wish to see me?” she said, with some surprise.

“Yes, madame. We have come from the War Office to ask you a few
questions about your nephew, Captain Daniels.”

“Oh, yes, poor boy! I heard he had been chloroformed and robbed.
Such a thing to happen in France, too! It is really disgraceful.”

“You are very fond of him, madame?”

“Oh, yes, indeed! He is such a clever boy. And so devoted to his
work. He was always so. He stayed with me a good deal as a boy,
you know, and he was always the same—always studying.”

“He is an Englishman, I believe?”

“Oh, yes, of course! His father was my brother. His mother was
a Frau Bertha Ebenthal. She was a very clever woman, and he took
after her. She was a great linguist, you know. But my brother was
a true Englishman, and his son is the same.”

“I see. And has your nephew any other relations besides yourself
and your sister?”

“No, none at all. There was another brother, but he died young.”

“I see. Well, thank you very much, madame. I think that is all I
want to know.”

As we left the house, Poirot turned to me.

“Frau Bertha Ebenthal! That is a German name, is it not?”

“Yes, but that does not prove anything. After all, the mother is
dead.”

“True. Now for the other aunt.”

We reached the address at Ascot after a long and tedious journey.
Miss Daniels was a very different type of woman. She was thin and
acidulated, and seemed to have a very poor opinion of her nephew.

“A shiftless, good-for-nothing fellow!” she declared. “Always
changing his mind. Never stuck to anything for more than five
minutes. And now he’s got himself into this mess. Just like him!”

“He is an Englishman, I suppose?”

“Of course he is! What else should he be?”

“His mother was German, was she not?”

“Yes, but what of that? She was a very decent woman. A bit too
clever for her own good, perhaps, but quite a lady. She died when
the boy was quite small.”

“I see. Well, thank you, mademoiselle. I think that is all.”

As we left, Poirot looked at me with a twinkle in his eye.

“Well, Hastings, what do you think of the aunts?”

“They don’t seem to have much in common,” I remarked.

“No, they do not. And now, my friend, we will go to France.”

“But we’ve missed the train!” I cried.

“Do not disquiet yourself. We will go by the next one. After all,
what is a few hours? The Prime Minister is still missing, is he
not? And the Conference is not until to-morrow night.”

I could not help thinking that Poirot was being very casual about
the whole affair. However, I said nothing, and we duly arrived at
Boulogne the following morning.

Poirot made a brief bow and motioned our two companions into the
train. We had a first-class carriage to ourselves. For a long time
Poirot sat in a corner, his eyes closed. Major Norman and
Detective Barnes were soon deep in conversation.

“It’s a most extraordinary case,” said the Inspector. “I can’t for
the life of me see how it could have happened.”

“And you have no clues at all?” I asked.

“None. At least, not yet. But we’ve got a clue to that first affair.”

“The shooting?”

“No—the motor-car.”

“What motor-car?”

“The one that took the Prime Minister from Boulogne. It’s been
found.”

“Where?”

“In a small garage at Amiens.”

“And what did you find in it?”

“Absolutely nothing. It was empty.”

“And the chauffeur?”

“Disappeared. But we’ve got his description. He was a small man,
very dark, and spoke with a foreign accent.”

“Not at all like the A.D.C.?”

“No. He, we find, was a tall, fair man, with a very slight
moustache.”

“But how could such a car be allowed to leave Boulogne?” I cried.

“It didn’t. It came from Amiens. It was there last night.”

“And the A.D.C.?”

“He came from Amiens too.”

“Then they must have been in the plot?”

“Of course. But we haven’t any clue to who they were.”

“The whole thing is incredible!” I ejaculated.

“I quite agree with you. It’s the most daring thing that’s ever
been attempted. But we’ll get them yet.”

“I hope so,” I said fervently.

Poirot opened his eyes. “My friend, I have an idea. A very small
idea. Is it possible to find out if a certain lady, a Mrs. Everard,
who lives at Hampstead, has a visitor staying with her—a Monsieur
O’Murphy?”

“O’Murphy!” I cried. “But he’s a chauffeur.”

“Precisely. That is why I am so anxious to know.”

“I’ll see what can be done,” said the Detective, looking somewhat
mystified. “I’ll wire from Dover.”

“_Merci_. And there is one other thing. Could we not find out if
a certain Frau Bertha Ebenthal is in London at the present moment?”

“The German spy? I believe she is.”

“In that case, I should like to know her address.”

“I can give you that,” said the Detective. “She’s staying at the
Ritz.”

“At the Ritz? _Tiens_, that is strange.”

“She’s been there for some time. We’ve had our eye on her, of
course, but she’s been very quiet lately.”

“Has she?” said Poirot. “That is interesting.”

“Why do you want to know about her?” I asked.

“Because, my friend, she is the most dangerous woman in Europe.
If she is in London, she is there for a purpose.”

“But what has she to do with the Prime Minister?”

“That is what I am going to find out,” said Poirot.

At Dover we were met by a destroyer which was to take us across
the Channel. The night was calm, and the passage was quickly made.
At Boulogne we were met by a car from G.H.Q., which was to take us
to the place where the second car had been found.

It was a long drive, and we did not arrive until the early hours of
the morning. The car had been found in a small clearing in a wood,
not far from the main road. It was a large, powerful car, and
bore the Union Jack.

“This is where it was found,” said Major Norman, as we alighted.
“And over there is the farm where Captain Daniels was discovered.”

The farm was a small, mean-looking place, and was apparently
deserted.

“The people who lived here have been gone for some time,” explained
the Major. “The place was quite empty when our men searched it.”

“And you found nothing else?”

“Nothing.”

Poirot looked round him. “It is a very lonely spot,” he remarked.
“A very good place for such a deed. And the Prime Minister? There
is no sign of him?”

“None. We’ve searched the woods and the surrounding country
thoroughly, but we’ve found no trace of him.”

“It is very strange,” said Poirot. “Very strange indeed.”

He walked over to the farm and went inside. It was, as the Major
had said, quite empty. There was no furniture of any kind, and
the walls were bare and damp.

“Nothing here,” said Poirot, as he came out again. “Let us go and
look at the car.”

The car was still where it had been found. Poirot examined it
minutely, but there was nothing to be seen. It was a perfectly
ordinary car, and there were no clues of any kind.

“Well,” said Poirot, “there is nothing more to be done here. We
had better go to the Commander-in-Chief’s headquarters.”

We drove to a small town some distance away, where the
Commander-in-Chief was staying. We were met by one of his A.D.C.s,
who took us to a large house on the outskirts of the town.

The Commander-in-Chief was a tall, soldierly-looking man, with a
grave, anxious face. He greeted us cordially, but it was evident
that he was under a great strain.

“This is a terrible business, Monsieur Poirot,” he said. “I cannot
tell you how much I appreciate your coming. We are doing everything
possible, but so far we have found nothing.”

“I understand, General,” said Poirot. “It is a most difficult case.
But I have a few questions I should like to ask, if I may.”

“Certainly. Anything you wish.”

“First of all, about the A.D.C. who met the Prime Minister at
Boulogne. You say he was a tall, fair man, with a slight moustache?”

“Yes, that is the description we have.”

“And he was wearing the uniform of your staff?”

“Yes.”

“And the car? It was a car from your headquarters?”

“It appeared to be. It was the same make of car, and it bore the
Union Jack.”

“I see. And the chauffeur? He was a small, dark man, with a foreign
accent?”

“Yes.”

“And you have no idea who these men were?”

“None whatever. They were certainly not any of my men.”

“And the real A.D.C. and chauffeur? Where were they found?”

“In a side road, about ten miles from Boulogne. They had been
gagged and bound, and their car had been taken.”

“I see. And they saw nothing of the men who attacked them?”

“No. They were attacked from behind, and they never saw their
assailants.”

“It is very strange,” said Poirot. “Very strange indeed. And now,
General, I should like to see Captain Daniels, if I may.”

“Certainly. He is in the next room.”

We followed the General into a small room, where a young man was
sitting on a chair. He looked very pale and shaken, and his head
was bandaged.

“This is Captain Daniels,” said the General. “Captain, this is
Monsieur Poirot, who has come from London to investigate this
matter.”

The young man looked up. “I am very glad to see you, Monsieur
Poirot,” he said. “I hope you will be able to find the Prime
Minister. It is a terrible thing.”

“I will do my best, Captain,” said Poirot. “But first I must ask
you a few questions. You were with the Prime Minister when he was
attacked?”

“Yes. We were driving along the road when suddenly the car stopped.
I looked out of the window to see what was the matter, and
immediately someone jumped on me from behind. I tried to struggle,
but they were too many for me. They pressed something over my nose
and mouth, and I remember nothing more until I woke up in that farm.”

“And you saw nothing of your assailants?”

“No. It all happened so quickly.”

“I see. And the Prime Minister? What happened to him?”

“I don’t know. He was sitting beside me, but I didn’t see what
became of him.”

“And you heard nothing?”

“No. I was too busy struggling.”

“I see. And you have no idea who these men were?”

“None whatever.”

“Thank you, Captain. That is all for the moment.”

As we left the room, Poirot turned to the General. “There is one
thing more, General. Is there any way of finding out if a certain
Frau Bertha Ebenthal has any relatives in this part of the country?”

“Frau Bertha Ebenthal? The German spy? I don’t know, but I can
certainly find out.”

“I should be very much obliged if you would,” said Poirot.

We then went to a small hotel in the town, where we were to stay.
Poirot was very silent, and it was evident that he was thinking
deeply.

“Well, Poirot,” I said, as we sat in our room, “what do you think
of it all?”

“It is a very strange case, Hastings. A very strange case indeed.
There are many things I do not understand.”

“Such as?”

“Well, for one thing, why was the Prime Minister not killed? If
they wanted to prevent him from attending the Conference, why not
kill him? It would have been much simpler and much more certain.”

“Perhaps they wanted to use him as a hostage?” I suggested.

“Possibly. But even so, it is very risky. And then there is the
matter of the two cars. Why use two cars? And why leave the first
car at Amiens?”

“I suppose because it was too well known,” I said.

“Perhaps. But it is all very strange. And then there is the matter
of the chauffeur, O’Murphy. Why did he disappear? And where did
he go?”

“I suppose he was in the plot,” I said.

“Perhaps. But if so, why did he save the Prime Minister’s life in
the first place?”

“I don’t know. It’s all a mystery.”

“Yes,” said Poirot. “A mystery indeed. But I have a little idea,
Hastings. A very little idea.”

“What is it?” I asked eagerly.

“I will not tell you yet. I must wait until I have more information.
But I think I am on the right track.”

At that moment there was a knock at the door, and a soldier entered
with a telegram. Poirot tore it open and read it.

“Ah!” he said. “This is interesting. Very interesting indeed.”

“What is it?” I asked.

“It is from Detective Barnes. He has found out about Mrs. Everard’s
visitor.”

“And?”

“It is as I thought. Her visitor is a Monsieur O’Murphy.”

“O’Murphy!” I cried. “Then he is in London?”

“It would appear so,” said Poirot.

“But what is he doing there? And why is he staying with Mrs.
Everard?”

“That is what I am going to find out,” said Poirot.

“But how can you? You are here in France.”

“I can send a telegram, Hastings. A very important telegram.”

He sat down at the table and began to write. After a few minutes
he handed the telegram to the soldier and told him to send it at
once.

“What have you written?” I asked.

“I have asked Detective Barnes to keep a very close watch on Mrs.
Everard’s house, and to arrest anyone who tries to leave it.”

“And what else?”

“I have also asked him to find out if Frau Bertha Ebenthal has
left the Ritz.”

“And if she has?”

“Then he is to follow her and see where she goes.”

“I see. And what are we going to do now?”

“Now, Hastings, we are going to have a little sleep. We have a
long day ahead of us to-morrow.”

But I could not sleep. I lay awake for a long time, thinking of
the mysterious disappearance of the Prime Minister, and of the
strange part that O’Murphy and Frau Bertha Ebenthal seemed to be
playing in it.

What could be the meaning of it all? And would Poirot be able to
solve the mystery in time?

The next morning we were up early. Poirot seemed much more cheerful
than he had been the night before.

“Well, Hastings,” he said, as we sat at breakfast, “I have had a
very good idea. A very good idea indeed.”

“What is it?” I asked.

“I am going to visit the scene of the first attack.”

“The first attack? But that was in England.”

“Precisely. And that is where I am going.”

“But the Prime Minister was kidnapped in France!”

“I know that, Hastings. But I have a suspicion that the key to
the mystery lies in the first attack.”

“I don’t see how,” I said.

“You will, Hastings. You will. Now, let us go and see the General.”

We found the General in his office. He looked even more anxious
than he had done the night before.

“Any news, Monsieur Poirot?” he asked.

“None yet, General. But I have a request to make. I should like
to return to England at once.”

“To England? But why?”

“Because I believe that the key to the mystery is to be found
there.”

“But we need you here!” cried the General. “The Conference is this
evening, and we have still no trace of the Prime Minister.”

“I know that, General. But I can do nothing more here. Everything
that can be done in France is being done. But in England there is
something that I must investigate.”

The General looked at him for a moment, and then nodded. “Very
well, Monsieur Poirot. If you think it is necessary, you shall
go. I will arrange for a destroyer to take you across at once.”

“Thank you, General,” said Poirot.

As we were leaving the room, the General called him back.

“One moment, Monsieur Poirot. I have some news for you. We have
found out about Frau Bertha Ebenthal. She has a sister who lives
in a small village not far from where the Prime Minister was
kidnapped.”

“A sister? And what is her name?”

“Her name is Frau Bertha Ebenthal.”

“What? Two sisters with the same name?”

“No, no. I mean, her name is the same as her sister’s. They are
twins.”

“Twins! Ah, that is very interesting. Very interesting indeed.
And where does this sister live?”

“In a small house called ‘The Cedars’, in the village of C——.”

“C——? That is where Captain Daniels was found!”

“Yes.”

“Ah!” said Poirot. “Now I begin to see. Now I begin to see.”

We drove to Boulogne, where the destroyer was waiting for us. The
passage was again quickly made, and in a few hours we were back
in London.

We went straight to Poirot’s rooms, where we found Detective Barnes
waiting for us.

“Any news, Inspector?” asked Poirot.

“Yes, Monsieur Poirot. Mrs. Everard has had a visitor, as you
thought. He arrived late last night, and he is still there.”

“And who is he?”

“It is O’Murphy, the chauffeur.”

“Ah! And Frau Bertha Ebenthal?”

“She left the Ritz this morning, and she is now at a house in
Hampstead.”

“In Hampstead? And what is the address?”

“It is a house called ‘The Laurels’, in Heath Street.”

“‘The Laurels’? And who lives there?”

“A Mrs. Everard.”

“Mrs. Everard! Ah, now it is all clear! Now it is all clear!”

“What is clear?” I asked.

“Everything, Hastings. Everything. Now, Inspector, I want you to
come with us to ‘The Laurels’ at once. We have no time to lose.”

We drove to Hampstead in a taxi. When we arrived at ‘The Laurels’,
Poirot told the taxi to wait, and we walked up to the front door.

Poirot rang the bell, and a servant opened the door.

“Is Mrs. Everard at home?” asked Poirot.

“Yes, sir. But she is engaged at the moment.”

“Tell her that Monsieur Hercule Poirot is here, and that it is
most urgent.”

The servant went away, and a few minutes later she returned and
asked us to follow her. She took us to a large, well-furnished
room, where a middle-aged woman was sitting at a table.

“Mrs. Everard?” said Poirot, bowing.

“Yes. What can I do for you?”

“I have come to see your visitor, Mrs. Everard. The Monsieur
O’Murphy.”

The woman’s face turned pale. “I don’t know what you mean,” she
said. “I have no visitor of that name.”

“Come, come, Mrs. Everard,” said Poirot. “It is no use. We know
that he is here. And we also know that Frau Bertha Ebenthal is
here.”

The woman looked at him for a moment, and then she suddenly burst
into tears.

“It’s not my fault!” she cried. “They forced me to do it! They said
they would kill me if I didn’t!”

“Who forced you?” asked Poirot.

“The Germans! They said they would kill me if I didn’t let them
use my house.”

“And where is the Prime Minister?” asked Poirot.

“He is upstairs,” she sobbed. “In the back bedroom.”

We rushed upstairs, and in the back bedroom we found the Prime
Minister. He was lying on the bed, gagged and bound, but he was
unharmed.

We quickly released him, and he told us what had happened. He had
been kidnapped by a band of men, who had taken him to the farm in
France, and then brought him back to England in a submarine.

“In a submarine!” I cried. “So that is how they did it!”

“Yes,” said Poirot. “It was a very clever plan. But they made one
mistake.”

“What was that?” I asked.

“They forgot that Hercule Poirot has the little grey cells.”

We took the Prime Minister back to London, and he was able to
attend the Conference after all. It was a great triumph for him,
and for England.

And what of the kidnappers? They were all captured, including
O’Murphy and Frau Bertha Ebenthal. It turned out that O’Murphy had
been a German spy all along, and that he had been the one who had
led the Prime Minister into the trap.

And the first attack? That had been a clever trick to divert
suspicion from the real kidnapping. The masked men had been
O’Murphy’s accomplices, and the whole thing had been carefully
planned to make it look like an unsuccessful attempt.

“But what about the bullet wound?” I asked.

“That was a very small wound, Hastings. A mere scratch. It was
easily done.”

“And Captain Daniels?”

“He was an innocent victim. He knew nothing of the plot, and he
was lucky to escape with his life.”

“And Mrs. Everard?”

“She was a weak woman who had been coerced into helping the Germans.
She was not a criminal in the true sense of the word.”

“And the twin sisters? What about them?”

“Ah, that was a very clever idea of Frau Bertha Ebenthal’s. She
used her sister to create an alibi for herself, so that she could
be in two places at once. But it did not fool Hercule Poirot.”

“Well, Poirot,” I said, as we sat in his rooms that evening, “you
have done it again. You have saved the Prime Minister, and you
have saved England.”

Poirot smiled. “It was nothing, Hastings. Nothing at all. It was
merely a matter of using the little grey cells. And now, if you
will excuse me, I must go and finish mopping my grey suit. There
is still a small spot of grease that I have not yet removed.”

And so ended the case of the Kidnapped Prime Minister. It was one
of the most remarkable cases in which Poirot was ever involved,
and it was a testament to his extraordinary genius.

But for Poirot, it was just another case. A case that had been
solved by the use of the little grey cells. And that, after all,
was all that mattered.

The end.

We entered the special train, which had been placed at our
disposal. Detective Barnes was a tall, fair man, with a very
professional air; and Major Norman, of the Intelligence Department,
was a dark, alert young officer. Both were evidently keenly
interested in the case.

“I suppose you’ll want to go straight to the abandoned farm,
Monsieur Poirot?” asked the Major.

Poirot thought a moment.

“No, I think not. I should prefer to visit the scene of the
shooting first.”

Major Norman looked surprised. “But that happened this morning!
It can have very little to do with the abduction, can it?”

“It is possible,” replied Poirot. “At any rate, I shall be
interested to see the spot. Can we get there easily?”

“Oh, yes. We can go by car from London.”

“_Très bien_! I will go with you, Major Norman. Captain Hastings
and Detective Barnes will proceed to France.”

“What?” I cried, in dismay. “And leave you?”

“It must be so, my friend. I have a little idea—a very little
idea—which I must follow up. And I cannot be in two places at once.
You will keep your eyes and ears open, and you will report to me
from time to time by telegram. You understand?”

I did not. But I knew better than to argue with Poirot. He had a
habit of keeping his own counsel until he was ready to speak.
So, with a heavy heart, I saw the train pull out of the station,
leaving my friend and the Major behind.

We chatted in a desultory fashion with Major Norman. In the centre
of the little group of men on the platform I recognized a little
ferret-faced fellow talking to a tall, fair man. He was an old
acquaintance of Poirot’s—Detective-Inspector Japp, supposed to be
one of the smartest of Scotland Yard’s officers. He came over and
greeted my friend cheerfully.

Poirot leaned back in his seat and closed his eyes, his fingers tapping a rhythmic tattoo upon his knee. “Tell me, Inspector,” he said suddenly, “this O’Murphy—what is his record? Is he a man of many friends? A man of the home? Or is he one who frequents the cafés and the clubs?” Japp pulled a notebook from his pocket. “An excellent record, Monsieur Poirot. Ten years in the force, three years as a special guard. He’s a widower with no children, lives alone in lodgings in Pimlico. Quiet sort of chap, usually. No known political leanings, though his family in Ireland are said to be a bit ‘hot’ on the national question. We’ve found nothing in his past to suggest he’d sell out to the Boche, but that Soho business is black—very black.”

Poirot sat in silence for some time, his eyes closed, his hands folded over his cane. Then, with a suddenness that made Japp jump, he leaned forward. “The movement of the train, it is not good for the digestion,” he remarked, “but for the brain, perhaps it provides a necessary stimulus. Tell me, Inspector, what have you learned of the chauffeur O’Murphy? Beyond his disappearance, I mean. And what of these aunts of Captain Daniels? A Mrs. Everard of Hampstead, was it not?”

Poirot settled himself into his seat, his eyes half-closed. “And what of the woman, Bertha Ebenthal?” he asked, his voice barely a whisper. Detective Barnes stiffened. “We’ve had our eye on her for months, Monsieur Poirot. She’s the most dangerous German agent in England. We know she’s behind half the pacifist propaganda in the country, but she’s as slippery as an eel. We’ve never been able to pin a thing on her. At the moment, she’s believed to be in London, but we’ve lost track of her.” Poirot nodded slowly. “A woman of great ability, no doubt. It is interesting, is it not, that she should be at liberty at such a moment? One wonders if her path has crossed that of our friend O’Murphy—or perhaps the excellent Captain Daniels?”

The journey was a silent one. Poirot sat with his eyes closed, his hands folded over his stomach. He appeared to be sleeping, but the occasional twitch of his eyebrows told me that his “little grey cells” were working at high pressure. As for myself, I was consumed by a fever of impatience. Every moment that passed brought us nearer to the fatal hour of the Conference, and yet we seemed no nearer to solving the mystery. It was not until we were nearing Dover that Poirot broke the silence. He turned to Detective-Inspector Japp. “Tell me,” he said, “about this shooting affair. You saw the Prime Minister’s wound?”

Poirot sat in silence for a few moments, the rhythmic clicking of the wheels seemingly aiding his thoughts. Suddenly he turned to Japp. "The restaurant in Soho, my friend—the place where O’Murphy’s car was found. What do we know of it?" Japp shrugged. "It is a small place, the 'Chat Noir'. The proprietor is a woman, a Frau Bertha Ebenthal. We have had our eye on her for some time; she is undoubtedly a German agent of some importance, but she is as slippery as an eel. We raided the place an hour after the car was found, but she had a perfect alibi, and there was no sign of O’Murphy. She claimed she had never seen the car before." Poirot’s eyes twinkled. "An alibi? I have always a great deal of interest in an alibi. It is so often too perfect."

It was a curious journey. The Scotland Yard men crowded together.
Maps of Northern France were spread out, and eager forefingers
traced the lines of roads and villages. Each man had his own pet
theory. Poirot showed none of his usual loquacity, but sat staring
in front of him, with an expression on his face that reminded me
of a puzzled child. I talked to Norman, whom I found quite an
amusing fellow. On arriving at Dover Poirot’s behaviour moved me
to intense amusement. The little man, as he went on board the boat,
clutched desperately at my arm. The wind was blowing lustily.

“_Mon Dieu!_” he murmured. “This is terrible!”

“Have courage, Poirot,” I cried. “You will succeed. You will find
him. I am sure of it.”

“Ah, _mon ami_, you mistake my emotion. It is this villainous sea
that troubles me! The _mal de mer_—it is horrible suffering!”

“Oh!” I said, rather taken aback.

The first throb of the engines was felt, and Poirot groaned and
closed his eyes.

“Major Norman has a map of Northern France if you would like to
study it?”

Poirot shook his head impatiently.

The detective officers and the military men who were awaiting us
seemed to me very efficient. A car was provided for us and, with
Major Norman and Detective-Inspector Japp, we were soon tearing
along the road towards C——. I thought that we were wasting time,
for surely the Prime Minister was not still in that neighbourhood?

“If the Prime Minister had been anywhere near C——, his presence
must have been discovered long ago,” I remarked.

Japp shook his head. “I’m not so sure. They say it’s a big area of
downland, very wild and lonely, and there’s any amount of disused
farms and cottages. Our people have been through a good many, but
it’s a slow business.”

“Yes,” Poirot interrupted, “and, besides, there are many little
ways of concealing a man.”

“Then you think he _is_ there?” I said, in some surprise.

“I? I think nothing at all. I am just a little Belgian, with no
ideas. But I should like to see the farm where Captain Daniels
was found.”

“The car is already there, monsieur,” said the driver, turning his
head.

I looked out of the window. We were passing through a small village.
The car turned off the main road, and, after a few minutes, we
came to a lonely farm-house, which had obviously been derelict for
some time. Several cars were standing in the yard, and a couple
of gendarmes were on guard.

We got out. A tall, dark man, with a very keen, clever face, came
forward and greeted us.

“This is Monsieur Lefebvre, of the Sûreté,” said Major Norman,
introducing us. “He has the case in hand.”

The Frenchman shook hands with us cordially.

“I am glad to see you, Monsieur Poirot. Your reputation has preceded
you. We are working hard, but, so far, we have found nothing. The
Prime Minister has vanished, as though into thin air!”

“And the car?”

“Ah, the car! We have found that, as you know. It was abandoned
about two miles from here. But as for the Prime Minister——”

He shrugged his shoulders.

“And Captain Daniels?”

“He is in the house. He is still very much upset, but he will tell
us all he can.”

We followed Monsieur Lefebvre into the farm-house. In a small,
bare room a young man was sitting, his head in his hands. He looked
up as we entered. He was a good-looking young fellow, with a
clever, mobile face.

“This is Captain Daniels,” said Lefebvre.

Poirot stepped forward. “I am Hercule Poirot. I have been sent by
the British Government to find the Prime Minister. Can you tell
me anything—anything at all—that may help me?”

The young man shook his head. “I’m afraid not. I’ve told the French
police everything I know. It all happened so suddenly. We were
driving along, and then—well, the next thing I knew I was being
gagged and bound. I tried to struggle, but it was no use. There
were several of them, and they were all masked.”

“Did you hear any names mentioned?”

“No.”

“And you saw nothing?”

“Nothing. It was quite dark.”

“Did you notice anything about the car?”

“It seemed a very powerful one. And it was driven at a great pace.”

“And you have no idea where the Prime Minister is?”

“None whatever. I wish to God I had!”

Poirot looked at him for a moment in silence. Then he turned to
Monsieur Lefebvre.

“I should like to see the place where the car was found.”

“Certainly. It is about two miles from here, as I said. If you will
come with me, I will show you.”

We all got into the car again, and drove for a few minutes along
a narrow, winding road. Then Monsieur Lefebvre pointed to a spot
where the grass was trampled and torn.

“There,” he said. “The car was standing there. It had evidently
been driven off the road.”

Poirot got out and examined the ground carefully.

“Yes,” he said, “I see. And which way did it go?”

“We cannot tell. The tracks are lost on the hard road.”

Poirot nodded. “I see. Well, there is nothing more to be done here.
Let us return to the farm.”

When we got back, Poirot asked to see the room where Captain Daniels
had been found. It was a small, dark room, with a single window.
On the floor were some pieces of rope and a dirty handkerchief.

“That is where he was lying,” said Monsieur Lefebvre.

Poirot picked up the rope and examined it.

“A very stout rope,” he remarked. “And the handkerchief?”

“It was used as a gag.”

Poirot smelled it. “Chloroform,” he said. “Yes, it is as you said.”

He looked round the room. “Is there anything else?”

“Nothing.”

Poirot walked to the window and looked out.

“A very lonely spot,” he said. “No houses for miles.”

“Yes. That is why they chose it, no doubt.”

Poirot turned away from the window. “Well,” he said, “I have seen
all I want to see. Now, if you will be so good, I should like to
go to Boulogne.”

“To Boulogne?” I cried in surprise. “But the Prime Minister is not
there!”

“Perhaps not, Hastings. But I have a little idea. Monsieur Lefebvre,
is it possible for me to have a few words with the chauffeur of
the car that was found in the side road—the real car, I mean?”

“Certainly. He is in Boulogne now. I will take you to him.”

We drove back to Boulogne, and were soon in the presence of the
chauffeur. He was a young man, with a very honest, open face.

“Now, my man,” said Poirot, “I want you to tell me exactly what
happened this morning.”

“Well, sir, it was like this. We were driving along, about five
miles from Boulogne, when we saw a car standing in the middle of
the road. A man was standing beside it, waving his arms. I pulled
up, and as I did so, several men rushed out from the side of the
road. They were all masked, sir. They dragged me and the A.D.C. out
of the car, and then they gagged and bound us. They put us into
the other car—the one that was standing in the road—and drove off.
After a bit, they stopped and lifted us out, and left us in a ditch
by the side of the road. We managed to get free after a while, and
then we found the car—our own car, I mean—in a side road.”

“I see. And did you notice anything about the men?”

“No, sir. They were all masked, as I said.”

“And the car—the one they put you into?”

“It was a big, powerful car, sir. I couldn’t say what make it was.”

“I see. Well, thank you. That will do.”

When the man had gone, Poirot turned to Monsieur Lefebvre.

“Now, monsieur, I have a request to make. I should like to see the
A.D.C. who was with the chauffeur.”

“Certainly. He is also in Boulogne.”

The A.D.C., a young Captain named Arbuthnot, was soon found. His
story was the same as the chauffeur’s.

“And you saw nothing else?” asked Poirot.

“Nothing. It was all over in a few minutes.”

“I see. Well, thank you, Captain.”

When we were alone again, Poirot turned to me.

“Well, Hastings, what do you think of it all?”

“It’s a most extraordinary case,” I said. “I can’t make head or
tail of it.”

“Neither can I,” said Poirot. “But I have a little idea. Hastings,
I want you to go to the telegraph office and send a telegram for
me.”

“A telegram? To whom?”

“To London. To Lord Estair.”

“What do you want me to say?”

“Just this: ‘Please send me the address of Mrs. Everard at
Hampstead.’ That is all.”

“Mrs. Everard? But what has she to do with it?”

“Perhaps nothing, Hastings. But I have a little idea. Go and send
the telegram, and then meet me at the hotel.”

I did as I was told, and half an hour later I found Poirot in his
room at the hotel. He was sitting in an armchair, staring into
space.

“Well,” I said, “I’ve sent the telegram. Now, tell me, what is this
idea of yours?”

Poirot shook his head. “Not yet, Hastings. It is only a little idea.
We must wait for the answer to the telegram.”

It was not until late that evening that the answer arrived. Poirot
tore it open and read it.

“Ah!” he said. “That is good. Now, Hastings, we must go back to
England.”

“To England?” I cried. “But we’ve only just come!”

“I know, I know. But there is nothing more for us to do here. We
must go back to London.”

“But the Prime Minister?”

“He will be found, Hastings. Do not fear. He will be found.”

We caught the night boat to Dover, and by the next morning we were
back in London. Poirot went straight to his rooms, and I followed
him.

“Now,” I said, “will you tell me what it’s all about?”

“In a little minute, Hastings. But first, I must make a telephone
call.”

He went to the telephone and was soon in communication with Lord
Estair.

“Is that you, milord? It is Hercule Poirot. Yes, I have returned.
No, I have not found the Prime Minister yet, but I am on his track.
I want you to do something for me. I want you to find out if
Captain Daniels has an aunt living at Hampstead—a Mrs. Everard.
Yes, that is right. And I want the address. You have it? Thank
you. And one more thing. I want you to find out if anyone has
called at that address in the last twenty-four hours. A doctor,
perhaps? Or a nurse? Thank you, milord. I will wait.”

He hung up the receiver and turned to me.

“Now, Hastings, we shall see.”

“But I don’t understand,” I said. “What has Mrs. Everard to do with
it? And why a doctor or a nurse?”

“Wait, Hastings, wait. All will be clear in good time.”

A few minutes later the telephone rang. Poirot answered it.

“Yes? Yes, milord. I see. A doctor called there this morning? And
he is still there? Thank you, milord. That is all I wanted to know.”

He hung up the receiver and turned to me, his eyes sparkling with
excitement.

“Now, Hastings, we must go to Hampstead! There is not a moment to
lose!”

We jumped into a taxi and were soon tearing through the streets of
London. Poirot was in a state of great suppressed excitement.

“Quickly, quickly!” he cried to the driver. “It is a matter of life
and death!”

We reached Hampstead in record time. Poirot directed the driver to
a small, quiet street, and we stopped in front of a neat little
house.

“This is it,” said Poirot. “Stay in the taxi, Hastings. I shall
not be long.”

He jumped out and ran up the steps of the house. He rang the bell,
and a few minutes later the door was opened by a neat-looking maid.
Poirot spoke to her for a moment, and then he was admitted.

I waited in the taxi, my heart beating fast with excitement. What
was Poirot doing? What had he found out?

Ten minutes passed—twenty minutes—half an hour. I was just
beginning to get anxious when the door opened and Poirot appeared.
He was supporting a tall, elderly man, whose face was pale and
drawn.

I gasped in astonishment. It was the Prime Minister!

Poirot helped him into the taxi, and then he jumped in beside him.

“To Downing Street!” he cried to the driver. “And drive like the
wind!”

As we sped through the streets, Poirot turned to the Prime Minister.

“You are safe now, monsieur. All is well.”

The Prime Minister nodded feebly. “Thank you,” he murmured. “Thank
you.”

“But how—how did you find him?” I cried.

“It was very simple, Hastings. But I will tell you all about it
later. First, we must get the Prime Minister to Downing Street.”

We reached Downing Street in a few minutes, and the Prime Minister
was soon in the care of his friends. Poirot and I were ushered into
a small room, where we were joined by Lord Estair and Mr. Dodge.

“Monsieur Poirot!” cried Lord Estair, shaking him warmly by the
hand. “How can we ever thank you? You have saved the country!”

“It was nothing, milord,” said Poirot modestly. “It was just a
little matter of the grey cells.”

“But how did you do it?” asked Mr. Dodge. “We were all completely
at sea.”

“It was the shooting affair that first gave me the clue,” said
Poirot. “As I told you, it was so—how do you say?—melodramatic. It
did not ring true. And then there was the disappearance of
O’Murphy. Why should he disappear? If he were a traitor, why should
he save the Prime Minister’s life? It did not make sense.”

“But then, who was the traitor?” asked Lord Estair.

“There was no traitor, milord. At least, not in the way you mean.”

“What do you mean?”

“I mean that the shooting affair was a—what do you call it?—a
‘put-up job.’ It was arranged by the Prime Minister himself!”

“What?” we all cried in unison.

“Yes,” said Poirot. “The Prime Minister wanted to disappear. He
wanted to go somewhere where he would not be disturbed, where he
could think out his policy for the Conference. And so he arranged
this little comedy. He told O’Murphy to take that turning, and he
had his friends—or perhaps they were not his friends, but people
he could trust—to play the part of the masked men. He even fired
the shots himself—or rather, he had them fired. And then he went
to France, as arranged. But he did not go to the Commander-in-Chief’s
house. Instead, he went to a little house in Hampstead, the house
of Mrs. Everard, the aunt of his secretary, Captain Daniels.”

“But why Mrs. Everard’s house?” I asked.

“Because it was the last place anyone would think of looking for
him. And Captain Daniels was in on the secret, of course. He
arranged the whole thing in France—the bogus car, the gagging and
binding—all to make it look like a kidnapping. It was very clever,
very clever indeed.”

“But the Prime Minister—why did he do it?” asked Lord Estair.

“Because, as I said, he wanted to be alone. He was tired,
overworked, and he felt that he could not face the Conference
without some rest and time for thought. And so he took this
extraordinary way of getting it.”

“But the doctor?” I asked. “Who was the doctor who called at the
house?”

“That was the Prime Minister’s own doctor, whom he had summoned to
attend to his wound—the wound that was supposed to have been caused
by the assassin’s bullet, but which was really only a slight cut
he had given himself.”

“Well,” said Mr. Dodge, “it’s the most extraordinary story I’ve ever
heard!”

“Yes,” said Lord Estair. “But the important thing is that the Prime
Minister is safe, and he will be able to attend the Conference.”

“Thanks to Monsieur Poirot,” said Mr. Dodge.

“It was nothing, messieurs,” said Poirot, bowing. “And now, if you
will excuse me, I think I will return to my rooms. I have a little
matter of a ‘charlady’ and her husband to attend to.”

And with a twinkle in his eye, the little Belgian detective led
the way out of the room.

The first news we heard on arrival at the quay was that there was
still no news of the Prime Minister. A car was waiting for us,
and Poirot and I, with Inspector Japp and Major Norman, were
whirled away through the dark lanes.

“It’s a most extraordinary thing,” said Japp, as he sat with his
notebook on his knee. “Here’s the car—found in the road. Here’s the
driver and the A.D.C., both gagged and bound, and unable to give
any information. Here’s the second car—found in the farmyard, with
the secretary, Daniels, also gagged and bound. But where’s the
Prime Minister? It’s enough to make a cat laugh!”

“That’s a very sound remark, Japp,” said Major Norman. “I’m glad
you’re able to see the humorous side of things.”

Japp grunted. “Wait until you’ve been at this sort of thing as long
as I have, and you won’t feel like laughing then. It’s no joke to
lose a Prime Minister!”

Poirot had not spoken. He was looking out of the window, at the
leafless trees and the dark sky. Suddenly he spoke.

“What is the time?”

“A quarter past three.”

“In the morning?”

“Yes.”

“And the Conference is at nine o’clock to-night?”

“Yes.”

“Then we have just seventeen hours and three-quarters!”

“Exactly.”

Poirot sighed. “What I want to know is, where is the third car?”

“The third car?” I asked.

“But yes! There was the real car, and the bogus car. And then
there must have been a third car, to take away the Prime Minister
and his captors.”

Japp nodded. “We’re on the track of that now. A car was seen near
here about four o’clock yesterday afternoon.”

“_Tiens!_” said Poirot. “That’s interesting.”

“It was a big car—a dark-coloured one. It was seen going towards
the coast.”

“The coast? Then they’ve taken him back to England?”

“It looks like it.”

“Or perhaps they’ve taken him to some little fishing village, and
got him away by boat?”

“That’s possible too.”

Poirot relapsed into silence. He seemed to be deep in thought.

“We’ll be at General Headquarters in a few minutes,” said Major
Norman. “I’ve arranged for rooms for you all.”
