“That is most kind of you, Major,” said Poirot. “But, if you do
not mind, I would prefer to go on at once to the farm where they
found the secretary, Daniels.”

“The farm? But it’s miles away!”

“No matter. I wish to see it.”

“Very well. I’ll tell the driver.”

We went straight to the scene of the kidnapping, and the abandoned
farm where the chauffeur and the A.D.C. had been found. Then to
another farm, some ten miles away, where the second car and Captain
Daniels had been discovered.

Poirot examined both places with his usual thoroughness. He spent
some time in the farm where Captain Daniels had been found, and I
found him intently studying a small, dark object on the floor of
the room. He did not say anything, but I saw his eyes sparkle as
he put it into his pocket.

The French police were most helpful. M. Lefebvre, of the _Sûreté_,
had the case in hand. He and Poirot had many long and whispered
consultations. They seemed to agree perfectly.

“Ah,” I said, as we stood together in the dusk of the evening, “at
last there is light!”

“Light?” said Poirot, his eyes twinkling. “I don’t know. I see it
not.”

“But Lefebvre?”

“He and I, we have much in common. He is a man of method. He has
his own ideas. He and I—we are in accord. But I do not see the
light—yet.”

“And you think the Prime Minister will be found in time for the
Conference?”

Poirot shrugged his shoulders. “I should say—no.”

“What?”

“The time is too short. But, _n’importe_! One must do what one
can.”

We were staying in a small hotel at C——. We had just finished a
late and somewhat hurried dinner when Poirot was called to the
telephone. When he came back his face was grave.

“There is more news. O’Murphy has been found.”

“Where?”

“In London. At the very restaurant where his car was discovered.
He has been there all the time—but he is dead.”

“Dead?”

“Yes, shot through the heart. He was discovered in a small upstairs
room. It is a bad business.”

“Then he was a traitor, after all?”

“Wait, wait, _mon ami_! One must be sure. He was shot through the
heart, remember.”

“But what does that prove?”

“It proves that he was a man who knew too much. If he had been a
traitor, why should they kill him? No, no, I begin to think that
O’Murphy was an honest man.”

“Then why was he at that restaurant?”

“That is what we have to find out. But, come, we must go to the
Conference. The time is short.”

“But what can you do there?”

“Who knows? One may at least see—and hear.”

We drove to Versailles. The great Salle des Glaces was a scene of
intense and suppressed excitement. The delegates of the Allied
Powers were all there, but the one man who could have dominated the
situation was missing. The atmosphere was one of gloom and
foreboding.

Lord Estair and Mr. Dodge were there, looking pale and anxious.
They came up to us at once.

“Well?”

Poirot shook his head. “I have nothing to tell you—yet.”

“But the time? It is nearly nine o’clock!”

“I know, I know. But one must have patience.”

At that moment a stir went through the room. A tall, dark man had
just entered. He was followed by a small, fair-haired woman,
exquisitely dressed.

“Who is that?” I whispered to Major Norman.

“That is the German delegate, Baron von Hoehm. And the lady with
him is his wife.”

“She is very beautiful,” I said.

“Yes, and as clever as she is beautiful. They say she is the real
power behind the German Government.”

Poirot was looking at the lady with intense interest.

“_Tiens!_” he murmured. “That is interesting.”

“What is interesting?”

“The lady’s face. I have seen it before.”

“Where?”

“In a photograph. But where—where?”

He tapped his forehead impatiently.

“Wait—I have it! It was in the dossier of the Prime Minister’s
secretaries.”

“What?”

“Yes. She is the aunt of Captain Daniels—Frau Bertha Ebenthal!”

“Frau Bertha Ebenthal? But Lord Estair said his aunts were a Mrs.
Everard and a Miss Daniels!”

“Exactly. And Frau Bertha Ebenthal is Mrs. Everard!”

“Then Captain Daniels is a traitor?”

“It would seem so. But wait—there is more.”

Poirot was watching the lady intently. She was talking to one of
the French delegates, her eyes sparkling, her whole face full of
animation. Suddenly she turned and looked straight at Poirot. For
a moment her face went deadly pale. Then she recovered herself and
continued her conversation.

“She knows me,” whispered Poirot. “She knows who I am. That is
well. Now we shall see.”

He moved towards the lady, bowing low.

“Madame, I think we have met before?”

The lady looked at him with a cold, haughty stare.

“I think not, monsieur. You are mistaken.”

“I think not, madame. It was in London—at the house of your nephew,
Captain Daniels.”

The lady’s eyes flashed with anger.

“I have no nephew of that name, monsieur. You are making a mistake.”

“I think not, madame. And I think you know more of the Prime
Minister’s disappearance than you care to say.”

The lady laughed scornfully.

“You are absurd, monsieur! I know nothing of the Prime Minister’s
disappearance. Why should I?”

“Because, madame, you are a German spy!”

A gasp of astonishment went through the room. Lord Estair and Mr.
Dodge hurried forward.

“Monsieur Poirot! What are you saying?”

“I am saying the truth, milord. This lady is Frau Bertha Ebenthal,
the most dangerous German spy in Europe. And she is the aunt of
Captain Daniels!”

The lady drew herself up to her full height.

“This is an insult! Baron, come!”

She turned to her husband, but Poirot stepped in front of her.

“One moment, madame. I have something to show you.”

He drew from his pocket the small, dark object he had found in the
farm. It was a small, gold-mounted scent-bottle.

“This was found in the room where Captain Daniels was discovered.
It has your initials on it, madame—B. E.”

The lady’s face went white. For a moment she looked as though she
would faint. Then, with a sudden, swift movement, she snatched the
bottle from Poirot’s hand and flung it onto the floor, where it
shattered into a thousand pieces.

“It is a lie!” she cried. “A lie! I know nothing of it!”

“But the bottle was there, madame,” said Poirot quietly. “And now,
messieurs, I think we have the key to the mystery. Captain Daniels
is a traitor, and he has been working in league with his aunt, Frau
Bertha Ebenthal. They have kidnapped the Prime Minister, and they
are holding him somewhere—heaven knows where!”

“But where? Where?” cried Lord Estair.

“That we have to find out. But first we must arrest this lady.”

But Frau Bertha Ebenthal had already disappeared. In the confusion
that followed she had managed to slip out of the room.

“Quick! After her!” cried Mr. Dodge.

But it was too late. The lady had vanished.

“She must be found!” cried Lord Estair. “She is the only one who
can tell us where the Prime Minister is!”

“I am not so sure of that,” said Poirot thoughtfully. “There is
another person who may know.”

“Who?”

“Captain Daniels.”

“But he is at the farm, under guard!”

“Is he? I wonder.”

Poirot turned to Major Norman.

“Major, will you tele-phone to the farm and see if Captain Daniels
is still there?”

In a few minutes Major Norman returned, his face pale.

“He is gone! He managed to escape an hour ago!”

“I thought as much,” said Poirot. “Then they are together. And
they have the Prime Minister with them.”

“But where? Where?”

Poirot shook his head. “I do not know. But I have an idea. A very
small idea.”

He turned to Lord Estair.

“Milord, you said that Captain Daniels had an aunt who lived near
Ascot—a Miss Daniels?”

“Yes.”

“And you have searched her house?”

“Of course. But there was nothing there.”

“And Mrs. Everard’s house at Hampstead?”

“Yes. Nothing there either.”

“And you are sure there are no other relatives?”

“None that we know of.”

Poirot nodded thoughtfully. “Then it must be one of those two.
But which? Which?”

He sat down and buried his face in his hands. For a long time he
remained motionless. Then, suddenly, he looked up, his eyes
sparkling.

“I have it! I have it! The spot of grease!”

“The spot of grease?” I cried. “What do you mean?”

“Do you not remember, Hastings? The spot of grease on my suit! I
could not remove it! And then I realized—it was not grease at all!
It was something else!”

“But what has that to do with the Prime Minister?”

“Everything! Everything! Come, we must go to London at once!”

“To London? But the Prime Minister is in France!”

“Is he? I wonder. Come, there is no time to lose!”

We drove to the station and caught the midnight train to London.
During the journey Poirot was silent and absorbed in thought. When
we arrived at Charing Cross it was early morning.

“Now,” said Poirot, “to Hampstead! To the house of Mrs. Everard!”

We drove to a small, quiet house in a suburban street. Poirot rang
the bell, and a neat-looking maid opened the door.

“Is Mrs. Everard at home?”

“No, sir. She is away in the country.”

“And Captain Daniels?”

“He is away too, sir.”

Poirot nodded. “I see. And is there anyone else in the house?”

“Only the cook, sir.”

“May we come in? I am a friend of Captain Daniels.”

The maid hesitated, but Poirot’s charming manner soon overcame her
scruples. We were shown into a small, comfortably furnished
drawing-room.

Poirot began to wander round the room, examining everything with
the greatest interest. Suddenly he stopped in front of a large
mahogany cabinet.

“_Tiens!_” he murmured. “That is interesting.”

“What is it?” I asked.

“This cabinet. It is very fine, is it not?”

He began to feel along the edges of the cabinet with his deft
fingers. Suddenly there was a click, and a secret door swung open.

Inside was a small, dark space, and in it, gagged and bound, was a
man!

“The Prime Minister!” I cried.

It was indeed Mr. MacAdam. He was unconscious, but alive.

Poirot quickly cut his bonds and removed the gag. In a few minutes
the Prime Minister opened his eyes.

“Where am I?” he murmured.

“You are safe, monsieur,” said Poirot. “You are in London.”

“In London? But I was in France!”

“No, monsieur. You never left England.”

“What?”

“It was all a clever plot, monsieur. You were kidnapped on your way
to Charing Cross, and brought here. The man who went to France in
your place was an impostor—a man who had been carefully coached
to play the part.”

“But the wound? The bullet?”

“That was part of the plot, monsieur. To give the impostor a reason
for wearing a bandage, which would hide his face.”

“But who was the impostor?”

“O’Murphy, the chauffeur! He was a man of the same height and
build as yourself, and with the bandage on his face he could easily
pass for you.”

“And Captain Daniels?”

“He was the leader of the plot. He and his aunt, Frau Bertha
Ebenthal. They had everything arranged—the bogus car in France,
the abandoned farms—everything to make it seem as though you had
been kidnapped in France.”

“But why did they kill O’Murphy?”

“Because he knew too much. Once he had played his part, he was no
longer of any use to them. And they could not afford to take any
risks.”

“And where are they now?”

“They are gone, monsieur. But we shall find them. Hercule Poirot
does not fail!”

At that moment the door opened, and Lord Estair and Mr. Dodge
entered. They had followed us from France.

“The Prime Minister!” they cried. “Thank God!”

“Yes, messieurs,” said Poirot. “He is safe. And now, if you will
excuse me, I have a little matter to attend to.”

He turned to the Prime Minister.

“Monsieur, you will be able to attend the Conference after all.
There is still time.”

“But how? The Conference is at Versailles!”

“We have a special train waiting for you, monsieur. And a
destroyer. You will be there in time.”

The Prime Minister smiled. “Thank you, Monsieur Poirot. England
owes you a great debt.”

Poirot bowed low. “It was a small matter, monsieur. A mere matter
of the ‘little grey cells’.”

As we left the house, I turned to Poirot.

“But how did you know, Poirot? How did you know the Prime Minister
was here?”

“It was the spot of grease, Hastings! Do you not remember? I said
it was not grease. It was—chocolate!”

“Chocolate?”

“Yes. A small piece of chocolate that had been dropped on my suit.
And then I remembered—Captain Daniels was always eating chocolate!
It was his one weakness. And when I found a similar spot of
chocolate in the drawing-room of Mrs. Everard’s house, I knew that
he had been there recently. And if he was there, the Prime
Minister must be there too!”

“But what about the scent-bottle in France?”

“That was a ‘red herring’, Hastings! A little device of my own to
frighten Frau Bertha Ebenthal and make her reveal herself. I had
found the bottle in the Prime Minister’s car, and I knew it
belonged to her. But it was not found in the farm—I put it there
myself!”

“Poirot! You are incredible!”

“No, Hastings. I am only—Hercule Poirot!”

And so it was that the Prime Minister of England arrived at
Versailles just in time to save the Conference—and the world—from
a disastrous peace. And the secret of his disappearance was well
guarded, until today.

“I have much to do, and I must not be hampered by the _mal de mer_.
Now, Hastings, you must go at once to the Commander-in-Chief’s
headquarters, where you will be met by his A.D.C. and find all the
latest news. As for me, I have a little something to do here. I
shall not be more than half an hour.”

“What are you going to do?”

“_Eh bien!_ I am going to see the hospitals.”

“The hospitals! But why? The Prime Minister is not in hospital.”

Poirot smiled. “One never knows. It is as well to be sure. There
was a little matter of a scratch, you remember. Now, don’t argue,
my friend. Go—go!”

I went. At General Headquarters I found everyone in a state of
intense excitement. The Prime Minister’s car had been found, in a
shed at a small farm not far from the spot where the bogus car had
been discovered. There was no sign of the Prime Minister, however.
The search was being redoubled. Every inch of ground for miles
round was being explored.

When Poirot rejoined me, he looked more like a puzzled child than
ever.

“_Rien_!” he murmured. “It is unbelievable! Can he have been
carried to Paris?”

“Not a chance. Every car is being stopped and searched.”

“Then he must be in this neighbourhood. But where—where?”

He sat down and buried his face in his hands.

“Think, Poirot—think!” I cried.

“I do think, my friend. But there is something I have missed—some
small detail that would make all the difference. What is it? I
cannot find it.”

“Perhaps there is some other clue?”

“None. We have the cars—the bogus A.D.C.—the real A.D.C.—and the
real chauffeur——”

“And the Prime Minister,” I added.

“Yes, and the Prime Minister. But he is the only thing we have
_not_ got!”

“Where are you going now?”

“I am going to see the secretary, Daniels.”

“But he can tell you nothing.”

“Perhaps. But one never knows.”

We drove to the farm where the secretary was being guarded. He
looked very white and ill, and his head was bandaged. He could,
however, tell us nothing more than we already knew. He had been
attacked from behind, and had known nothing more until he found
himself in the farm, gagged and bound.

“And the Prime Minister?”

“I know no more than you do. He was with me in the car. That is
all I can tell you.”

Poirot turned away, with a sigh.

“It is no use,” he said. “We must go back to London.”

“Back to London!” I cried, in astonishment. “But the Conference—the
Prime Minister——?”

“We can do nothing here. The Prime Minister is not in France. I
am sure of it now.”

“But where can he be?”

“In London. We must go back.”

“But this is madness! How could he be in London?”

“I do not know—but he is. We are wasting our time here. Come,
Hastings, we must catch the next boat.”

I followed him, still protesting, but Poirot was not to be moved.
On the boat he was again a prey to the _mal de mer_, and I could
get nothing more out of him.

When we reached London it was already morning. Poirot drove
straight to his rooms.

“Now, Hastings, I must think. Do not disturb me.”

I left him, and went to my own room. I was tired out, and fell fast
asleep. When I awoke it was nearly midday. I went to Poirot’s room.
He was sitting in his chair, with a look of triumph on his face.

“I have found it, Hastings! I have found it!”

“The Prime Minister?”

“No—the clue! The little detail that I had missed!”

“What is it?”

“It is so simple—so very simple! Why did I not see it before?”

“But what is it?”

“The Prime Minister’s wound!”

“His wound?”

“Yes. Do you not see, my friend? It was a scratch—a mere scratch.
And yet he went to a hospital to have it dressed! Why?”

“Because he is a very cautious man, I suppose.”

“No, no! That is not the reason. He went to the hospital because
he wanted to be seen—because he wanted people to know that he was
the Prime Minister!”

“But he didn’t reveal his identity.”

“Exactly! He wanted to be recognized—without appearing to wish it.
It was a very clever piece of work. But it was a mistake—a great
mistake!”

“I don’t understand.”

“You will, my friend—you will. Now, we must go to Hampstead.”

“To Hampstead? Why?”

“To see Mrs. Everard—Captain Daniels’ aunt.”

“But what has she to do with it?”

“Everything, my friend—everything!”

We drove to Hampstead in a taxi. Mrs. Everard’s house was a small,
unpretentious-looking villa. We were shown into a small drawing-room,
where we were joined by a middle-aged lady with a pleasant,
rather vacant face.

“Monsieur Poirot?” she said, looking at my friend. “I have heard
of you. My nephew has often spoken of you.”

“Ah! You are Captain Daniels’ aunt?”

“Yes. I am so worried about him. This terrible affair——”

“Quite so, madame. But I have come to see you on a rather different
matter. I believe you have a guest staying with you?”

Mrs. Everard looked surprised. “A guest? No, I have no one staying
with me.”

“Are you sure, madame?”

“Of course I am sure! Why should you think I have a guest?”

Poirot smiled. “Because, madame, I have reason to believe that the
Prime Minister is in this house!”

Mrs. Everard stared at him in amazement. “The Prime Minister! In
my house! You must be joking, Monsieur Poirot.”

“I am not joking, madame. I have reason to believe that he is here.”

“But I tell you he is not! I haven’t seen the Prime Minister for
years.”

Poirot looked at her keenly. “Are you sure, madame? Think again.
Has no one come to this house lately?”

“No one—except, of course, the doctor.”

“The doctor? What doctor?”

“Dr. Benson. He came to see my maid, who has been ill.”

“And where is this Dr. Benson now?”

“I don’t know. He left about an hour ago.”

“And the maid—where is she?”

“In her room, upstairs.”

“I should like to see her, if I may.”

“Certainly, if you wish. But I don’t see what she has to do with
the Prime Minister.”

Poirot did not answer. He followed Mrs. Everard upstairs to a small
bedroom at the back of the house. On the bed lay a woman, her head
swathed in bandages.

Poirot went up to the bed and looked at her. Then he turned to Mrs.
Everard.

“This is not your maid, madame,” he said quietly.

“Not my maid? Of course it is my maid! Who else should it be?”

Poirot reached out and pulled the bandages from the woman’s head.
As he did so, a cry of astonishment broke from my lips. For there,
lying on the bed, was the Prime Minister!

“Mr. MacAdam!” I cried.

The Prime Minister opened his eyes and looked at us. He seemed
dazed and confused.

“Where am I?” he murmured.

“You are safe, sir,” said Poirot. “You are in London.”

“In London? But I was in France——”

“No, sir. You have never been in France. You have been in this
house ever since you were kidnapped.”

“Kidnapped? Yes, I remember. . . . The car. . . . The masked men. . . .
And then—nothing more.”

“They chloroformed you, sir,” said Poirot. “And then they brought
you here.”

“But how did you find me, Monsieur Poirot?” asked Lord Estair,
who had just entered the room, accompanied by Mr. Dodge and several
other gentlemen.

Poirot smiled. “It was the wound, milord. The scratch that was not
a scratch.”

“I don’t understand,” said Lord Estair.

“It was very simple,” said Poirot. “The whole thing was a plot—a
very clever plot. The shooting affair was a blind—a piece of
theatricality to divert suspicion. The Prime Minister was never
shot at all. The man who was shot—or rather, who appeared to be
shot—was a double—an actor who had been hired for the purpose.”

“A double?”

“Yes. He was dressed to look like the Prime Minister, and he had
a small wound on his cheek, which had been carefully prepared
beforehand. He was the man who went to the hospital, and who
crossed to France in the destroyer. The real Prime Minister was
kidnapped in the lane, as you know, and brought here. The double
took his place, and it was he who was ‘abducted’ in France.”

“But why?”

“To gain time, milord. To keep the police and the military busy
searching for the Prime Minister in France, while he was safely
hidden here in London. It was a very clever idea.”

“And who was the mastermind behind all this?” asked Mr. Dodge.

Poirot’s face grew grave. “There were several people involved,
monsieur. But the leader—the one who planned it all—was someone
very close to the Prime Minister.”

“Who?”

Poirot turned and looked at a woman who was standing in the doorway.
She was tall and dark, with a hard, clever face.

“It was you, was it not, Frau Bertha Ebenthal?”

The woman started, and a look of fear came into her eyes.

“I—I don’t know what you mean!” she cried.

“I think you do,” said Poirot. “You are a German agent, madame.
You have been working for the German Government for years. It was
you who planned the kidnapping of the Prime Minister, and it was
you who hired the double to take his place.”

“It’s a lie!” cried the woman.

“Is it?” said Poirot. “Then perhaps you can explain why you are
here, in this house?”

“I—I am a friend of Mrs. Everard’s.”

“A very convenient friendship, madame. And I suppose it was also
a coincidence that you were seen in the company of Captain Daniels
and O’Murphy?”

The woman did not answer. She stood staring at Poirot, her face
pale and set.

“You are under arrest, madame,” said Detective-Inspector Japp,
stepping forward. “And I think you’d better come with me.”

As the woman was led away, Lord Estair turned to Poirot.

“Monsieur Poirot, I don’t know how to thank you. You have saved
England from a great catastrophe.”

Poirot bowed. “It was nothing, milord. A little matter of the
‘little grey cells,’ that is all.”

“But how did you know it was her?” I asked, as we drove back to
Poirot’s rooms.

“It was the restaurant in Soho, Hastings. The ‘unsavoury little
restaurant’ where O’Murphy’s car was found. It is a well-known
meeting-place for German agents. And I knew that Frau Ebenthal
was often to be found there. When I heard that O’Murphy had been
seen there, I began to suspect that he might be working for her.
And when I found the Prime Minister in Mrs. Everard’s house, I
knew I was right.”

“But what about Captain Daniels and O’Murphy?”

“They were both in it, Hastings. Daniels was the one who
arranged for the Prime Minister to be kidnapped, and O’Murphy was
the one who drove the car. They were both working for Frau Ebenthal.”

“And the double—what happened to him?”

“He is still in France, I expect. But I don’t think he will be
there for long. The French police are very clever, and they will
soon find him.”

Poirot leaned back in his seat and closed his eyes.

“It has been a long day, Hastings. And I am tired. But I am
satisfied. The Prime Minister is safe, and the Conference will go
on. England is saved!”

I looked at my friend with admiration. Once again, the “little grey
cells” of Hercule Poirot had triumphed.

We were met by a French officer and a chauffeur. Poirot looked
with interest at the car. It was a large, grey, powerful machine.

“You see,” said the Frenchman, “it is an exact replica of the
Commander-in-Chief’s own car. It even has the Union Jack on the
bonnet, as the other had.”

“_Tiens!_” said Poirot. “That is most interesting. And you have
discovered nothing of the real car?”

“Nothing. But there are hundreds of such cars, and many of them
are in the service of the British and French authorities. It is
extremely difficult to track them.”

“That is so,” agreed Poirot. “The problem is a very difficult one.
Where do you propose to take us?”

“To the farmhouse where the secretary was found. It is on the
outskirts of the village of C——, some ten miles from here.”

The car set off at a good pace, and in about twenty minutes’ time
we were at the scene of the tragedy. It was a lonely, dilapidated
building, which had evidently not been inhabited for some years.
The door was guarded by a French gendarme.

We went inside, and through into the kitchen, where a table and
two chairs had been placed for our convenience.

“The secretary was found in an upstairs room,” said the French
officer. “He was gagged and bound, as Lord Estair has told you.
There was no one else in the house. The villagers say that a car
was seen to stop there late in the afternoon, but they saw no one.”

“And the Prime Minister?”

“There was no trace of him.”

“Have you searched the neighbourhood?”

“The whole district has been scoured. Every wood and every field
has been searched. Every house has been visited.”

“And you have found nothing?”

“Nothing.”

“Then,” said Poirot, “I am afraid we are wasting our time here.”

“Wait a moment, Monsieur Poirot. There is something I should like
to show you.”

The officer led the way into a small room at the back of the house.
On the floor lay a small, dark object.

“What is that?” I asked.

“It is a piece of the Prime Minister’s tie. It was found on the
floor of this room.”

Poirot picked it up and examined it carefully. “Yes,” he said,
“it is indeed a piece of his tie. I recognize it from the
photographs I have seen. But what does it mean? Why should a piece
of his tie be here?”

“It was evidently torn off in the struggle,” suggested the officer.

“Perhaps. But it is strange. If there was a struggle, why did no
one hear anything? The villagers say they saw the car stop, but
they heard no cries, no sounds of a struggle.”

“The Prime Minister may have been chloroformed,” I suggested.

“Perhaps. But even so, one would expect to find some other traces
of a struggle. This piece of tie—it is so small. It is as though
it had been deliberately cut.”

“But why should anyone do that?”

“I do not know. It is very strange.”

Poirot stood for a moment in thought. Then he turned to the officer.

“I should like to see the room where the secretary was found.”

“Certainly. It is this way.”

We followed the officer up a narrow flight of stairs to a small
room on the first floor. In one corner of the room was a heap of
straw.

“This is where he was found,” said the officer. “He was lying on
the straw, gagged and bound.”

Poirot looked round the room. “There is nothing else?”

“Nothing.”

“_Très bien_. Then I think we have seen all there is to see here.”

We went downstairs again and out to the car.

“Where to now?” asked the officer.

“To the place where the real car was found,” said Poirot.

“That is some five miles from here, on the road to G.H.Q.”

We set off once more, and in a few minutes’ time we were at the
spot where the real car had been discovered. It was a narrow,
winding lane, with high hedges on either side.

“The car was found here,” said the officer, pointing to a spot
where the hedge was somewhat broken. “The chauffeur and the A.D.C.
were lying in the ditch, gagged and bound. The car was standing in
the middle of the road.”

“And the Prime Minister’s car—the bogus one—it was seen to pass
this way?”

“Yes. A peasant who was working in a field nearby saw it pass.
He noticed the Union Jack on the bonnet.”

“And it was going towards the farmhouse?”

“Yes.”

“And the real car—where was it going?”

“It was going towards G.H.Q.”

“I see. So the two cars must have passed each other?”

“Yes, they must have done so.”

“And yet no one saw them?”

“It is a very lonely road, Monsieur Poirot. There are very few
people about.”

“That is true. But still, it is strange.”

Poirot walked up and down the road for a few minutes, his eyes
fixed on the ground. Then he stopped and looked at the officer.

“There is one thing I do not understand. Why did the kidnappers
leave the real car here? Why did they not take it with them?”

“I suppose they thought it would be easier to escape in the bogus
one. It was less likely to be noticed.”

“Perhaps. But it seems a risky thing to do. If the real car had
been found sooner, the whole plot might have been discovered.”

“That is true. But luckily for them, it was not found until some
hours later.”

“Yes, luckily for them.”

Poirot fell into a fit of abstraction. He stood staring at the
ground, his brow furrowed in thought. Then he looked up.

“I should like to go to the Commander-in-Chief’s headquarters.”

“Certainly. It is about twenty miles from here.”

The journey to G.H.Q. was a silent one. Poirot seemed lost in
thought, and I did not care to disturb him. When we arrived, we
were met by a young A.D.C. who informed us that the
Commander-in-Chief was away, but that he had left instructions
that we were to be given every assistance.

“I should like to see the Prime Minister’s room,” said Poirot.

“Certainly. It is this way.”

The A.D.C. led the way upstairs to a large, comfortable room.

“The Prime Minister was to have stayed here to-night,” he said.
“His luggage has already arrived.”

Poirot looked round the room. “Has anything been touched?”

“No. Everything is just as it was when it arrived.”

Poirot went over to the dressing-table and began to examine the
articles upon it. He picked up a hairbrush and looked at it
closely. Then he picked up a small bottle of medicine.

“What is this?” he asked.

“It is some medicine for the Prime Minister’s throat,” said the
A.D.C. “He has been suffering from a slight cold.”

Poirot uncorked the bottle and smelt it. “_Tiens!_ It is very
strong.”

He replaced the cork and put the bottle back on the dressing-table.
Then he turned to the A.D.C.

“I should like to see the Prime Minister’s secretary, Captain
Daniels.”

“He is in the next room. He has only just recovered from the
effects of the chloroform.”

We followed the A.D.C. into the adjoining room, where we found
Captain Daniels lying on a sofa. He looked pale and exhausted.

“Monsieur Poirot,” he said, as we entered, “I am glad you have come.
This is a terrible business.”

“It is indeed, Captain Daniels. Can you tell us anything about it?”

“I am afraid I can tell you very little. As I told the police, I
remember nothing after the car was held up. Something was pressed
over my nose and mouth, and I lost consciousness. When I came to,
I was in that farmhouse, gagged and bound.”

“And you saw no one?”

“No one.”

“And you heard nothing?”

“No.”

“You did not hear the Prime Minister’s voice?”

“No.”

“You did not hear any sounds of a struggle?”

“No.”

Poirot looked at him keenly. “You are quite sure of that, Captain
Daniels?”

“Quite sure.”

“And you have no idea who your captors were?”

“None whatever.”

“It is very strange.”

Poirot turned to the A.D.C. “I should like to speak to Captain
Daniels alone for a few minutes.”

“Certainly.” The A.D.C. and the French officer withdrew.

Poirot sat down beside the sofa. “Now, Captain Daniels, I want you
to tell me the truth.”

Daniels looked at him in surprise. “The truth? I have told you the
truth.”

“Pardon me, but I do not think you have. There is something you are
withholding.”

“I don’t know what you mean.”

“I think you do. You are a very clever man, Captain Daniels. You
speak seven languages. You are an expert linguist. And yet, you say
you heard nothing, you saw no one. Is that not a little strange?”

“I told you, I was unconscious.”

“Yes, so you say. But was it really chloroform?”

“Of course it was.”

“Then why do you not smell of it?”

Daniels started. “What do you mean?”

“Chloroform has a very strong and persistent odour. If you had
been chloroformed, the smell would still be hanging about you.
But there is no smell of chloroform in this room, nor on your
clothes.”

Daniels turned pale. “I—I don’t understand.”

“I think you do. I think you were never chloroformed at all. I
think you were an accomplice in this business.”

“That’s a lie!” cried Daniels, starting up from the sofa.

“Is it? Then perhaps you can explain why a piece of the Prime
Minister’s tie was found in that farmhouse?”

“I—I don’t know.”

“I will tell you why. It was put there to make it look as though
there had been a struggle. But there was no struggle. The Prime
Minister went with his captors quite willingly.”

“That’s impossible!”

“Is it? We shall see. Now, Captain Daniels, I will give you one
more chance. Tell me where the Prime Minister is, and it will be
the better for you.”

“I tell you, I don’t know!”

“Very well. Then I shall have to find him myself.”

Poirot rose and walked to the door. “Hastings, come with me.”

I followed him out of the room. When we were outside, I asked:

“Poirot, do you really think Daniels is an accomplice?”

“I am sure of it, my friend. His story is full of holes. And did
you notice his hands?”

“His hands? No, what about them?”

“They were quite clean. If he had been lying on a heap of straw in
a dirty farmhouse, his hands would have been dirty. But they were
perfectly clean.”

“But he might have washed them?”

“He has only just recovered from the effects of the ‘chloroform,’
remember. He would hardly have had time to wash his hands.”

“That’s true. But where can the Prime Minister be?”

“That is what we have to find out, my friend. And we have very
little time. Only twenty-four hours.”

“But where are we to look? The whole of Northern France has been
searched.”

“Then we must look elsewhere.”

“But where?”

“In London.”

“In London? But the Prime Minister is in France!”

“Is he? I wonder.”

“But he was seen to go on board the destroyer at Dover. He was
seen to arrive at Boulogne.”

“Was he? Or was it someone who looked like him?”

“But Captain Daniels was with him!”

“Exactly. And Captain Daniels is an accomplice. It would be easy
for him to arrange for a substitute to take the Prime Minister’s
place.”

“But why? What would be the object of such a trick?”

“To gain time, my friend. To gain time. While the police of two
countries are searching France, the real Prime Minister is being
hidden in London.”

“But where? Where could they hide him?”

“That is what we must find out. And I think I know where to start
looking.”

“Where?”

“At the house of Captain Daniels’ aunt—Mrs. Everard, at Hampstead.”

“But the police have already searched it!”

“Perhaps they did not search it thoroughly enough. We will go
there at once.”

We hurried downstairs and out to the car.

“To Boulogne!” cried Poirot to the chauffeur. “As fast as you can!”

We reached Boulogne in record time, and were lucky enough to find
a destroyer just about to leave for Dover. We went on board, and
in less than two hours we were back in London.

We took a taxi straight to Hampstead. Mrs. Everard’s house was a
small, semi-detached villa in a quiet street. We were met at the
door by a middle-aged woman with a pleasant, motherly face.

“Mrs. Everard?” asked Poirot.

“Yes, that is my name.”

“I am Monsieur Poirot. I have come to see you about your nephew,
Captain Daniels.”

“Oh, yes. I have been so worried about him. The police were here
this morning, asking all sorts of questions. I hope he is all
right?”

“He is quite well, Madame. But I should like to ask you a few
questions, if I may.”

“Certainly. Come in.”

She led the way into a small, neatly furnished parlour.

“Now, Madame, when did you last see your nephew?”

“He was here last night. He came to see me for a few minutes
before he went to Windsor.”

“And was he alone?”

“Yes, he was alone.”

“And did he say anything about the Prime Minister?”

“Only that he was going to France with him to-day.”

“I see. And has anyone else been to see you lately?”

“Only a lady who came this afternoon. She said she was a friend of
my nephew’s.”

“A lady? What was her name?”

“She said her name was Frau Bertha Ebenthal.”

Poirot’s eyes flashed. “Frau Bertha Ebenthal! And what did she
want?”

“She said she had a message for my nephew. She seemed very
disappointed when I told her he wasn’t here.”

“I see. And where is she now?”

“I don’t know. She left about an hour ago.”

“And did she leave an address?”

“No.”

“_Tiens!_ That is a pity. Now, Madame, I have one more question to
ask you. Have you any other visitors in the house?”

“No, none at all.”

“Are you quite sure? No one in the upstairs rooms?”

“Quite sure. You can go and look if you like.”

“I think I will, if you don’t mind.”

We followed Mrs. Everard upstairs. She showed us into all the
rooms, but they were all empty.

“You see,” she said, “there is no one here.”

Poirot looked disappointed. “Yes, I see. Well, thank you, Madame.
I am sorry to have troubled you.”

We went downstairs and out into the street.

“Well, Poirot,” I said, “it looks as though your theory was wrong.”

“Perhaps, Hastings, perhaps. But I am not beaten yet. There is
still the other aunt—Miss Daniels, at Ascot.”

“But that is a long way from here. It will take us hours to get
there.”

“No matter. We must go. It is our only hope.”

We took another taxi and set off for Ascot. It was a long and
tiresome journey, and by the time we arrived it was after midnight.

Miss Daniels’ house was a small cottage on the outskirts of the
town. It was dark and silent. We knocked at the door, but there
was no answer. We knocked again, more loudly this time. Still no
answer.

“It looks as though there is no one at home,” I said.

Poirot did not reply. He was busy examining the lock of the door.

“It is a very simple lock,” he murmured. “I think I can manage it.”

He took a small tool from his pocket and began to work on the lock.
In a few minutes the door flew open.

“Poirot!” I cried. “We can’t go in like this! It’s housebreaking!”

“It is more than that, my friend. It is a matter of life and death.
Come!”

We entered the house and closed the door behind us. Poirot struck
a match and looked around. We were in a small hall. To the right
was a door, which Poirot opened. It was a small sitting-room,
meanly furnished.

“Wait here, Hastings,” said Poirot. “I am going to explore.”

He went out of the room, and I heard him going upstairs. A few
minutes later he came back, his face alight with excitement.

“Hastings! I have found him!”

“Found him? Found who?”

“The Prime Minister!”

“What? Where?”

“In a room upstairs. He is gagged and bound, but he is alive!”

I followed Poirot upstairs and into a small bedroom. There, lying
on the bed, was the Prime Minister. He was gagged and bound, just
as Poirot had said.

We quickly released him, and Poirot gave him a little brandy from
a flask he carried.

“Monsieur MacAdam,” said Poirot, “you are safe. I am Hercule
Poirot, and this is my friend Captain Hastings.”

The Prime Minister looked at us in bewilderment. “Where am I? What
has happened?”

“You have been kidnapped, Monsieur. But you are safe now. We must
get you back to London at once.”

We helped the Prime Minister downstairs and out to the taxi. As we
were about to drive away, a car drew up at the gate and a woman
got out.

“Frau Bertha Ebenthal!” cried Poirot.

The woman started and turned to flee, but Poirot was too quick for
her. He seized her by the arm and held her fast.

“No, Madame, you shall not escape so easily! Hastings, call the
police!”

In a few minutes a policeman arrived, and Frau Ebenthal was taken
into custody.

We drove the Prime Minister back to London, where we were met by
Lord Estair and Mr. Dodge.

“Monsieur Poirot!” cried Lord Estair. “You have done it! You have
saved the Prime Minister!”

“It was nothing, milord,” said Poirot modestly. “A little matter
of the ‘little grey cells,’ that is all.”

“But how did you find him?” asked Mr. Dodge.

“It was quite simple. I realized that the whole affair in France
was a trick to gain time. The Prime Minister never left England.
The man who went to France was a substitute—probably O’Murphy, the
chauffeur.”

“O’Murphy?” cried Lord Estair. “But he is a Scotland Yard man!”

“He was also a German agent,” said Poirot. “He and Captain Daniels
were working together. They arranged the whole thing. The
attempted assassination was a sham, to give them an excuse to take
the Prime Minister to that hospital, where he was chloroformed and
taken to Miss Daniels’ house. Then O’Murphy took his place and
went to France.”

“But the piece of tie?” I asked.

“That was put there by Daniels to lead the police to believe that
there had been a struggle in the farmhouse. He wanted to keep them
searching in France as long as possible.”

“And Frau Ebenthal?”

“She was the mastermind behind the whole plot. She is a well-known
German spy. I had been on her trail for some time.”

“Well, Monsieur Poirot,” said Lord Estair, “England owes you a
great debt. You have averted a national catastrophe.”

“I am happy to have been of service, milord,” said Poirot.

As we walked away, Poirot turned to me with a smile.

“You see, Hastings, it is as I always say. One must use the little
grey cells. Without them, one is nothing!”

The next day, the Prime Minister attended the Conference at
Versailles, and the peace of the world was secured. And, although
the story of his kidnapping was never made public, the name of
Hercule Poirot was held in high honour by those who knew the truth.

Japp’s forefinger was still tracing imaginary routes on his map.
“Nonsense! The car started from Boulogne—here they branched off.
Now, my idea is that they transferred the Prime Minister to another
car. See?”

“Well,” said the tall detective, “I shall make for the seaports.
Ten to one, they’ve smuggled him on board a ship.”

Japp shook his head. “Too obvious. The order went out at once to
close all the ports.”

The day was just breaking as we landed. Major Norman touched Poirot
on the arm. “There’s a military car here waiting for you, sir.”

“Thank you, monsieur. But, for the moment, I do not propose to
leave Boulogne.”

“What?”

“No, we will enter this hotel here, by the quay.”

He suited the action to the word, demanded and was accorded a
private room. We three followed him, puzzled and uncomprehending.

“Well, I think most people would expect it,” said Major Norman
coldly.

“But no, but no! That is the _romance_ of the detective! The
_reality_ is far otherwise. One must use the little grey cells.
Wait—I will send for some coffee.”

He went to the door and gave an order. In a few minutes the coffee
was brought. Poirot leaned back in his chair and blew a cloud of
smoke into the air.

“Now, let us examine the case with method. Let us begin at the
beginning. It is a long journey to Dover—then there is the sea
voyage. The Prime Minister is tired, he is wounded. He reaches
Boulogne. He finds there a car and an A.D.C. he knows—or _thinks_
he knows. Is it not so?”

“Yes.”

“And that car, we are told, was a bogus car. But why was it not
perceived to be a bogus car? At least ten or a dozen people saw
it, and yet no one suspected it for a moment! Why?”

“Because it was a very clever imitation,” I suggested.

“No, no, my friend. Not at all. It was not an imitation. It was
the _real_ car.”

“What?”

“The Prime Minister’s car—the one that had left him at Charing
Cross! That car was not found until some time after the boat had
sailed from Dover. It was then discovered in Soho. How it got there
no one knows.”

“Then you think O’Murphy was the traitor?” I suggested.

“It is not a question of thinking. It is a certainty! O’Murphy
was the only man who could have driven that car to Boulogne.”

“But how could he? He would have had to get it on board the boat,
and that would be impossible!”

“Not if he had the assistance of some one in authority. And who
more likely to have it than the Prime Minister’s own chauffeur?”

“But the car was found in Soho!”

“Exactly! That is where the cleverness of the scheme comes in.
O’Murphy’s disappearance, the discovery of the car in Soho—it was
all part of a very clever plot to put us on a false scent.
O’Murphy, of course, was never in Soho at all.”

“Then where was he?”

“He was on the boat, with the car!”

“But how did he get the car on board?”

“With the greatest ease. The Prime Minister’s car is a privileged
one. No one would think of questioning it. It would be taken on
board as a matter of course.”

“And once at Boulogne?”

“The rest was easy. He has only to drive to a prearranged spot,
and there the Prime Minister is transferred to another car. The
first car is then abandoned, and O’Murphy and his accomplices
disappear.”

“It’s a very clever theory,” said Major Norman, “but I’m afraid it
won’t hold water. In the first place, the car was seen in Soho.”

“By whom?”

“By the police.”

“And how did they know it was the Prime Minister’s car?”

“By the number, of course.”

“Ah! And you think it is difficult to change a number-plate?”

Major Norman was silent.

“Then there’s another thing,” I put in. “The A.D.C. who was with
the car—he was recognized by the Prime Minister.”

“Was he? Are you sure of that?”

“Well, Lord Estair said so.”

“Pardon me, he said the Prime Minister was met by one of the
Commander-in-Chief’s A.D.C.s. He did not say he was recognized by
the Prime Minister.”

“But surely he must have been!”

“Not necessarily. A man in uniform, with his hat pulled down over
his eyes—it is very easy to be mistaken.”

“But the Prime Minister must have known him!”

“Does the Prime Minister know every A.D.C. at Headquarters? No, of
course not. He would merely see a young officer in uniform, and
take him for granted.”

“It’s possible,” admitted Major Norman. “But what about the real
car and the real A.D.C.?”

“They were found, as you know, in a side road, gagged and bound.
The A.D.C. was a young fellow named Murphy—not the same name as
the chauffeur, but near enough to be confusing. He had only just
arrived at Headquarters, and was not known to the Prime Minister.
That was another point in their favour.”

“Then you think the Prime Minister is still in France?”

“I am sure of it.”

“But where?”

“Ah, that is the question! But I have a little idea. . . . Tell
me, Major Norman, is there not a lady—a very celebrated lady—who
lives not far from Boulogne? A certain Frau Bertha Ebenthal?”

Major Norman started. “Frau Bertha Ebenthal? Yes, she has a villa
at C——, on the coast.”

“Aha! And C—— is not far from the spot where the second car was
found, is it not?”

“It is about five miles away.”

“_Precisely!_ Now, my friend, we will go to C——.”

“But the French police have already searched the Villa Ebenthal!”

“No doubt. But they did not find what I shall find!”

“And what is that?”

“The Prime Minister!”

“But he’s not there! They searched the house from top to bottom!”

“Ah, but they did not search the _right_ place! Come, let us go.”

In a few minutes we were spinning along the road to C——. Poirot
was silent and absorbed in thought. When we reached the Villa
Ebenthal, he did not even wait to be announced, but strode
straight into the house. In the hall we were met by a tall,
handsome woman, with a very pale face and dark, haunting eyes.

“Frau Ebenthal?” said Poirot.

The lady bowed. “I am she. What is it you want?”

“I want the Prime Minister,” said Poirot quietly.

The woman laughed. “The Prime Minister? You are late, monsieur!
He is no longer here!”

“_Comment?_ No longer here?”

“No. He was here, it is true, but he has been moved. He is now far
away.”

Poirot’s face went very white. “Where is he?”

“That I shall not tell you! You may kill me if you like, but I
shall not speak!”

“We shall see!” said Poirot. “Major Norman, will you and Captain
Hastings search the house? I will remain here with this lady.”

We did as he directed, but our search was fruitless. There was no
sign of the Prime Minister anywhere. When we returned to the hall,
we found Poirot and the woman standing as we had left them.

“Well?” said Poirot.

“We have found nothing,” I replied.

Poirot turned to the woman. “You hear? Now, tell me, where is the
Prime Minister?”

She only laughed.

Poirot’s eyes flashed with a sudden light. “So! You will not
speak? Then I must make you!”

He stepped forward and seized her by the wrist.

“Where is he?”

“I shall not tell you!”

“_Très bien!_ Then I shall have to find him for myself!”

He turned to us. “Come, my friends. We have no more time to lose!”

As we left the house, I saw that Poirot was very much upset. His
hands were trembling, and he was muttering to himself in French.

“It is terrible!” he said. “Terrible! If we do not find him in
time, it will be a catastrophe! And that woman—she knows, she
knows!”

“But where can he be?” I asked.

“I do not know! I do not know! But we must find him! We must!”

We spent the rest of the day in a fruitles search. We visited
every house and cottage for miles around, but there was no trace
of the missing man. As the evening drew on, Poirot’s despair
became more and more evident.

“It is the end!” he cried. “The Conference begins in an hour, and
we have not found him! England is ruined!”

“Don’t give up hope, Poirot!” I said. “There is still a chance!”

“No, no! It is too late! We have failed!”

He sank into a chair and buried his face in his hands.

Suddenly he jumped up. “Wait! I have an idea! The car—the first
car! Where was it found?”

“In a side road, as you know,” said Major Norman.

“Yes, but _where_?”

“About two miles from here.”

“Take me there! At once!”

In a few minutes we were at the spot. It was a lonely, deserted
road, with thick woods on either side. Poirot jumped out of the
car and began to examine the ground.

“Look!” he cried, pointing to some tyre-marks in the mud. “The car
came this way—and then it turned—so!”

He followed the tracks into the wood. We followed him, our hearts
beating with excitement. After a few hundred yards, the tracks
stopped in front of a small, dilapidated cottage.

Poirot ran to the door and burst it open. The room inside was
empty, but in one corner there was a trap-door leading to a cellar.
Poirot tore it open and ran down the stairs.

A moment later, he reappeared, carrying a limp, unconscious figure
in his arms.

“The Prime Minister!” I cried.

“Yes!” said Poirot. “And he is alive! Quick, Major Norman, we must
get him to Versailles at once!”

We lifted the Prime Minister into the car and drove as fast as we
could. We reached Versailles just as the clock was striking nine.
The Conference was saved!

The next day, the Prime Minister was well enough to tell us his
story. He had been kidnapped, as we had suspected, and taken to
the Villa Ebenthal. But, just as they were about to move him to
another hiding-place, they had been interrupted by our arrival.
They had managed to smuggle him out of the house and into the
woods, where they had hidden him in the cellar of the cottage.

“But who was the traitor?” I asked.

“It was O’Murphy,” said the Prime Minister. “He had been in the pay
of the Germans for years. He was the one who led me into the
trap.”

“And what about Captain Daniels?”

“He was an innocent victim. He was chloroformed and left behind to
divert suspicion.”

“And Frau Ebenthal?”

“She was the leader of the gang. She is now in the hands of the
French police.”

“Well, Poirot,” I said, as we sat in his rooms a few days later,
“you’ve done it again! You’ve saved England!”

Poirot smiled. “It was nothing, my friend. A mere matter of using
the little grey cells!”

“But how did you know he was in that cottage?”

“I didn't. It was just a guess. But, as I always say, a good
detective must have a little imagination!”

And with that, he went back to mopping his grey suit with the
minute sponge.

“I admit I expected you to be a little more active,” said Major
Norman, with a touch of sarcasm.

“I am very sorry to disappoint you,” said Poirot, “but it is not
my way. See you, I believe that the Prime Minister is still in the
country.”

“Where?”

“Ah, that I cannot tell you. But I believe he is here—somewhere.
And I have an hour, maybe two, to spare. We will stay here.”

The major and the two Scotland Yard men looked at each other in
silent amazement.

“If you will excuse me,” said the tall detective, “I must be moving.
I think I’ll try the seaports, as I said.”

He went out, and was followed by Japp, who was still muttering over
his map.

“Well, Monsieur Poirot,” said Major Norman, “what do you propose to
do?”

“At present, nothing,” said Poirot. “I will wait for news.”

“What news?”

“Ah, that I cannot tell you. But if you would be so kind as to find
out for me the names of any people who have been staying in this
hotel lately?”

Major Norman looked at him in surprise. “I can do that, certainly.
But what can it possibly have to do with the Prime Minister?”

“Nothing, probably. But one never knows. One must have method,
_mon ami_.”

I knew by the twinkle in his eye that he was enjoying himself
immensely.

Presently Major Norman returned with a list of names. Poirot ran
his eye over them, and then handed it to me. There were a few French
names, one or two Americans, and several English.

“Any of these known to you, Hastings?”

“No,” I said, after a quick glance. “I don’t recognize any of them.”

“Well,” said Poirot, with a sigh, “it was a chance. Now let us see
if the others have found anything.”

He was about to ring the bell when the door was burst open and Japp
and the other detective rushed in.

“They’ve found him!” they cried in one breath.

“What?”

“Yes, in a little cottage near the coast. He was drugged and
unconscious, but otherwise unhurt. They’re bringing him along
now.”

“And the kidnappers?”

“Gone. But we’ve got a clue. A woman’s glove was found on the
floor.”

“A woman’s glove!” I cried. “Then there’s a woman in it?”

“So it would seem,” said Japp. “But, any way, the great thing is
that the Prime Minister is safe.”

He hurried out again, followed by the others. Poirot and I were
left alone.

“Well, Poirot,” I said, “I must congratulate you. You were right.
The Prime Minister _was_ still in the country.”

Poirot shook his head. “It is too easy,” he murmured. “It is too
easy. Why should they leave him where he could so easily be found?
And why leave a woman’s glove? It is like a story in a magazine.”

He sat for a moment in silence, then his eyes suddenly lit up.

“Hastings, did you notice the names on that list?”

“Yes.”

“Was there one that struck you?”

“No.”

“Think again. A name that we have heard before this evening?”

I thought hard, but could remember nothing.

“Wait,” said Poirot. “I will show you.”

He drew the list from his pocket and pointed to a name.

“_Frau Bertha Ebenthal_,” he read.

“Frau Bertha Ebenthal!” I cried. “But that is a German name!”

“Precisely. And do you not remember Lord Estair telling us that
there were two aunts of Captain Daniels—a Mrs. Everard and a Miss
Daniels?”

“Yes, but what has that to do with it?”

“Mrs. Everard—Ebenthal! Do you not see? It is the same name! Mrs.
Everard is the English for Frau Ebenthal. And she was staying in
this hotel—the very hotel where we are now!”

“By Jove!” I cried. “Then you think she is the woman who was
concerned in the kidnapping?”

“It is possible,” said Poirot. “But we must not jump to
conclusions. Let us go and see this cottage where the Prime
Minister was found.”

We were driven to a small, lonely cottage on the cliffs. It was
surrounded by a cordon of police and soldiers. Inside, we found
Japp and the other detective, who were busily searching the rooms.
The Prime Minister had been taken to a neighbouring château.

“Found anything?” asked Poirot.

“Nothing more,” said Japp. “Only this glove.”

He held up a small, daintily perfumed lady’s glove.

“May I see it?” asked Poirot.

He took it and examined it closely.

“A very small hand,” he remarked. “And a very expensive glove. Not
the sort of thing a cottage woman would wear.”

“No,” said Japp. “It belongs to some lady of fashion, I should say.”

“Or a very clever woman,” said Poirot.

He looked round the room. It was poorly furnished, with a deal
table and a few chairs. On the table was a bottle of wine and two
glasses.

“They seem to have been making themselves comfortable,” remarked
Japp.

Poirot picked up one of the glasses and smelt it.

“_Laudanum_,” he said. “That explains the Prime Minister’s
unconsciousness. And the other glass?”

He picked up the second glass. It was empty, but there was a faint
smell of wine.

“One person drank wine, and the other laudanum,” he said. “It is
very simple.”

“But who was the other person?” I asked.

“Ah, that is the question!” said Poirot. “But I think I can guess.”

He turned to Japp. “Have you any description of the people who were
seen here?”

“Yes. A woman and a man. The woman was tall and dark, and wore a
heavy veil. The man was short and thick-set. They arrived in a car
late last night.”

“And the car?”

“A large, dark-coloured car. No one seems to have noticed the
number.”

“_Tiens!_” said Poirot. “It is very mysterious.”

He walked over to the window and looked out.

“The sea is very close,” he said. “A boat could easily land here.”

“That’s what I thought,” said the other detective. “They probably
came by sea.”

“And went by sea,” said Poirot. “But why leave the Prime Minister
behind?”

“Perhaps they were disturbed,” suggested Japp.

“Perhaps,” said Poirot. “But I have another idea. Let us go to the
château and see the Prime Minister.”

We found the Prime Minister in bed, still under the influence of
the drug. A doctor was in attendance.

“He will be all right in a few hours,” he said. “It was a fairly
heavy dose, but he has a strong constitution.”

“Can we speak to him?” asked Poirot.

“Not yet. He is still unconscious.”

“Then we will wait,” said Poirot.

We sat in the hall of the château, waiting for news. It was a
long, weary wait. Major Norman and the two detectives had gone
back to Boulogne to continue their investigations.

Suddenly Poirot stood up.

“Hastings, I have a little idea. I am going back to the hotel for
a few minutes. Will you stay here?”

“Of course,” I said. “But what is your idea?”

“I want to have another look at that list of names,” he said.

He was away for about an hour. When he returned, his eyes were
shining with excitement.

“I have found it!” he cried.

“What?”

“The clue! The clue that I was looking for!”

“What is it?”

“I will tell you later. Now, let us go and see the Prime Minister.
The doctor says he is regaining consciousness.”

We were shown into the Prime Minister’s room. He was sitting up in
bed, looking pale and exhausted.

“Monsieur Poirot?” he said, as we entered.

“Yes, monsieur.”

“I have heard of you. They tell me you have found me.”

“It was the police who found you, monsieur. I only assisted.”

“I am very grateful to you. It was a terrible experience.”

“Can you tell us what happened?”

“I remember very little. We were driving along when suddenly the
car stopped. Some men appeared—they were masked. I remember a
struggle—then something was pressed over my face. I knew no more
until I woke up here.”

“And Captain Daniels?”

“I don’t know what became of him. Is he safe?”

“He was found gagged and bound in an abandoned farm,” said Poirot.

“Poor fellow! He must have put up a fight.”

“He did, monsieur. But tell me, do you remember anything else? Any
small detail?”

The Prime Minister thought for a moment.

“No, I don’t think so. Stay—there was one thing. Just before I lost
consciousness, I heard a woman’s voice.”

“A woman’s voice?”

“Yes. She said something in German.”

“What did she say?”

“I couldn’t quite catch it. But it sounded like ‘_Gott sei Dank!_’”

“Thank God!” translated Poirot. “That is very interesting.”

He turned to the doctor. “How long do you think it will be before
the Prime Minister is able to travel?”

“He should be able to move in a few hours,” said the doctor. “But
he must have rest.”

“He shall have it,” said Poirot. “Now, Hastings, we must go.”

As we left the room, Poirot turned to me.

“You see, Hastings? A woman’s voice—and speaking German! It all
fits in.”

“With Frau Ebenthal?”

“Exactly. But there is one thing that does not fit in.”

“What is that?”

“The shooting affair. Why should they try to shoot him if they
wanted to kidnap him?”

“I thought we had decided that it was a separate attempt,” I said.

“No, no! I cannot believe that. There is some link between the two.
And I think I know what it is.”

“What?”

“The bandage!”

“The bandage?” I cried, in amazement.

“Yes. Do you not remember Lord Estair telling us that the Prime
Minister’s wound was dressed and bound up at a cottage hospital?”

“Yes, but what of it?”

“It was a very slight wound—a mere scratch. Why should it be
bound up so carefully?”

“I suppose because it was a wound,” I said.

“No, no! It was more than that. It was a disguise!”

“A disguise?”

“Yes. Think, Hastings! If you wanted to hide someone, what better
way than to cover their face with a bandage? No one would see their
features. And if that person was supposed to be the Prime Minister,
who had been wounded in an attempt on his life, no one would
suspect anything.”

“But the Prime Minister was kidnapped in France!” I cried.

“Was he?” said Poirot. “Or was it someone else?”

“I don’t understand.”

“Wait, and you shall see. Now, we must go back to London.”

“To London? But we have only just arrived!”

“I know. But our work here is finished. The rest must be done in
England.”

We caught the afternoon boat for Dover. On the way across, Poirot
was very silent. He sat with his eyes closed, his face set in deep
thought.

When we arrived in London, we went straight to the Home Office.
Lord Estair and Mr. Dodge were waiting for us.

“Well, Monsieur Poirot?” they cried. “What news?”

“The Prime Minister is safe,” said Poirot. “He is at a château near
Boulogne.”

“Thank God!” said Lord Estair. “Then he will be able to attend the
Conference?”

“I fear not,” said Poirot.

“Why not?”

“Because the man at the château is not the Prime Minister.”

“What?” they cried in one breath.

“It is true,” said Poirot. “The man you have found is an impostor.”

“But how is that possible?”

“It is very simple. The real Prime Minister was kidnapped in
England—on his way from Windsor to London.”

“But the shooting affair——?”

“That was a blind. The men who held up the car were not German
agents. They were the kidnappers. They took the Prime Minister,
and in his place they put another man—a man who was carefully
made up to look like him, with a bandage over his face to hide his
features.”

“And O’Murphy?”

“O’Murphy was in it, of course. He drove the car to the cottage
hospital, where the ‘wound’ was dressed. Then he drove to Charing
Cross, where the impostor took the train for France. The real
Prime Minister was meanwhile being taken to some secret hiding-place.”

“But where?”

“That is what we have to find out. But I think I know where it is.”

“Where?”

“At the house of Mrs. Everard—the aunt of Captain Daniels!”

“But she lives at Hampstead!” cried Lord Estair.

“Exactly,” said Poirot. “And that is where we are going now.”

We drove to Hampstead at breakneck speed. The house was a large,
isolated one, surrounded by a high wall. We were met at the door by
a tall, dark woman.

“Mrs. Everard?” asked Poirot.

“Yes,” she said. “What do you want?”

“We have come for the Prime Minister,” said Poirot.

She turned pale and tried to shut the door, but Poirot was too
quick for her. He pushed his way into the hall, followed by the
rest of us.

“Where is he?” he demanded.

“I don’t know what you mean,” she said.

“It is no use,” said Poirot. “We know everything. Your nephew,
Captain Daniels, has confessed.”

It was a bold stroke, but it worked. The woman’s face crumpled.

“He told you?” she whispered.

“Yes. Now, take us to him.”

She led the way upstairs to a locked door. She produced a key and
opened it.

Inside, sitting in a chair, was the Prime Minister. He looked
haggard and worn, but he was undoubtedly the real Mr. MacAdam.

“Lord Estair!” he cried, as we entered. “Thank God you have come!”

“Are you all right, sir?” asked Lord Estair, rushing to his side.

“Yes, yes—only a bit shaken. They have been keeping me here for
the last twenty-four hours.”

“And the man in France?”

“A double, I suppose. They must have had it all planned out.”

“It was a very clever plot,” said Poirot. “But they forgot one
thing.”

“What was that?”

“The bandage. It was too clever. It was that which first made me
suspicious.”

“But how did you find this house?” asked Mr. Dodge.

“By the list of names at the hotel in Boulogne,” said Poirot. “I
saw the name of Frau Bertha Ebenthal. I remembered that Captain
Daniels had an aunt named Mrs. Everard. Ebenthal—Everard. It is
the same name. I knew then that she must be the woman concerned
in the plot.”

“And the culprit?” asked Lord Estair. “Who was the mastermind
behind it all?”

Poirot looked at the woman, who was standing by the door, her face
sullen and defiant.

“The mastermind,” he said, “was Frau Bertha Ebenthal—alias Mrs.
Everard. She is a very dangerous German agent. But she had an
accomplice—someone who was close to the Prime Minister, someone
who could arrange everything.”

“Who?”

“Captain Daniels,” said Poirot.

“Daniels!” cried the Prime Minister. “I can’t believe it!”

“It is true, monsieur. He was the one who suggested the route
from Windsor. He was the one who arranged the ‘assassination’.
He was the one who saw that the impostor took your place.”

“And O’Murphy?”

“O’Murphy was also an accomplice. He was the one who drove the
car to Soho, to give the impression that he was a German agent.
But he was merely a tool in the hands of Daniels and Frau Ebenthal.”

“It is incredible,” said Lord Estair. “But what about the woman’s
glove in the cottage?”

“That was another blind,” said Poirot. “It was left there to make
the police think that a woman was involved in the kidnapping in
France. But, as I told you, the kidnapping in France was a sham.
The real kidnapping had already taken place in England.”

“And the man at the château?”

“He was also an accomplice—probably a German actor who was paid
to play the part. He will, no doubt, disappear as soon as he can.”

“Well, Monsieur Poirot,” said the Prime Minister, “you have done
England a great service. I don’t know how we can ever thank you.”

“It was a pleasure, monsieur,” said Poirot, bowing. “And now, if
you will excuse me, I think I will return to my rooms. I have a
spot of grease on my new grey suit that needs my attention.”

And, with a twinkle in his eye, the little man led the way out of
the house.

I laughed. “Not quite that, Poirot. But I expected you to be on
the track, at least.”

“But I am on the track! For the first time, I see. . . .”

“You see what?”

“The truth. . . . The little grey cells of the brain—they are
beginning to work!”

“What do you mean?”

“Wait! I will tell you. There were several points which bothered
me. For instance, why should the kidnappers leave Captain Daniels
behind? Why should they not have taken him as well as the Prime
Minister?”

“Because he would have been a nuisance,” I suggested.

“No, no! A second person is an asset, not a nuisance. It is easier
to guard two than one. Then, again, why should they have left the
car in a place where it was certain to be found?”

“I suppose they couldn’t help themselves.”

“Ah, but they could! They could have driven it into a wood, or
covered it with brushwood. But no, they left it in a most
conspicuous place.”

“Well, what does that prove?”

“It proves that they _wanted_ it to be found!”

“I don’t see it.”

“Naturally you do not. It is because you have not the little grey
cells, my friend. Now, there is another thing. Lord Estair told us
that the Prime Minister’s car did not return to the garage after
depositing him at Charing Cross. Why? Because the chauffeur,
O’Murphy, was a traitor! He went straight to a house in Soho.
Now, _why_ did he do that?”

“To get his instructions, I suppose.”

“But he had his instructions already! He must have had. The whole
plot was beautifully organized. No, he went there to give
information. Now, what information could he have to give?”

“I don’t know.”

“Think, Hastings! What information could a chauffeur have to give
that would be of any use to the enemy?”

“I give it up.”

“The Prime Minister’s destination, of course!”

“But that was already known!”

“Was it? Are you sure? The exact house where he was to stay? The
very road he was to take? The moment of his arrival? All those
things were only known to a very few people.”

“But O’Murphy would not know them!”

“No, but Captain Daniels would! And O’Murphy was in his service!”

“What? I don’t follow.”

“_Listen_! O’Murphy disappears. Why? Because he is a traitor? No,
because he is a _danger_! He knows something. What does he know?
He knows that Captain Daniels is not what he seems! He knows that
Captain Daniels is in league with the enemy!”

“But Daniels was found gagged and bound!”

“Aha! We come back to that! Why was he left behind? To give the
alarm, of course! To tell the story of the bogus car and the bogus
A.D.C.! To set the police of two countries on a false scent!”

“Then the Prime Minister was never in that car at all?”

“Precisely! He was kidnapped in England!”

“In England?” I cried, in amazement. “But he was seen to go on
board the destroyer at Dover!”

“Was he? Think, Hastings, think! A man with his head and face
swathed in bandages! Who could say it was the Prime Minister? No
one had a good look at him. And the bandages were a perfect
disguise.”

“Then you mean——?”

“I mean that the whole scene in France was a gigantic sham,
staged to divert attention from the real scene of the crime. The
shooting affair, the bogus car—all that was a well-rehearsed play.
The Prime Minister was never in France. He was kidnapped in England,
between Windsor and London.”

“But the bandages? He had those before the kidnapping took place.”

“Of course he had! That was the first step. The shooting affair
was part of the plot. It provided the excuse for the bandages.
Then, on the way to Charing Cross, the real Prime Minister was
spirited away, and a substitute, already waiting, took his place.
The substitute, with his face well muffled up, went on board the
destroyer, and was eventually ‘kidnapped’ in France. Meanwhile,
the real Prime Minister was being safely hidden in England.”

“But where?”

“Ah, that is the question! Where? Let us see. Where would he be
taken? Not to a place that could be easily searched. To some quiet,
unobtrusive house, probably. Now, what did Lord Estair tell us?
Captain Daniels has two aunts. One lives at Hampstead, and the
other at Ascot.”

“Ascot! That is near Windsor!”

“Precisely. And it was on the road from Windsor that the shooting
affair took place. Now, let us suppose that the Prime Minister’s
car, instead of merely ‘deviating’ from the main road, actually
went to the house of this Miss Daniels? The Prime Minister is
imprisoned there. A substitute is ready, his head already
bandaged. He takes the Prime Minister’s place, and the car goes
on to London. O’Murphy, who is an honest man, suspects something.
He follows the car to Charing Cross, and then, instead of
returning to the garage, he goes to Soho to find out what he can
about this Captain Daniels. He is discovered, and—well, we don’t
know what has happened to him, but I fear the worst.”

“But this is incredible!” I cried.

“It is the only explanation that fits all the facts. And we have
no time to lose. We must return to England at once.”

“But the Conference? It is at nine o’clock to-night!”

“I know, I know! We must hurry. Major Norman, can you get us a
special boat back to Dover?”

“I think so, sir. But are you sure? It seems so—so——”

“It is the truth! I, Hercule Poirot, have said it! There is no
time to argue. Every moment is precious!”

The next few hours were a whirl of excitement. We crossed the
Channel in a special boat, and a fast car was waiting for us at
Dover. Poirot was like a man possessed. He urged the driver to
ever-increasing speed. As we flew through the Kentish lanes, I
could not help wondering if he were right. It seemed so
fantastic—so impossible. And yet, as he had said, it was the only
theory that fitted the facts.

We reached London in record time, and Poirot at once telephoned to
Scotland Yard. A few minutes later, we were joined by Japp, who
had also returned from France.

“You’ve got it, Poirot!” he cried. “We’ve just had a report from
Ascot. A car answering the description of the Prime Minister’s was
seen at a small house called ‘The Cedars’ on the morning of the
kidnapping. It’s the house of a Miss Daniels!”

“Quick!” cried Poirot. “There is not a moment to lose!”

We jumped into the car and raced towards Ascot. As we drew near the
house, Poirot’s excitement became almost uncontrollable.

“The little grey cells!” he murmured. “They have not failed me!
But we must be careful. These people are desperate.”

We reached “The Cedars,” a small, secluded house, surrounded by
trees. Japp and two other detectives jumped out and surrounded the
house. Poirot and I followed them to the front door. Japp knocked
loudly.

There was no answer. He knocked again. Still no answer.

“Break it in!” cried Poirot.

A few sturdy blows, and the door gave way. We rushed into the hall.
A middle-aged woman, with a terrified face, came running down the
stairs.

“What is it? What is the matter?” she cried.

“We are the police,” said Japp shortly. “We have a warrant to
search this house.”

The woman shrank back, her face deathly pale. “I—I don’t know what
you mean.”

“Where is the Prime Minister?” demanded Poirot.

The woman did not answer. She seemed to be on the point of
fainting.

“Search the house!” ordered Japp.

We went from room to room, but there was no sign of the Prime
Minister. My heart sank. Was Poirot wrong after all?

“The cellar!” cried Poirot suddenly.

We rushed down to the basement. There, in a small, dark cellar, we
found him—the Prime Minister of England! He was gagged and bound,
but alive.

With a cry of joy, we released him. He was weak and exhausted, but
his spirit was unbroken.

“Thank God!” he murmured, as we lifted him up. “I thought my last
hour had come.”

“You are safe, sir,” said Poirot gently. “And you will be at the
Conference in time.”

The Prime Minister’s eyes flashed. “Then England is saved!”

As we led him out of the house, Japp turned to the woman, who was
crouched in a corner of the hall.

“And now, Mrs. Everard,” he said sternly, “perhaps you will tell
us where your nephew, Captain Daniels, is?”

The woman burst into tears. “I don’t know! I don’t know! He told
me it was all for the good of the country—that the Prime Minister
was a traitor!”

“A traitor!” cried the Prime Minister. “The scoundrel!”

“He is the traitor!” said Poirot. “But he has not escaped yet.”

“We’ll get him,” said Japp grimly. “We’ve got his description, and
every port is closed.”

“And O’Murphy?” I asked.

Poirot’s face saddened. “I fear we shall find him in that house in
Soho—but it will be too late to save him.”

We hurried the Prime Minister to the waiting car. It was now six
o’clock. We had three hours in which to get him to Versailles.

“Can we do it?” I asked.

“We must!” said Poirot.

The journey that followed is one I shall never forget. We reached
the coast in time to catch a fast destroyer, and as the clock
struck nine, the Prime Minister walked into the Conference room at
Versailles.

The sensation was profound. The German agents, who had been
confidently expecting his absence, were confounded. The Conference
was a triumph for England, and the “Peace by negotiation” party
was utterly routed.

A few days later, Poirot and I were sitting in his rooms. The news
of the Prime Minister’s rescue had been made public, and Poirot
was the hero of the hour.

“And Captain Daniels?” I asked.

“He was captured at Liverpool, trying to get on board a ship for
America. He will be tried for high treason.”

“And Mrs. Everard?”

“She was merely a tool in his hands. She will be dealt with
leniently, I expect.”

“And the real culprit?” I asked. “The man behind it all?”

Poirot smiled. “Ah, that is a different matter. But I think we
can safely say that the brain of the whole plot was a certain Frau
Bertha Ebenthal, one of the most dangerous German agents in
Europe. It was she who planned the whole affair, and Captain
Daniels was merely her instrument.”

“And how did you know it was her?”

“Because, my friend, the whole plot bore the stamp of her
originality. The shooting affair, the bandages—it was all so
theatrical—so like her! And then, there was the house in Soho.
It is well known as her headquarters in London.”

“Well, Poirot,” I said, “you have done a great service to your
country.”

“Not my country, Hastings—yours! But I am glad to have been of
service to the brave England. And now, let us talk of something
else. I have a most interesting case—a young lady who has lost a
diamond ring. . . .”

I laughed. “From the Prime Minister to a diamond ring! You are
truly amazing, Poirot!”

“But why not? To the little grey cells, all cases are of equal
interest. It is the method—the method that matters!”

And so the great crisis passed, and England was saved—thanks to the
marvellous brain of Hercule Poirot.

I smiled. “It is, Poirot.”

“_Eh bien_, but I, Hercule Poirot, have a better way. I sit
here—quite quiet. I use the little grey cells. I tell you, it
could not have been done—that abduction! It is impossible.
Therefore, it was not done.”

“But it _was_ done!” I cried.

“_Ecoutez_, my friend! The police of two countries have searched.
They have found nothing. That is because there was nothing to
find. Therefore, the Prime Minister cannot be in France.”

“But he was seen to land at Boulogne!”

“No, no! A man _believed_ to be the Prime Minister was seen to
land at Boulogne. A man who sat in a car, with his face and head
bandaged, and a Union Jack on the car. And who was that man?”

“The Prime Minister!”

“But no—it was the Prime Minister’s double! The man who had been
acting the part ever since the shooting affair.”

“But,” I cried, “the shooting affair happened in England!”

“Exactly. Let us go back. The Prime Minister, on the way from
Windsor, is attacked. He is wounded. He goes to a cottage hospital.
A bandaged and muffled figure comes out, gets into the car and
proceeds to Charing Cross. He is seen by many people. He goes to
France. But the _real_ Prime Minister—he never left that cottage
hospital.”

Major Norman’s face was a study in amazement. “Then, where is he?”

“I should say,” said Poirot, “that he is at this moment in a
certain house at Hampstead—the house of a Mrs. Everard, the aunt
of Captain Daniels.”

“What?”

“The Prime Minister was never kidnapped. He was abducted at the
cottage hospital. That is why O’Murphy—the Prime Minister’s
chauffeur—went to Soho. To tell his friends that the first part
of the plot had been successful. The shooting affair was a plant.
It was a means of getting the Prime Minister to the hospital and
substituting the double. The double then went to France, and was
‘kidnapped’ to gain time. The Prime Minister himself was taken
quietly back to London in another car.”

“But this is incredible!” I cried.

“It is the only possible explanation. You will find it is as I
say.”

“I admit I’m surprised you aren’t doing something,” said Major
Norman.

“But I _am_ doing something! I am using the little grey cells of
the brain! See, I sit here, and I look at the case with method.
Where is the Prime Minister? He is in France. Where in France?
In that little space that we call the ‘Area of the Armies.’ He is
