held a prisoner there. How? By someone who has the means of doing
so—somebody who can command a house, a car, a hiding-place. Who
is that somebody? A German agent? No, for that he must have a
safe place, and it is almost impossible for a German agent to keep
one in that part of the country. Is he, then, a man of our own
Army? That is better—much better.”

“Good heavens!” I cried. “You don’t mean that?”

“I mean that he must be a man with a house, or a villa, or a
château, at his disposal. Some person of importance. Who is
important in that part of the country?”

“Everyone,” said Norman, with a laugh.

“No, not everyone. Someone with a house. A woman, perhaps. Women
have played a great part in this war. They are clever, the women.
Think of the famous Frau Bertha Ebenthal. She has the brain of a
man. She has been in this country, I know. Is she in France now?
It is possible. If so, where?”

His eyes challenged us. “But I—Hercule Poirot—tell you that it is
not so! The true clues are within—_here_!” He tapped his forehead.
“See you, I need not have left London. It would have been sufficient
for me to sit quietly in my rooms there. All that matters is the
little grey cells within. Secretly and silently they do their part,
until suddenly I call for a map, and I lay my finger on a
spot—so—and I say: the Prime Minister is _there_! And it is so!
With method and logic one can accomplish anything! This frantic
rushing to France was a mistake—it is playing a child’s game of
hide-and-seek. But now, though it may be too late, I will set to
work the right way, from within. Silence, my friends, I beg of
you.”

Presently Poirot’s face underwent a sudden change. He became alert.
His hand stole to his pocket. He drew out a small silver case,
containing two of his little Russian cigarettes. He lit one with
meticulous care. Then he rose, with a long, contented sigh.

“_C’est fait!_ I have it. It is simple, _tout à fait simple_!”

“You know where the Prime Minister is?” I cried, jumping up.

“I have a very strong suspicion. But it is more than a suspicion,
it is a certainty. Let us return to the station. We must catch the
next train for London.”

“What?”

“The next train. We have no time to lose. It is essential we should
reach London by four o’clock this afternoon.”

Major Norman’s face was a study in amazement. “Do I understand you
to say that we are to return to London?”

“That is so. The Prime Minister is not in France. He is in London.”

“What?”

“Ah, I see your surprise. But it is even so. Let us go.”

I was as amazed as anyone. Was the man mad? Or was he really
telling the truth? I looked at my friend, but Poirot’s eyes were
shining with a light that I had never seen in them before. It was
clear that he had some secret, of which he alone was the possessor.

Suddenly, however, Poirot sat up and looked at his watch.

“Twenty minutes to ten. . . . Ten minutes to ten. . . . It is time.
Now, my friends, I have found the Prime Minister! He is in London!
Come! We will go back at once!”

“What?”

“The boat leaves in fifteen minutes. I have just time to catch her.
Hurry!”

“You are mad!” cried Major Norman, starting up. “The Prime Minister
disappeared _here_, in France, and you go to London to find him?”

“Precisely. It is the only way.”

“But it’s impossible! He must be here!”

“_Mon Dieu!_” Poirot’s voice was like a scream. “I have told you
he is not! My brain tells me so!”

I caught his arm. “Poirot, you are overwrought! You have been doing
too much.”

“_Nom d’un nom d’un petit bonhomme!_ But I tell you I know!”

He rushed from the room, and we perforce followed. It was an
extraordinary sight—a little man running for the boat and three
others running behind him. But he reached her just as she was
casting off. We followed suit.

Poirot did not even look back at the receding shore. He sat in a
corner of the saloon with a smile on his face that was almost
divine.

“_Maintenant, c’est tout_,” he remarked. “The rest is easy.”

He took out a little book and began to jot down figures. We three
stared at him in amazement. Was he mad? Or was there some method
in his madness?

“But tell me,” I cried, “how do you know?”

“Method, my friend, and logic! If it is not so, it must be so.
There is no other way. Therefore it is so! It is simple, is it
not?”

“But I don’t see it!”

“No, you do not use your little grey cells, as I do. Now, follow
my reasoning. The car was found abandoned at C——. Captain Daniels
was gagged and bound. Why? To make it appear that he was a victim.
But, as I have told you, if he was a victim, why was he not
disposed of? Why leave him to be found? The answer is: because he
was _not_ a victim. He was an accomplice. He was the one who
delivered the Prime Minister into the hands of the enemy. But, if
he was an accomplice, why was he gagged and bound at all? Why not
disappear with the others? Because he had still a part to play!”

“What part?”

“The part of the witness! He was to tell the story of the kidnapping.
He was to make us believe that the Prime Minister had been spirited
away in France. But, if the Prime Minister was not kidnapped in
France, where was he kidnapped?”

“In England?”

“Precisely. Now, think. What happened in England? An attempted
assassination. A very clumsy, amateurish affair, as I told you at
the time. Why was it so clumsy? Because it was not an assassination
at all! It was a kidnapping! The masked men did not try to shoot
the Prime Minister—they tried to take him! But they failed. The
chauffeur, O’Murphy, was too quick for them. He drove on, and the
Prime Minister escaped. But the kidnappers did not give up. They
had another card up their sleeve. And that card was Captain
Daniels! He was the traitor in the camp. He saw his opportunity
and took it.”

“But how?”

“Think of what happened at the hospital. The Prime Minister’s wound
was dressed and bound up. He was not, you remember, recognized.
Why? Because his face was covered with bandages! Now, suppose that,
after the bandages were put on, the man who came out of the hospital
was _not_ the Prime Minister at all, but someone else?”

“But who?”

“Captain Daniels, of course! He is, as Lord Estair told us, a
wonderful linguist. He could easily personate the Prime Minister.
The bandages would hide his face, and his voice would be muffled.
He would only have to say a few words. The real Prime Minister,
chloroformed and helpless, was left behind in the hospital!”

“But the chauffeur? O’Murphy?”

“Ah, O’Murphy was in it too! He was the one who drove the car to
the hospital. He was the one who saw to it that the Prime Minister
was left behind. And then, what did he do? He drove the bogus Prime
Minister to Charing Cross! He saw him on to the train! And then,
his work done, he disappeared—to Soho, to report to his German
masters!”

“And the man who went to France?”

“Was Captain Daniels, of course! He went to France, he was met by
the bogus car, he was ‘kidnapped’—and then he was found gagged and
bound, to tell his story and put the police on the wrong scent! It
was a masterpiece of deception!”

“But the Prime Minister? Where is he?”

“He is still in that hospital, of course! They are keeping him
there, under drugs, until the Conference is over. But they have
reckoned without Hercule Poirot! We shall be in London by eight
o’clock, and by nine we shall have the Prime Minister at Versailles!”

“But it’s impossible! Even if we find him, we can’t get him to
Versailles by nine o’clock!”

“Wait and see, my friend, wait and see!”

And indeed, it was as Poirot had said. We reached London at eight
o’clock, and at half-past eight we were at the little cottage
hospital near Windsor. There, in a private room, we found the
Prime Minister, still unconscious, but otherwise unharmed.

“But how are you going to get him to Versailles?” I cried.

“By the air, of course! There is a special plane waiting for us at
Hendon. We shall be there in time!”

And we were. As the clock struck nine, the Prime Minister, looking
a little pale but otherwise himself, walked into the Conference
Chamber at Versailles. The situation was saved!

The next day, Poirot and I were sitting in his rooms, when the door
opened and Lord Estair and Mr. Dodge entered.

“Monsieur Poirot,” said Lord Estair, “we have come to thank you.
You have saved England.”

“It was nothing,” said Poirot modestly. “A little matter of the
grey cells, that is all.”

“But how did you know?” asked Mr. Dodge. “How did you know it was
Captain Daniels?”

“It was the languages, monsieur! You told me he spoke seven
languages. Now, no honest Englishman speaks seven languages! It
is not done! And then, there was the matter of the aunts. One aunt
at Hampstead, and one at Ascot. Ascot is very near Windsor, is it
not? It was there that the Prime Minister was taken. It was all
very simple.”

“And O’Murphy?”

“O’Murphy was a traitor, of course. He was in the pay of the
Germans. But he will not trouble you again. He has been arrested
in Soho.”

“And what about the other two?” I asked. “Mrs. Everard and Frau
Bertha Ebenthal?”

“Ah, they were the ones who were keeping the Prime Minister in the
hospital! Mrs. Everard was the ‘nurse,’ and Frau Ebenthal was the
‘doctor.’ They are both in custody now.”

“Well, Poirot,” I said, when our visitors had left, “you’ve done
it again! You’re a wonderful man.”

“I am, am I not?” said Poirot, complacently. “But then, I have the
method and the logic! And now, if you will excuse me, I must go and
attend to that spot of grease on my grey suit. It is still there,
and it annoys me!”

I smiled as I watched him go. He was a strange little man, but
there was no doubt about it—he was a genius!

The afternoon drew on. I had been out and about the little town,
but when I returned Poirot was still sitting in the same
position—still motionless, still blinking.

The clock on the mantelpiece struck five. Poirot’s eyes suddenly
opened.

“_Bon!_” he said, and he began to move.

He rose to his feet.

“Come, my friends, it is enough!”

“You’ve found him?”

“No, I have not found him. But I think I see a little way. . . .
You have a car, Major Norman? We will go to the place where the
two cars were found.”

The major led the way. We were soon speeding along the road, and
presently reached the spot.

“A lonely place,” observed Poirot, looking round. “But I cannot
see much. It is too dark.”

“Is that all?” asked the major.

“Yes, that is all. Now we will return to the town.”

Major Norman looked at his watch.

“If you want to be at the Conference at nine o’clock, we should
start at once.”

“I have no intention of being at the Conference,” said Poirot
sharply.

“But the Prime Minister——?”

“He will not be there.”

“But if he is found?”

“If he is found, it will be by others, not by me. For me, the
Conference is no longer of interest.”

Suddenly Poirot’s eyes flashed with a new light. He pulled out his
watch.

“It is half-past one. In eight hours the Conference will be held
at Versailles. Is it too late? Perhaps. . . . But we will try.
Major Norman, I must have a car. And I must have it at once.”

“At once? Certainly.”

“I will go to Paris, then. But first I must visit a certain
place—it is on the way.”

“_Where?_”

“A small farm near C——. The place where Captain Daniels was
found.”

“What? But that has been thoroughly searched already! It’s only
wasting time!”

“It may be so, but I have a little idea that I should like to
verify for myself. We will take the Scotland Yard man with us.”

Major Norman was clearly doubtful of the wisdom of this proceeding,
but he did not say anything. In less than ten minutes a car was at
the door, and we were spinning along the roads of France. Poirot
kept his eyes closed, and his lips were moving. He seemed to be
rehearsing some speech or other to himself.

We reached the farm in record time, and were greeted by a French
officer of police.

“Ah, Monsieur Poirot! I have heard of you. But I fear you will find
nothing here. We have searched with the utmost care, but there is
nothing to be found.”

“_Bien, bien_! Let me look at the room where the Capitaine was
found.”

The officer led the way into a small, dark room, with stone walls.
It was empty. Poirot walked to the window and looked out.

“The road is quite near, then? And the car was seen to stop here?”

“Yes, Monsieur Poirot. It was a large, grey car. Two men got out,
carrying something between them. They went into the house. Ten
minutes later they came out and drove away at a great pace.”

“And it was then that you found the Capitaine Daniels?”

“Precisely. He was lying on the floor, as I have described. The
door was locked on the outside.”

“And there was no sign of the Prime Minister?”

“None. We searched every corner of the farm.”

Poirot nodded. He seemed to be looking for something. Suddenly he
stooped and picked up something from the floor. It was a small,
white, downy feather. He held it up to the light.

“_Tiens!_ What is this?”

The French officer smiled. “A feather, Monsieur Poirot. There are
many fowls in the yard outside.”

“Is it a chicken’s feather?”

“I—I suppose so.”

Poirot shook his head. “No, no, my friend. This is a very different
kind of feather. It is a downy feather—a very small, downy
feather—from a pillow!”

He looked at us with a curious expression.

“Wait here for me, my friends. I will return in a little moment.”

He hurried out of the room. We looked at each other in surprise.
What was the meaning of this?

Ten minutes later he returned, his eyes dancing with excitement.

“Now, my friends, for Paris! There is no time to be lost! We must
be there by eight o’clock!”

“But what have you found?” I cried.

“The Prime Minister!”

“The Prime Minister? Where?”

“Wait, wait, my friend! You shall see!”

At length, after what seemed an eternity, Poirot stirred himself.
His green eyes had never been more brilliant.

“Now, my friends, I have found him!”

“What?”

“The Prime Minister is at a house called ‘The Cedars,’ near
Putney!”

“But, Monsieur Poirot, it is impossible! He is in France!”

Poirot shook his head. “I tell you, _non_! He is at Putney—with
Mrs. Everard!”

“Mrs. Everard! Captain Daniels’ aunt!”

“Precisely.”

Major Norman’s face was a study in incredulity. “But—but, look
here, Monsieur Poirot, the Prime Minister was seen to land here!”

Poirot smiled. “A man _resembling_ the Prime Minister, yes. But
the Prime Minister—_non_!”

“But we have his secretary’s evidence!”

“Exactly—his secretary’s evidence. And his secretary, as I told
you, speaks seven languages!”

“But—the Prime Minister was shot!”

“_Enfantillage_! He was shot in England—early this morning.
_Mon Dieu_, what a chance for a substitute! The Prime Minister
with his head and face all bandaged up! Who would know him?”

“But—but—what about the Prime Minister?”

“I have told you. He is at ‘The Cedars,’ Putney. He has never left
England.”

“But—how did they get him there?”

“He was kidnapped in the lane. The ‘masked men’ were his own
detectives—at least, they thought they were! Daniels and O’Murphy
had it all arranged. They took him to Mrs. Everard’s. The ‘Prime
Minister’ who came to France was a substitute. It was a simple
matter to have him ‘kidnapped’ again. And, as I told you, he would
be bandaged up—no one would see his face.”

“And O’Murphy?”

“O’Murphy is with him at Putney. They are all together—the Prime
Minister, O’Murphy, and Mrs. Everard. It was a well-laid plot.”

“And where is Captain Daniels?”

“He is at the farm at C——, I expect. He will be found there when
the police go to look for him.”

“Then—the Prime Minister is safe?”

“If you go to Putney at once, yes.”

“But—but—how did you find it all out?”

“By the little grey cells, my friend! It was the only way. The
whole thing was too complicated, too elaborate. It had to be
something simpler. And then I remembered Mrs. Everard—the aunt at
Hampstead. It was a little clue, but it was enough.”

“And the Conference?”

“The Prime Minister will be there. There is still time. If you
hurry, messieurs, you will be in time.”

Major Norman and the Scotland Yard man did not wait to hear any
more. They rushed from the room. I followed them.

“Poirot,” I cried, “it is wonderful! How did you do it?”

Poirot smiled. “It was the only way, my friend. The only way.”

“But—but—is it true?”

“We shall see, Hastings—we shall see!”

And we did see. Two hours later a telegram was received from London:
“Prime Minister found at ‘The Cedars,’ Putney. All well. O’Murphy
and Mrs. Everard in custody. Captain Daniels escaped.”

The Conference was a great success. The Prime Minister’s presence
saved the situation. And, as Lord Estair said to me later, England
owed a debt of gratitude to Hercule Poirot that it could never
repay.

“But how did you find it out, Poirot?” I asked him again, as we
sat in his rooms a few days later.

“It was the only way, my friend. The only way.”

“But—the clues? The map?”

“The map was a little piece of—how do you call it?—bluff! I did
not need the map. I knew the Prime Minister was in England all the
time. It was the only way he _could_ be hidden so long. And then
I remembered the aunt at Hampstead—and the other aunt at Ascot.
It was a little clue, but it was enough.”

“But—the shooting?”

“_Enfantillage_, as I said. A little piece of melodrama to
divert our attention. It was well done—very well done. But it did
not deceive Hercule Poirot!”

And my friend smiled, and began to mop his grey suit with a minute
sponge.

Finally, I got up, and strolled as noiselessly as I could to the
window. The matter was becoming a farce. I was secretly concerned
for my friend. If he failed, I would have preferred him to fail in
a less ridiculous manner. Out of the window I idly watched the
daily leave boat, belching forth columns of smoke, as she lay
alongside the quay.

Suddenly I was aroused by Poirot’s voice close to my elbow.

“_Mes amis_, let us start!”

I turned. An extraordinary transformation had come over my friend.
His eyes were flickering with excitement, his chest was swelled to
the uttermost.

“I have been an imbecile, my friends! But I see daylight at last.”

Major Norman moved hastily to the door. “I’ll order the car.”

“There is no need. I shall not use it. Thank Heaven the wind has
fallen.”

“Do you mean you are going to walk, sir?”

“No, my young friend. I am no St. Peter. I prefer to cross the sea
by boat.”

“To cross the _sea_?”

“Yes. To work with method, one must begin from the beginning. And
the beginning of this affair was in England. Therefore, we return
to England.”


  •   •   •   •   •   •   •

Lord Estair was waiting for us, his face drawn with the suspense of the last few hours. He looked at Poirot with a kind of desperate hope, which turned to bewilderment as he realized we had returned empty-handed. “Monsieur Poirot!” he exclaimed. “What does this mean? Every moment is precious! Why are you not in France?” Poirot bowed with his usual punctiliousness. “Because, milord, the clue is not in France. It is here. I have a great desire to visit the lady who is the aunt of Captain Daniels—this Mrs. Everard of Hampstead. And I would also like the address of the small hospital where the Prime Minister’s wound was so capably dressed yesterday morning.”

Upon our arrival, Poirot’s first action was to consult a small notebook. Then, with a decisive nod, he hailed a taxi and gave an address in Hampstead. Major Norman and I followed him, my mind a whirl of conjectures. Why Hampstead? Why not Scotland Yard? As the taxi threaded its way through the London traffic, Poirot remained enigmatically silent, his eyes fixed on some internal vision. At length, we drew up before a small, detached villa of suburban respectability. “Here, my friend,” said Poirot, “is the residence of Mrs. Everard, the aunt of Captain Daniels. It is here that we shall find the first thread of our tangled skein. Courage, Hastings; the little grey cells are beginning to march in step!”

At the exit of the station, a powerful car was waiting. Poirot gave a brief direction, and we were soon threading our way through the afternoon traffic. I was surprised to find that we were heading towards Hampstead. As we climbed the hill, Poirot turned to me with a small, cryptic smile. “You wonder, Hastings, why we come here? You think it is a waste of time? But I tell you, it is the only way. To understand the end, one must understand the beginning. And the beginning, it is here, at the house of the aunt of Captain Daniels.”

“Now, my friends,” said Poirot, as we stepped into a waiting car, “we have exactly six hours. Let us not waste them. We go first to Hampstead.”
“To see Mrs. Everard?” I asked, surprised.
“Precisely. The aunt of the Captain Daniels. The official police, they have visited her, yes—but they have seen only what she wished them to see. Me, I wish to see what she seeks to hide. It is an intuition of mine that in that house we shall find the first thread of our skein.”

"Now," said Poirot, as we emerged into the bustling Strand, "we have no time to lose. A taxi, if you please, Major Norman. We go to Hampstead."

"To see the aunt?" I asked, remembering the name Lord Estair had mentioned.

"Exactly. Mrs. Everard. I have a great desire to make the acquaintance of that lady. It is possible she may be able to tell us something of her nephew's habits—and perhaps of his friends."

"But the Prime Minister!" I protested. "Every moment we spend here, he is in greater danger over there!"

"Calm yourself, Hastings. The 'over there' and the 'here' are more closely related than you imagine. In this affair, the distance is a mere bagatelle."

Owing to the special passes held by Norman, we got through
everywhere in record time. In London, a large police car was
waiting for us, with some plain-clothes men, one of whom handed a
typewritten sheet of paper to my friend. He answered my inquiring
glance.

“A list of the cottage hospitals within a certain radius west of
London. I wired for it from Dover.”

We pulled up at a small, neat building standing back from the road. A brass plate informed us that this was the “Ascot Cottage Hospital.” Poirot hopped out of the car with the agility of a grasshopper and was up the steps in a moment. I followed him, my mind a whirl of conjectures. What did he expect to find here? The Prime Minister had only stayed a few minutes to have his wound dressed. Surely there could be no clue of importance after all these hours?

The car slowed as we approached the leafy outskirts of Ascot. Suddenly, Poirot called upon the driver to halt in front of a small, unpretentious building—the Ascot Cottage Hospital. Without a word of explanation, my friend skipped from the car and disappeared through the swing doors. Major Norman sighed heavily and checked his watch. “I fail to see, Hastings, how visiting a hospital where a scratch was dressed yesterday can lead us to the Prime Minister in France to-day.” I shook my head, equally mystified, but within five minutes Poirot was back, his face a study in suppressed excitement. “To the villa of Miss Daniels!” he commanded. “It is close by, is it not? _Vite, vite_, for the clock, he does not stop!”

The car slowed as we reached the outskirts of a quiet village. Poirot consulted his list with a small grunt of satisfaction. We drew up before a modest red-brick building—the local cottage hospital. With a sharp “Follow me, my friends,” Poirot sprang from the car, his movements characterized by a sudden, feverish energy. We were conducted immediately to the matron’s office, where Poirot, with his most gallant bow, began his inquiries concerning a certain patient brought in on the previous morning.

We pulled up in front of a small, neat building standing back from the road. A brass plate on the gate informed us that this was the "Ascot and District Cottage Hospital." Poirot hopped out of the car with the agility of a grasshopper and rang the bell. A trim nurse appeared at the door, her face expressive of some surprise at our sudden arrival and the imposing appearance of our motor-car. Poirot, with a flourish of his hat and a stream of polite apologies, requested to see the Matron on a matter of the most urgent national importance.

The car drew up before a small, neat building—the cottage hospital Poirot had inquired about. He sprang out, his eyes alight with a purposeful green fire. We followed him inside, where a starched nurse met us with an air of professional inquiry. Poirot wasted no time. He described the "gentleman" who had come in early the previous morning to have a slight facial wound dressed—a graze from a bullet. He was particularly interested in the bandage. Was it a large one? Did it cover much of the face? The nurse confirmed that indeed, the dressing had been somewhat extensive to ensure protection, effectively masking much of the patient's jaw and cheek.

We duly stopped at the gate of a trim villa. Poirot jumped out and
rang the bell. I saw a perplexed frown dimming the radiance of his
face. Plainly, he was not satisfied. The bell was answered. He was
ushered inside. In a few moments he reappeared, and climbed into
the car with a short, sharp shake of his head. My hopes began to
die down. It was past four now. Even if he found certain evidence
incriminating Daniels, what would be the good of it, unless he
could wring from some one the exact spot in France where they were
holding the Prime Minister?

We reached the bridge, and there, as Norman had predicted, a second car was waiting. Two men in plain clothes stepped out and reported to Poirot in low tones. My friend’s eyes flashed with a sudden, green fire. He gave a sharp order, and our car, followed by the other, crept cautiously along a narrow lane. At last, we halted before a small, isolated house, half-hidden by a screen of trees. Poirot stepped out, his face set in lines of grim determination.

We reached the bridge, where a second car was waiting in the gathering dusk. Two men stepped forward, and a brief, whispered consultation took place between them and Major Norman. Poirot nodded as if satisfied, his eyes gleaming with a strange light in the shadows. We were soon speeding back towards London, but not towards the heart of the city; instead, our course was directed towards the heights of Hampstead. I realized then that we were heading for the residence of Mrs. Everard, the aunt of Captain Daniels. My heart hammered against my ribs—could the solution really be so close at hand, and had the Prime Minister never crossed the Channel at all?

We turned off the main road, and a few minutes later we reached the bridge. Two other cars were drawn up there in the shadows. A man in plain clothes stepped out and exchanged a few words with Major Norman. Poirot nodded with satisfaction. “Everything is in readiness? Good. We must not lose a second. The time is short, but if we move with the precision—the clockwork precision—we shall yet arrive.” He turned to the driver. “To Hampstead, my friend! To the house of Mrs. Everard!”

Our return journey was accomplished in record time. As we entered the quiet, tree-lined streets of Hampstead, the car slowed. Near a small stone bridge, we encountered the men Norman had mentioned. They were plain-clothes detectives, and their leader stepped forward to report that the house in question had been under constant surveillance since the receipt of the telegram from Dover. Poirot’s eyes shone with a cold, green light. “Excellent,” he murmured. “The net is drawn. Now, let us see what fish we have caught.”

We sped along a narrow lane, the car's headlights beginning to flicker in the gathering dusk. At a signal from Major Norman, the chauffeur slowed down. We were approaching a small, ivy-covered house that stood in a somewhat isolated position. It was a villa of the type one sees around Ascot, well-screened by high hedges of laurel. As we drew closer, I noticed a second car waiting in the shadows of a side turning. Poirot’s eyes were like green lamps as he peered through the window. "It is here," he whispered. "The house of the aunt—the Mrs. Everard of whom Lord Estair spoke. Now we shall see if the intuition of Hercule Poirot is as formidable as the German espionage."

We turned up a side road, and in the failing light I discerned a
second car, waiting by the side of the road. It contained two men
in plain clothes. Poirot got down and spoke to them, and then we
started off in a northerly direction, the other car following close
behind.

Norman and I waited in the car, our pulses racing. The quietude of the street seemed a mockery of the frantic search we knew must be taking place within those walls. It was perhaps five minutes later that the door opened again and Poirot beckoned us with an imperious gesture. We hurried up the steps and into the hall. The tall woman, whom I took to be Mrs. Everard, was standing by the mahogany table, her face pale but her eyes blazing with an unquenchable fire. She said nothing, but watched us with a look of cold calculation that made my blood run cold. Poirot, however, was in a state of suppressed exaltation, his chest heaving with excitement as he pointed toward the staircase.

The search of the villa was conducted with a swiftness that spoke of long practice. While the detectives ransacked the upper rooms, the woman—whom I rightly took to be Mrs. Everard—alternated between shrill protests and a stony, defiant silence. Poirot, however, seemed to have lost interest in the mistress of the house. He stood in the hall, his eyes fixed upon a heavy door that led, apparently, to the basement. At a signal from him, two of the men joined him, and the door was forced. We descended the stairs into a well-lit, comfortably furnished suite of rooms that had been carved out of the original cellars. And there, sitting at a table with a tray of tea before him, sat the Prime Minister!

Norman and I waited in a fever of impatience. What was happening inside? Was this another false scent? I looked at my watch. It was nearly six o’clock. In three hours the Conference was due to begin. At that moment, the door opened and Poirot reappeared. His face was radiant. He beckoned to us, and we hurried up the steps. In the hall, the tall woman sat in a chair, her face a mask of fury, while a detective stood over her. Poirot led the way upstairs to a room on the second floor. There, lying on a bed, his face pale and his head swathed in bandages, but undoubtedly himself, was the Prime Minister of England.

The house was in an uproar. The woman, who we now knew to be Mrs. Everard, the aunt of Captain Daniels, stood in the hall, her face a mask of fury. “What is the meaning of this?” she demanded. “How dare you force your way into my house?” Poirot stepped forward, his eyes shining with a green light. “It is simple, Madame. We seek the guest you have been so carefully guarding. Or perhaps I should address you by your more famous name—Frau Bertha Ebenthal?” The woman’s face went deadly pale, and for a moment I thought she would collapse, but she recovered herself with a supreme effort of will.

Inside the house, the air was thick with the scent of old dust and something sharper—the sickly sweet smell of chloroform. Mrs. Everard stood in the hall, her face a mask of frozen defiance, but she fell back as the detectives surged past her. Poirot, led by some unerring instinct, bypassed the drawing-room and headed straight for a small door concealed behind a heavy velvet portière. With a sharp command, the door was forced open. There, in a small, windowless room, sat the Prime Minister, looking remarkably like his own photograph, though strangely dazed and silent. Beside him, his face pale and his eyes shifting like a trapped animal’s, was Captain Daniels. Poirot stepped forward, a smile of immense satisfaction playing on his lips, and made a low, mocking bow. “The journey to Versailles, it is not yet cancelled, messieurs!”

Norman and I spent about five minutes cursing our forced inactivity.
Finally the door reopened, and the men emerged, escorting three
prisoners—a woman and two men. The woman, and one of the men, were
taken to the second car. The other man was placed in our car by
Poirot himself.

“I must go with the others, my friend. But have great care of this
gentleman. You do not know him, no? _Eh bien_, let me present to
you, Monsieur O’Murphy!”

The car raced through the gathering dusk, and I watched the street lamps beginning to flicker into life. Beside me, O’Murphy remained motionless, his eyes fixed on some point in space. I was burning to ask a thousand questions—where was the Prime Minister? Who were the other prisoners? What had Poirot discovered in those cottage hospitals? But the presence of Major Norman, and the grim silence of our captive, acted as a check upon my tongue. We were heading, I realized, toward the heart of the government—Downing Street itself. The gravity of the situation pressed upon me; it was now nearly seven o'clock, and in two hours the Conference at Versailles would commence, with or without the man who held the destiny of Europe in his hands.

I gazed with a feeling of deep repugnance at the man’s sullen face. This, then, was the trusted C.I.D. officer, the chauffeur who had supposedly vanished into the murky depths of Soho. What part had he played in this international drama? He remained obstinately silent, despite my attempts to draw him into conversation, staring straight ahead with a look of dazed bewilderment. Major Norman, too, seemed gripped by a tense excitement, his eyes constantly seeking the clock on the dashboard. We were tearing through the streets at a breakneck speed, for the hands of the clock were moving with a sinister rapidity. It was now half-past seven. In an hour and a half, the Conference was due to begin at Versailles, and we were still in London with nothing but a captured traitor in our custody.

We drove in silence. I looked at the man beside me—the man who had held the life of the Prime Minister in his hands and had, apparently, betrayed his trust. He seemed dazed, his eyes fixed on some point in space. My mind whirled with a thousand questions. If O’Murphy was here, in a house in North London, then who was it that had been kidnapped in France? And where, in the name of all that was wonderful, was the Prime Minister himself? My eyes sought the clock on the dashboard. It was nearly half-past six. In less than three hours, the Conference was to meet at Versailles, and we were still in the heart of England with a captive traitor and a missing leader. Our car swung into the well-lit streets of the West End and finally drew up before a large, somber house.

“To Downing Street!” cried Norman to the chauffeur.
We tore through the streets of London at a breakneck speed. O’Murphy remained obstinately silent, staring straight ahead with an expression of grim apathy. I watched him closely, my mind racing. Was this the man who had betrayed the England that trusted him? And what of the others? The woman, presumably the Mrs. Everard mentioned by Lord Estair, and the second man, whose identity I could only guess at. My thoughts flew to the Prime Minister—was he still alive, or had we come too late?

We whirled through the darkened streets, finally coming to a halt in front of a small, unpretentious house in a quiet suburb. Poirot’s car was already there. He was waiting on the pavement, and he motioned us to follow him, while O’Murphy was brought along behind us by the two detectives. We entered the house, which seemed strangely silent, and Poirot led the way upstairs. At the door of a room on the first floor, he paused and turned to us, a look of immense gravity upon his face.

To my surprise, we still kept a northerly route. We were not
returning to London, then! I was much puzzled. Suddenly, as the
car slowed down, I recognized that we were close to Hendon
Aerodrome. Immediately I grasped Poirot’s idea. He proposed to
reach France by aeroplane.

It was a sporting idea, but, on the face of it, impracticable. A
telegram would be far quicker. Time was everything. He must leave
the personal glory of rescuing the Prime Minister to others.

As we drew up, Major Norman jumped out, and a plain-clothes man
took his place. He conferred with Poirot for a few minutes, and
then went off briskly.

I, too, jumped out, and caught Poirot by the arm.

“I congratulate you, old fellow! They have told you the hiding-place?
But, look here, you must wire to France at once. You’ll be too late
if you go yourself.”

Poirot looked at me curiously for a minute or two.

“Unfortunately, my friend, there are some things that cannot be
sent by telegram.”


  •   •   •   •   •   •   •


At that moment Major Norman returned, accompanied by a young
officer in the uniform of the Flying Corps.

“This is Captain Lyall, who will fly you over to France. He can
start at once.”

“Wrap up warmly, sir,” said the young pilot. “I can lend you a
coat, if you like.”

He indicated the passenger we had brought with us from the house in Hampstead. In the glare of the aerodrome lamps, I saw the man’s face clearly for the first time. I gasped. It was the Prime Minister! The bandages from the “shooting” were gone, and though he looked haggard and grey, it was unmistakably “Fighting Mac” himself. He stepped toward the waiting aeroplane, then turned and caught Poirot’s hand in both of his. Not a word was spoken, but the look of gratitude in his eyes was enough. A moment later, the pilot started his engine, and the little craft took to the air, bearing away the man on whom the hopes of England rested.

He indicated the man he had called O’Murphy. The latter, still seemingly in a state of collapse, was helped into the aeroplane by the two detectives. He was muffled in a greatcoat, and his face was almost entirely hidden by a thick bandage. As the engine started its rhythmic throb and the plane began to taxi away into the night, Poirot turned to me with a look of immense satisfaction. “You are still in the dark, Hastings? You do not see that the man who has just departed is the only man who can save the situation—the real Prime Minister of England!”

He indicated the man we had just brought from the villa in Hampstead. As the light of the aerodrome lamps fell upon his face, I uttered a cry of astonishment. It was not O’Murphy at all! The face was older, more weary, but there was no mistaking those famous features. It was the Prime Minister himself!

“But—but,” I stammered, “the man who went to France—who was kidnapped there——?”

“An impostor, Hastings! A double! The Prime Minister has been here, in London, all the time. Now, Captain Lyall, I beg of you—lose not a second! The destiny of Europe is in your hands!”

He pointed to the silent man in our car. I looked at the man again, more closely this time. His face was pale and drawn, and he seemed to be recovering from the effects of a powerful drug. Poirot reached out and, with a deft flick of his fingers, removed a false mustache and a pair of heavy, obscuring eyebrows. I let out a cry of sheer amazement. The man sitting before us was not the Irish chauffeur O’Murphy at all; it was the Prime Minister, Mr. David MacAdam himself!

He indicated the man we had brought from the house in Hampstead. The latter, who had hitherto seemed dazed and shrinking, stepped forward. He took off his hat, and the light of a nearby lamp fell full upon his face. Major Norman fell back with a cry of astonishment. It was the Prime Minister!

He moved a little aside as he spoke, and a figure came forward out
of the darkness. It was the second male prisoner who had gone in
the other car, and as the light fell on his face, I gave a gasp of
surprise.

_It was the Prime Minister!_


  •   •   •   •   •   •   •


“For Heaven’s sake, tell me all about it,” I cried impatiently, as
Poirot, Norman, and I motored back to London. “How in the world
did they manage to smuggle him back to England?”

“There was no need to smuggle him back,” replied Poirot dryly. “The
Prime Minister has never left England. He was kidnapped on his way
from Windsor to London.”

“What?”

“I will make all clear. The Prime Minister was in his car, his
secretary beside him. Suddenly a pad of chloroform is clapped on
his face——”

“But by whom?”

“_Pas du tout!_ Have you not seen the celebrities of the Cinema
screen being ‘made up’? This was a masterly piece of work. The
substitute for the Prime Minister was perfect. His cheek was
bandaged—to serve the double purpose of hiding part of his face,
and of accounting for any slight change in his voice. O’Murphy’s
substitute was just as clever. Their task was easy. They had only
to drive to Charing Cross, and board the waiting train. Captain
Daniels accompanied them. But he, too, had to be replaced by a
substitute. The man who was found gagged and bound in the farm in
France was not the real Captain Daniels. He was a confederate.”

“And the original car?”

“The original car was driven to Soho, by another confederate, and
left there. The real O’Murphy was taken to the house of Daniels’
aunt, Mrs. Everard, at Hampstead. The Prime Minister was taken to
the house of his other aunt, Frau Bertha Ebenthal, who is a very
dangerous German agent, and who, under the name of Miss Daniels,
has lived at Ascot for years.”

“And the shot fired at the car?”

“Was simply a little bit of ‘eye-wash’ to make the story of the
kidnapping more plausible. It was never intended to hit anyone.
It was a master-stroke of the imagination on the part of the
organizers.”

“But how did you suspect?”

“_Pas du tout!_ Have you not seen the music-hall artistes do their
‘lightning changes’? A few deft touches, and the thing is done.
The part of the Prime Minister is played by a man who has made a
study of his face and manner—he may even be a professional actor.
He is already well padded and dressed in the same clothes. In a few
minutes, his face is also skilfully made up. He wears a bandage
round his face—that is a stroke of genius, for it serves the double
purpose of concealing his features and accounting for any lack of
familiarity in his voice. The other man is an exact double of
O’Murphy. He, of course, is the one who drives to the restaurant
in Soho, and there disappears, to resume his own personality. Now,
you see the reason for the attempted assassination. It was to
account for the bandage!”

“But the car that followed?”

“The substitutes’ car was already waiting at the turn of the road.
The car containing the detectives followed the _wrong car_. The
Prime Minister’s own car, with the real O’Murphy and the real Prime
Minister, was driven to the house of Daniels’ aunt at Hampstead—Mrs.
Everard.”

“And what of Daniels?”

“_Pas du tout!_ Have you not seen the ‘celebrity’ at a music-hall?
With a wig, a touch of the pencil, a grey suit, and a slightly
limping gait, the substitute for the Prime Minister was perfect.
As for O’Murphy’s double, no one would look at him. The police
car, following, sees the Prime Minister’s car turn the corner. It
follows. It sees the car stopped and a man approaching. It
naturally slows up. Then the Prime Minister’s car speeds away, and
the police car follows. It never doubts that the occupants are the
same. Then comes the ‘attempt’ on the life of the Prime Minister.
He is slightly wounded in the cheek. He stops at a cottage hospital.
Why? To set the seal of authenticity on the hoax. A small affair of
a bullet wound—the Prime Minister’s identity is not revealed—but
it gets into the papers. The police believe in the shooting affair,
and so they are more than ever certain that the person they are
escorting is the Prime Minister. He is conveyed to Dover, goes on
board the destroyer, and is met at Boulogne by another substitute
A.D.C., and a bogus car. He is driven away—and disappears.
And all the time the real Prime Minister is in London, in the
house of Captain Daniels’ ‘aunt’—who is, I suspect, no less a
person than the Frau Bertha Ebenthal herself.”

“Good heavens, Poirot!” I cried. “And you found this out by—?”

“By the fact that the shooting took place _before_ the abduction.
If the Prime Minister was to be kidnapped, why try to shoot him
first? It was not logical. Therefore, the ‘shooting’ must be part
of the kidnapping. But if the Prime Minister is shot at and wounded,
he will be more closely guarded than ever. That is not logical
either. But if the ‘shooting’ is to provide a reason for the Prime
Minister’s face being swathed in bandages, so as to disguise a
substitute—ah, then it is very logical indeed!”

“But how did you know where he was?”

“I searched the lists of cottage hospitals. I knew the area. I
found one where a gentleman had had a bullet wound in the cheek
dressed that morning. The description of the car didn’t match—but
I knew that they would use a different car. Then I looked for a
house nearby that might serve as a prison. The rest was easy.”

“And O’Murphy?”

“He was also in the house. Chloroformed and kept under until they
could decide what to do with him. Daniels is the man we want—but
I fear he has escaped us. He was the one who played the part of
the Prime Minister from London to Boulogne, then slipped away and
came back to London to help Frau Ebenthal. He is a very clever man,
that Captain Daniels!”

“What about the restaurant in Soho?”

“A plant, to throw us on the track of O’Murphy. The car was left
there—but it was never O’Murphy who drove it.”

“And the Prime Minister will be in time for the Conference?”

Poirot looked at his watch.

“He will be at Versailles by nine o’clock to-morrow night—in time
to win for England a Peace with Honour!”

“_Pas du tout!_ Have you not seen the celebrities of the Cinema
made up to resemble well-known public characters? With a few deft
touches, the substitute Chauffeur is made to look like O’Murphy,
and the substitute Prime Minister like Mr. MacAdam. The band of
masked men whose presence I found so unbelievable is easily
explained. They were there to give the substitutes a chance to
take their places. The shot is fired at the substitute Prime
Minister, to account for his bandaged face. The bandage then
serves the double purpose of hiding any slight lack of resemblance,
and of providing an excuse for the ‘Prime Minister’ to remain
silent and not speak to anyone. He is hurried off to France. In
the meantime, the real Prime Minister is taken to the house of
Daniels’ aunt at Hampstead.”

“Mrs. Everard?”

“Exactly. It was a clever idea. But Poirot is cleverer! I suspected
Daniels from the first. Why? Because he was the only person who
could have chloroformed the Prime Minister. Then I find that he
has an aunt at Hampstead and another at Ascot. I call at the villa
at Ascot. I find that no one of the name of Daniels has ever lived
there. _Très bien_! The aunt at Ascot is a ‘myth.’ But the aunt at
Hampstead is real. I go to the cottage hospitals between Windsor
and London, and I find a small car was seen to turn into a side
road on that morning. Finally, I visit the house in Hampstead,
and there I find the Prime Minister!”

“And the man in the car at Soho?”

“O’Murphy. They were not sure of him, you see. He had to be got out
of the way. He was chloroformed and taken to Soho, and the car
abandoned there to start a false scent. But they did not dare to
kill him. After all, he is a Scotland Yard man!”

“And the other man?”

“Frau Bertha Ebenthal herself. She was the ‘aunt’ in the Hampstead
house. A very dangerous woman, who has been at the bottom of many
a plot against England.”

“And the substitute Prime Minister?”

“He was a Mr. Bernard—a music-hall artist who has a marvellous
knack of mimicry. He, too, was a victim of the Ebenthal. He was
told it was a huge practical joke.”

“But the Conference?” I asked. “What happened there?”

Poirot smiled. “The Prime Minister arrived at Versailles at five
minutes to nine—just in time!”

“It was a near thing,” I said, with a sigh of relief.

“It was,” agreed Poirot. “But the little grey cells, they did not
fail me!”

“_Pas du tout!_ Have you not seen the music-hall artistes do their
‘quick-change’ acts? This was the same thing. The two substitutes,
carefully chosen for their great personal resemblance to the
Premier and O’Murphy, and acting their parts to perfection, drive
on to London. They stopped at the cottage hospital (the substitute
Premier had his face appropriately bandaged!) and then on to
Charing Cross and France. At Boulogne, the fake car was waiting
for them. The substitute Prime Minister is ‘abducted,’ and the
substitute chauffeur disappears. He and the fake A.D.C. meet at
the rendezvous in Soho. No doubt he has a different suit of clothes
under his chauffeur’s livery, and a few minutes later a very
different-looking man emerges from the restaurant in Soho. The
kidnapping of the Prime Minister is a _fait accompli_! No one
doubts but that it has taken place in France.”

“And the real Prime Minister?”

“He and O’Murphy were taken straight to the house of Daniels’ aunt,
Mrs. Everard, at Hampstead. But there was another accomplice. The
woman Bertha Ebenthal, of whom we have long been in search, was
at the head of the gang. It was she who posed as the aunt of
Daniels.”

“How did you find out?”

“I ask myself: what would be the best way to kidnap the Prime
Minister? And at once I see that the best way is to have him never
leave England at all. Then I look for the weak point in the case.
The shooting! Why the shooting? To give the ‘Prime Minister’ a
reason for having his face bandaged. At once I am on the track.
I find that a man, bandaged, has indeed been to a cottage hospital.
I say to myself: ‘If the man in the car was the real Prime
Minister, why should he be bandaged? He had only a tiny scratch.’
So I conclude that he was _not_ the Prime Minister. I visit all the
cottage hospitals. I find the one where the Prime Minister was
alleged to have gone. I see the surgeon who attended him. He
describes the patient. The man he describes is not the Prime
Minister. I have enough to go upon. I think of the aunts of Daniels.
I visit the one at Ascot. She is a charming old lady—quite
innocent. I go to the other, and—_voilà_!”

“But how did you know they had not killed him?”

“Because he is too valuable. If they kill him, they have nothing
to bargain with. As it is, they have a trump card.”

“And O’Murphy?”

“He was also at Hampstead. He had been heavily drugged, but was
unharmed. He will have a strange story to tell.”

“And the Conference?”

“It is now a quarter to nine. In a quarter of an hour the Conference
will open at Versailles. I think—yes, I think—that ‘Fighting Mac’
will be there!”

Poirot had been right. It was a close shave, but he was there. The
catastrophe was averted.

I may add that, while the other members of the gang were captured,
the woman Bertha Ebenthal managed to elude the police. But I have
a firm look-out for her. She is a dangerous woman. Some day,
perhaps, Poirot and she will meet again. Who knows?

Anyway, for the moment, my little friend was the hero of the hour.
And rightfully so. For without him—who knows?

“_Pas du tout!_ Have you not seen music-hall turns imitating
celebrities with marvellous accuracy? Nothing is easier than to
personate a public character. The Prime Minister of England is far
easier to understudy than Mr. John Smith of Clapham, say. As for
O’Murphy’s ‘double,’ no one was going to take much notice of him
until after the departure of the Prime Minister, and by then he
would have made himself scarce. He drives straight from Charing
Cross to the meeting-place of his friends. He goes in as O’Murphy,
he emerges as some one quite different. O’Murphy has disappeared,
leaving a conveniently suspicious trail behind him.”

“But the man who personated the Prime Minister was seen by every
one!”

“He ‘disappears’ also. As a matter of fact, he and the chauffeur
only had to take off their make-up. Now, as to the Prime Minister,
he was taken to the house of Daniels’ aunt, Mrs. Everard, at
Hampstead. Daniels had a sister, Miss Daniels, who lived near
Ascot, and who was in the plot. It was she who had the care of him
during the first few hours. But the real mastermind behind this
entire conspiracy was a woman known in the highest espionage
circles as Frau Bertha Ebenthal. It was she who directed the
operation from that very house in Hampstead, and it was she who
would have held the Prime Minister as a pawn for the German cause
had we not arrived when we did.”

“And how did you find the house?”

“I asked myself, what would be the best place to hide a famous
man? A place that was above suspicion. I had the list of cottage
hospitals to which the substitute Prime Minister had been taken.
(I knew it was a substitute because, as I told you, the shooting
affair was so unreal!) I found that one hospital was particularly
favoured. I also found that a certain woman, a Mrs. Everard, had
been very active in the neighbourhood. I took a little stroll in
Hampstead, and I saw a house that was very suitable. Then, I saw
a lady come out of it. She was not like the photographs of Mrs.
Everard. But I have a good memory for faces, and I recognized
her. It was the Fraülein Bertha Ebenthal. After that, the rest was
simple.”

“And O’Murphy?”

“He was also in the house, under guard. They had need of him—for
the same reason that they had need of the Prime Minister. If
their little plot had succeeded, O’Murphy would have been
conveniently ‘found’ later, with a well-concocted story of how
he had been kidnapped and escaped.”

Poirot puffed out his chest.

“And so, the Conference will be held—and the Prime Minister will
be there!”

“How did you know he had not been kidnapped in France?” I asked,
with some curiosity.

“Because he could not have been! If he had been kidnapped in
France, the kidnappers would not have been so long in making their
presence felt. To kidnap a man in a country which is under Military
Law is not an easy affair. No, the abduction must have taken
place in England.”

I looked at my friend. “You are a wonderful man, Poirot!” I
ejaculated.

“I am also a very cold one!” he replied, with a shiver. “And a
very hungry one! Hasten, I pray of you, to the restaurant. My
stomach, she is not yet at ease.”

But Poirot had once more saved England.

“He ‘disappears’ also. Daniels must, of course, have some help.
His aunt’s house was at Ascot, near the scene of the first attempt.
He is a clever man, this Daniels! But Hercule Poirot is cleverer!”

“How did you manage to track them down?”

“I asked myself, as I told you, why they should try to shoot him?
And at once I saw that it was a very clever bit of ‘camouflage.’
If the Prime Minister is shot at, and wounded, it at once gets rid
of the difficulty of his being recognized—for his face will be
bandaged. It also accounts for his being slightly different in
manner. Then I began to compare the two disappearances. The Prime
Minister—disappears in France; O’Murphy—disappears in London. Of
the two, which is the most likely to have taken place? The Prime
Minister’s, because it is more important. But, if the Prime
Minister had not been kidnapped in France, but in England, then the
disappearance of O’Murphy becomes significant. I had a list of the
cottage hospitals. I stopped at the one where the Prime Minister’s
face was dressed. They described the car to me. It was not the same
car as the one that arrived at Charing Cross! Then I knew! I
searched for the house that Daniels had taken, and which he had
cleverly described as his aunt’s. As for the ‘Mrs. Everard’ at
Hampstead, she was another German agent, no doubt. The rest was
easy.”

“And the man you arrested at the house?” I asked. “Was he the one
who had played the part of the Prime Minister?”

“No,” said Poirot, his eyes narrowing. “That individual had already
slipped away. The man we took was indeed the true O’Murphy, held
captive in that cellar. But as for the master of the house, the
true soul of the plot—that was none other than the woman I had
named to you: Frau Bertha Ebenthal.”

“He is a minor actor, named O’Farrell. He has had a certain amount
of success on the stage, but has been in low water for some time.
It was a clever idea. He was chosen, of course, for his power of
mimicry and his general resemblance to the Prime Minister. He
played his part well. It was only one little thing that betrayed
him.”

“What was that?”

“He used a different kind of disinfectant on his wound.”

“Disinfectant?”

“Yes. You remember my mentioning that the ‘Prime Minister’ stopped
at a cottage hospital? I visited all the cottage hospitals between
Windsor and London. At one of them, they remembered the case. The
doctor had dressed the wound, and, at the patient’s request, had
used a certain strongly-scented disinfectant. Now, the Prime
Minister, as I happen to know, has a great particularity in these
matters, and he never uses anything but a certain very mild
solution of a different kind. That first put me on the right track.
I knew then that the man who had been at the cottage hospital was
not the Prime Minister. After that, it was a matter of finding
where the real man was likely to be. I thought of the aunt of
Captain Daniels. We went there. I was not satisfied. I looked
elsewhere. I remembered the name of Mrs. Everard, the other aunt
at Hampstead. We went there—and we were successful.”

“Who was the woman?”

“Frau Bertha Ebenthal herself. A very dangerous woman. It was she
who was directing the whole affair. The house was, of course, the
headquarters of the German spy system in this country. It was
Daniels who had told O’Murphy to turn off the main road, and it
was Daniels who had drugged the Prime Minister. He is a clever
scoundrel.”

“And O’Murphy?”

“He was also at the house at Hampstead, but they had not been able
to make him speak. He is a brave man, that O’Murphy.”

“And the Conference?”

“The Prime Minister will be there. Captain Lyall will see to that.”

Poirot smiled.

“He is a great man, the Prime Minister, but it is a good thing he
has the small Hercule Poirot to look after him.”

“But how did you know it was O’Farrell?” I asked, still a little
bewildered.

“I did not know. But I knew that there must be an actor in the case.
And when I saw the name of O’Farrell in a list of ‘out-of-work’
actors who had been recently making inquiries at the Board of Trade
for work, I began to have my little ideas. Then, of course, his
personal appearance was easily verified.”

“It’s been a wonderful piece of work, Poirot,” I said admiringly.
“You’ve saved the situation.”

“I have used my little grey cells,” said Poirot, complacently. “And
now, my friend, let us go to dinner. I feel that I have earned a
most excellent meal.”

“He too ‘disappears.’ A boat is waiting for him. He steps into it,
rolls off his bandages, and emerges as—well, let us say, Frau
Bertha Ebenthal! It was a masterpiece of audacity. The substitute
Prime Minister, having played his part, simply vanishes into the
night, while the real David MacAdam lay all the while in the house
at Hampstead, guarded by the very woman whose name has been the
terror of the Secret Service for years.”

“And how did you find him?”

“I asked myself, as I told you, why the first attack was made?
From the first, I was suspicious of it. What was its object? To
delay? That could be done better by the abduction. To kill? No,
for they would have made sure of their work. There could be only
one reason—to provide a reason for the Prime Minister’s face being
bandaged! When I had arrived at that, the rest was simple. I
imagined a double, and I sought for a place where the Prime
Minister could have been changed. I found the cottage hospital.
The rest was a matter of simple deduction.”

“And O’Murphy?”

“He was also at the house at Hampstead. He had been drugged and
kept under, for they could not afford to let him go until their
plans were completed.”

“But how did you find the house?”

“By the list of cottage hospitals. I knew it must be within a
certain distance of one of them. I had also a list of the various
houses which had been rented by suspicious characters. Amongst
them was one rented by a Mrs. Everard. I took the risk. I was right.”

“And Captain Daniels?”

“He has not yet been caught. But we shall have him. He is a clever
man.”

“Well, Poirot,” I said, “you have certainly done it this time! You
must have the most extraordinary brain.”

“I? Not at all. It is only the little grey cells—the little grey
cells!”

“He ‘disappears’ also. Daniels must, of course, have some help.
His aunt’s house was used as a place of detention for the Prime
Minister. I suspected Daniels from the first. Why? Because he was
found gagged and bound in such a way as to suggest he was a victim,
yet his presence was essential to the success of the substitution.
And then there was the business of the bandages. If the Prime
Minister were truly wounded, why was there no record of him at any
nearby hospital? I visited the cottage hospitals, and at one I
found a lead. A man had been treated there, yes, but for a common
scratch, and his description did not match the Prime Minister,
save for the clothes. It was then I knew the shooting was a sham,
meant only to provide a reason for the bandages that would hide a
double's face.”

"But who was the double, Poirot?" I asked, leaning forward.

"A very clever actor, no doubt," Poirot mused, "but the brains
behind the operation—the one who organized the capture and the
imprisonment—that is what matters. To find the Prime Minister, I
had to find where Daniels would feel safest. He spoke of two aunts.
I visited the one in Ascot; she was a frail, innocent lady. But
the other, the Mrs. Everard of Hampstead..."

"Was she the culprit?" I exclaimed.

"She was the gaoler," Poirot corrected. "But the mistress of the
plot, the woman who has pulled the strings of German espionage in
this country for years, was none other than the lady I found
presiding over that house—the so-called Mrs. Everard, who is in
reality the notorious Frau Bertha Ebenthal."

“Rids himself of his disguise. He and the bogus chauffeur may be
arrested as suspicious characters, but no one will dream of
suspecting their real part in the drama, and they will eventually
be released for lack of evidence.”

“And the real Prime Minister?”

“At the very beginning, Hastings. The shooting affair—it was too theatrical, too much like a cinema film. Why shoot at a man you are about to kidnap? And then, the hospital. I visited every cottage hospital along that road. In none of them had a patient been treated for a graze on the cheek that morning. What did that mean? It meant that the shooting was a fake—a necessary ruse to permit the Prime Minister to have his face wrapped in bandages. Once he was bandaged, the substitution was easy. I knew then that the man who went to France was a double, and that the real Mr. MacAdam must still be in England. From there, it was but a matter of following the associations of Captain Daniels.”

“It was the first attack that was the key. Why shoot at the Prime Minister if you have a well-organized plan to kidnap him? It was not logical! And then, the nature of the wound—a graze on the cheek. So convenient, was it not? It necessitated the bandages, and the bandages were the soul of the substitution. They hidden the face of the double. Then I asked myself, who told the chauffeur to turn into that lane? Daniels. Who had an aunt living in the vicinity? Daniels. The little grey cells, they said to me: ‘Poirot, this is a comedy of the first water!’ I searched for the Prime Minister, not in France, where all the world was looking, but in England. The visits to the cottage hospitals confirmed my theory; the man who arrived at Charing Cross was already the substitute. After that, it was but a matter of finding where the real Mr. MacAdam was hidden. Frau Ebenthal—the so-called Mrs. Everard—was the obvious jailer, and the villa at Hampstead the most likely prison.”

“At the very beginning! The shooting, it was so dramatic, so—how you say—unreal! And then the bandage. It is a very old trick, that, to hide the face. And I said to myself: why should they try to shoot him in England and then kidnap him in France? It is not logical! And then there was the matter of the hospital. I visited those on the list, and at one of them, I discovered that the man who had been treated for a graze on the cheek was not the Prime Minister at all. From that moment, I knew that the man who crossed the Channel was an actor of great skill, and that the real Mr. MacAdam was still on this side of the water. To find him, I had only to look for the connections of the man who had the best opportunity—Captain Daniels. And so we arrived at the ‘aunt’ in Hampstead—who is in reality the German agent, Frau Bertha Ebenthal.”

“At the beginning, my friend. The shooting affair, it was too like a film of the cinema—not at all as such things happen in life. It was a clever stage-management to allow the ‘Prime Minister’ to be bandaged, and thus make the substitution easier. Once I realized that the man who went to France was an impostor, it was clear that the real Prime Minister must be in England. I visited the cottage hospitals to confirm my theory. At the third one, I discovered that the patient, though he acted the part of a great man, had forgotten that Mr. MacAdam is a teetotaler, and had asked for a nip of brandy! After that, the trail led to the ‘aunts’ of Captain Daniels. Ascot was a blind, but the house in Hampstead, belonging to the so-called ‘Mrs. Everard’—who is, as I suspected, the German agent Frau Bertha Ebenthal—was the true goal. She and Daniels were the masterminds of this most audacious plot.”

“At the very beginning, my friend! The shooting affair was so—how shall I say it?—melodramatic! It was a Cinema effect. If one wishes to kill, one kills. But if one wishes to hide a face, then a bullet that grazes the cheek and necessitates bandages—ah, that is a stroke of genius! It was then I said to myself: why the bandages? And the answer was: to hide the fact that the man who arrives at Charing Cross is not the Prime Minister. Once I had that, the rest was simple method and logic. I asked myself where the real man could be, and the answer was at once: near the place where the substitution took place. I looked for the ‘aunt’ of the clever Captain Daniels—and I found her, though the trail was well covered. The cottage hospitals I visited were those where the bogus Prime Minister had supposedly been treated; they knew nothing of him, which confirmed that the whole story of the wound was a fabrication to justify the bandages.”

“When I began to work the right way—from _within_! I could not make
that shooting affair fit in—but when I saw that the net result of
it was that _the Prime Minister went to France with his face bound
up_ I began to comprehend! And when I visited all the cottage
hospitals between Windsor and London, and found that no one
answering to my description had had his face bound up and dressed
that morning, I was sure! After that, it was child’s-play for a
mind like mine!”

  •   •   •   •   •   •   •

The following morning, Poirot showed me a telegram he had just
received. It had no place of origin, and was unsigned. It ran:

“In time.”
